Election night was a fever dream for Democrats. In January, reality will set in.
They had a reason to be giddy on Tuesday night: Next year, Democrats will take control of both chambers of Congress after a blowout victory.
"Today begins the great American comeback," an ecstatic Hakeem Jeffries, House Democratic leader, declared.
After months of promises on the campaign trail â to investigate corruption; lower the costs of healthcare, groceries and petrol; and curtail the Iran war â they will now begin the much tougher process of putting plans into action.
A shift in the balance of power in Washington doesn't necessarily mean Democrats will immediately get to start checking items off their legislative wish list. Democrats have Congress, but Republican President Donald Trump still has the power to reject legislation.
The Democrats should not consider what just happened "a mandate," US Senator Chris Coons told the BBC, warning that the party was still "deeply unpopular".
"We need to prove we can get stuff done, actually deliver answers to their concerns and questions about low wages and rising costs in particular."
What Democrats may be able to achieve
Congressman Robert Garcia of California will soon lead a powerful oversight committee in the House, with the power to make Trump's last two years in office quite difficult.
"Lawyer up," the Democrat said in a statement as victorious results poured in on election night.
Committees in both the US Senate and House have investigative powers, which they could use to delve into alleged conflicts of interest and other actions by the president and those close to him. On Tuesday, Garcia rattled off a list of possible targets: Trump's family, "corporate corruption", alleged abuses by the Department of Homeland Security and Immigration and Customs Enforcement, and the government's handling of the Epstein files.
The Senate also has the power to confirm or block the president's cabinet and judicial nominations.
Should a US Supreme Court vacancy, for example, arise during Trump's term, Senate Democrats could use their new power to block a nomination - or force Trump to choose a more moderate candidate who garners bipartisan support.
The House also has the power to impeach a president - the first step of Congress' process to remove an official from office.
Democrats twice impeached Trump during his first term, though the US Senate eventually voted to acquit him in both cases. But because it takes a two-thirds majority in the US Senate â or 67 votes â convicting a president in an impeachment case likely will remain out of reach for Democrats.
There's an active debate among Democrats about whether impeachment is a good idea. The first impeachment, in 2019, unleashed partisan rancor and allowed Trump to cast himself later as a victim of political persecution, which later helped build support for his second White House run.
Jeffries, who would almost certainly have to greenlight any Democratic impeachment effort, has kept his plans vague.
"Well, we've made clear: We haven't ruled anything in," he told CNN in August. "And we haven't ruled anything out".
What Democrats may struggle to do
Americans' frustration with Congress' productivity was palpable before the election. Only 14% of US registered voters approved of lawmakers' performance, an October Gallup poll suggested.
But with a Republican in the White House and Democrats running Congress, Americans may face even more deadlock.
"If you thought legislating was hard in the last Congress with unified Republican control, that will get much more complicated," said Casey Burgat, professor of legislative affairs at George Washington University.
Because they will control both chambers with a comfortable majority, Democrats will be able to pass legislation through Congress with relative ease.
Getting it enacted into law will be harder.
A president must sign most legislation in order for it to become law. Trump has the power to reject legislation passed by Congress that he does not support, and Congress can only override him with a supermajority from both chambers - margins Democrats alone will not have despite their success on Tuesday.
As his party lost Senate race after Senate race Tuesday night, Trump struck a conciliatory tone with the New York Times.
"We'll work with the Democrats, and we'll, you know, look forward to working with them. We'll probably work something out," he said.
But a few minutes later, Trump posted a picture on Truth Social of his red campaign hat with the word "VETO" emblazoned across the front. That Jekyll-and-Hyde approach to a Democratic Congress could become a theme.
While opposition to Trump led to Democrats' success, lawmakers acknowledged Tuesday night, it might not be enough.
"It is overwhelmingly a rejection of Donald Trump, and his agenda and policies," Coons told the BBC.
"But if we overreach, or if we fight too much internally, we could miss this moment."
Despite the veto threat, Jeffries has said that his party wants to restore significant cuts Republicans made to healthcare programmes like Medicaid, which is used by low-income groups, and the Obamacare marketplace.
"We're committed as a top priority as House democrats to reversing these Medicaid cuts and extending the Affordable Care Act tax credits," Jeffries said at a September event for healthcare workers.
On typically bipartisan issues â such as policies affecting affordability, regulating the AI industry, re-evaluating military funding for Israel and reining in the Iran War â talks could break down as lawmakers try to compromise. As they become the opposition heading into the 2028 presidential cycle, Republicans might not be in the mood to help Democrats achieve too many wins.

In a nationwide romp, Democrats ousted Republicans from coast to coast, with many surprising places in between, as voters rejected the president's party for the promise of something different for the country. Their majorities will be padded by wide margins in both the House and the Senate. The tally was decisive, at times bewildering, for the staggering scope of Democratic gains and the depth of Republican losses. For Jeffries and his leadership team, it will be their first time in the majority, managing a class of newcomers including a handful of far-left democratic socialists. With the majority in the 435-member House well past the 218 needed and the Senate Democrats holding at least 54 of 100 seats in that chamber, Jeffries and Senate Democratic Leader Chuck Schumer will have room to maneuver. "Five words for the American people: Relief is on the way," the New York senator said. A lame-duck session and leadership elections await Republicans For Republicans, their shriveled numbers will create a reckoning of their own, as they try to figure out what went so uniformly wrong. And the government could be headed toward a federal shutdown next month if Congress fails to pass a funding bill to keep operations running. In the weeks ahead, the parties will hold internal leadership elections as members-elect arrive for freshman orientation at the Capitol. The House will choose its speaker as one of the first votes when the new Congress convenes. Kansas woke up on Wednesday to sunny skies and historic new leadership after days of rain, hail and tornado warnings - amid a tempestuous election battle that ultimately swept a new brand of blue politics into the deep-red state.
Democrat and church pastor Adam Hamilton claimed victory Tuesday night over Republican incumbent and staunch Trump supporter Senator Roger Marshall, marking the first time a Democrat won the seat since 1932.
The 62-year-old leader of the US's largest United Methodist congregation - with 24,000 congregants - had promised voters civility, moderate policy stances and and open ear to their concerns. He'd invoked the state's most famous cultural touchstone, the Wizard of Oz, on the campaign trail, telling Kansans: "What we need in Washington right now is we need senators with a brain who use it, with a heart who feel with it, and who have courage and speak up because of it."
When the race was called in Hamilton's favour, voters all over Kansas - from lifelong Republicans in tiny unincorporated communities to dyed-in-the-wool liberals who'd felt disenfranchised for decades - erupted in cheers and sighs of relief.
In Wichita, a manufacturing city in the heart of the state, around 100 attendees celebrated as TV pundits onscreen spoke of a "blue tsunami" - cheering as Democrats swept not just Kansas seats but also races across the nation.
"I have lived in Kansas for 30-something years, and I have felt all of those years like I voted and my vote was never counted," said Laura Elliott, 71, sitting at a high-top table with three others.
"We did it!" shouted Chuck Schmidt, 76, hugging a younger voter as he credited upcoming generations with the party's success.
"People are fed up with the chaos and the corruption," Schmidt, a former state representative, told BBC. "People in Kansas, for some reason, have gotten conditioned to just vote for the R - and they haven't realised there was another alternative."
Faith has long been a deciding factor for many Kansas voters. A 2025 report from the Pew Research Center ranked the state as the 10th most religious in the US, with 70% of Kansans identifying as Christian and nearly 30% as evangelical Protestants - a group that has overwhelmingly backed Trump and the Republican Party in recent years.
In Great Bend, Marshall's hometown, Navy veteran Richard Elmore listed abortion, transgender issues, illegal immigration and "the gay rights issue" as some of the reasons he backed the Republican candidate.
"Anybody that'd say they were a Christian and not honour those things are lying to themselves and others," said the 77-year-old grandfather, who believes an angel is protecting Trump, otherwise "he'd be dead".
The Marshall campaign had painted Hamilton as a radical liberal whose views contradicted Biblical teachings â but the strategy failed to curb the Democrat's momentum.
In Marshall's concession speech, the outgoing senator quoted scripture â and called the loss "humbling".
"I don't have any answers," he said. "I'll just tell you it's been the greatest honour of my life to serve the state of Kansas for ten years."
As the founding pastor of the United Methodist Church of the Resurrection, Hamilton told voters his faith is what inspires his belief that the government should help care for the poor and vulnerable.
But some took issue with his positions; Richard Friedeman, a lawyer and Republican Party chair of Kansas' Barton County, accused the pastor of being "very, very liberal - and he has the ability that liberal pastors have of telling you one thing and turning right around and telling somebody else the opposite".
Friedeman was cautiously optimistic on election day as he discussed the race from his Great Bend home, saying he believed Marshall, a personal friend and "good Republican voter," had "done a good job" during his time in office.
But he conceded that the Republican party was embattled.
"I think there's going to be a reckoning for the way Trump has alienated so many people... I think it's going to be hard for awhile," he said.
His prediction proved true, as voters in Republican strongholds like Iowa, South Carolina and Texas turned out for Democratic candidates.
Even in Mississippi, the heart of America's bible belt, the race was neck and neck at the time of publication - a feat once thought nearly impossible for the Democratic Party.
Most pundits and pollsters are viewing these historic victories as rebukes of Trump's second-term agenda, such as aggressive immigration policies, a war in Iran and global tariffs that have contributed to the rising cost of living.
The day before the election, on a rainy afternoon filled with squalls and hail, dozens of Hamilton supporters turned out for a last-minute canvas in the university town of Lawrence, Kansas. Among them were retired teacher Sharron Witters, 77, and her husband Lynn, 78, a former forestry professor and pastor of 25 years.
As evangelical Christians, they said Hamilton's candidacy motivated them to put out signs on their lawn and knock on doors for the first time. They set out with maps and lists, as Sharron navigated their silver VW SUV from address to address in a well-heeled Lawrence neighbourhood.
Hamilton, Sharron said, "doesn't sound like a politician".
"What a delight to stand and listen to somebody whose sentences make sense," she said.
"Wouldn't it be wonderful if he actually motivated people to work across the aisle?
She noted how other evangelical Christians had backed Trump "because he said, 'I'm against abortion'".
But she and her husband, "felt, from the very beginning, that [Trump] was a wolf in sheep's clothing".
Hamilton's campaign galvanised a powerful cross-section of Kansas society - from Republicans voting blue for the first time to long-time liberals initially skeptical of his more moderate positions.

Joshua Wong, once the face of Hong Kong's democracy movement, has been sentenced to 10 years in jail for colluding with foreign forces under the city's sweeping national security law.
Wong is among hundreds of campaigners and ordinary Hongkongers arrested under the law, which was imposed in 2020 following explosive pro-democracy protests against Beijing's growing control.
Critics say the far-reaching law has silenced dissent, but authorities argue that it is needed to maintain stability and deny it has weakened the city's cherished autonomy.
Having already spent the last six years in jail, Wong, who was due to be freed in January, will now spend another decade behind bars.
Wong, who turned 30 last month, has already been imprisoned multiple times for his activism which started when he was a teen.
On Thursday, he arrived in court wearing a dark blue long-sleeved shirt, khaki trousers and black-rimmed glasses. He looked slimmer compared to his previous public appearances.
He nodded in greeting towards members of the packed public gallery, and took notes intermittently as the judge read out the reasons for his sentencing.
A crowd had gathered outside the court, with dozens of Hongkongers having queued for hours hoping to get a seat in the public gallery. There was also a heavy police presence.
Wong is already serving time for subversion and was due to be freed early next year when he was handed the latest charges, which he has pleaded guilty to earlier in September.
Two months and two days of the 10-year term will be served concurrently with his ongoing sentence, the judge said on Thursday.
Prosecutors said that Wong had conspired with other campaigners, including self-exiled activist Nathan Law, to lobby for foreign sanctions and blockades against Beijing.
These activities took place between July and late November 2020, the court heard.
Wong and Law had been co-founders of Demosisto, a now defunct pro-democracy political party.
On Thursday, Hong Kong's chief executive John Lee said Wong and Law were "among the primary culprits responsible for undermining Hong Kong's prosperity and stability".
Their actions "not only severely undermined national sovereignty, security, and development interests, but also directly prejudiced the well-being of the general public and the stability of society," Lee said in a statement issued after the ruling.
Wong's friend and fellow activist Frances Hui, now based in the US, says she is "heartbroken" and "outraged" by the verdict.
"Today's sentencing is not just about Joshua. It is part of a broader political crackdown that seeks to rewrite a chapter of Hong Kong's history and erase the contributions of an entire generation who believed they could shape the future of their city," she told the BBC.
Human Rights Watch described the ruling as "cruel and unjust".
"To keep Hong Kong society subdued, and to reduce the chance of an international outcry, the Hong Kong government appears to have adopted the tactic of stacking charges against influential pro-democracy leaders," said its Asia director Elaine Pearson.
The harshest sentence under the controversial national security law (NSL) thus far has been handed to former media tycoon Jimmy Lai, who was jailed for 20 years, also for colluding with foreign forces.
Who is Joshua Wong?
Born to IT professional Roger and homemaker Grace in October 1996, Wong was diagnosed with dyslexia as a child, which made him struggle with school.
However, he was quick to challenge established rules and norms when they didn't make sense. In secondary school, he rallied with his classmates to protest against the high prices of canteen lunches on Facebook.
In 2011, Wong, then 14, co-founded the pro-democracy student activist group Scholarism, which quickly grew in size and influence.
The following year, the group rallied more than 100,000 people to protest against Hong Kong's plans to implement mandatory "patriotic education" in schools, forcing the authorities to back down.
By 2014, Wong, who was then at the forefront of a civil disobedience movement known as the "Umbrella Movement", had already become one of the most recognisable faces of Hong Kong's pro-democracy movement.
In 2016, he co-founded Demosisto with Law and Agnes Chow, an activist who is now also in exile.
But he often expressed discomfort at being labelled a "protest leader".
"We have a lot of facilitators in this movement and I'm one of them...âInstead of having a top-down command, we now have a bottom-up command hub," Wong told The Financial Times in November 2019.
Demosisto disbanded in 2020, the year Beijing introduced the NSL in Hong Kong.
Law left for the UK and continued his advocacy abroad, while Wong stayed on in Hong Kong and tried to run for a seat in its legislature â but was barred, with authorities citing his opposition to the NSL as one of the reasons.
Meanwhile, the court cases against Wong were stacking up.
On 23 November 2020, he pleaded guilty to several charges related to his involvement in protests outside the Hong Kong police headquarters in 2019.
Then came the NSL charges. While still in prison in February 2021, Wong was among 47 people charged with "conspiracy to commit subversion". The group became known as the Hong Kong 47 and remains the largest prosecution so far under the NSL.
Wong was still serving his 56-month sentence for the subversion conviction when he was charged with collusion under the NSL last year.
On 22 November 2020, the day before he pleaded guilty to the protest charges, Wong wrote in a post on Instagram addressed to "the people of Hong Kong": "To be honest, I have never had much faith in Hong Kong's politics, but I have every confidence in the people of Hong Kong.
"Even as political power now poses a comprehensive challenge to the resilience of our civil society, I believe the people of Hong Kong will, as always, find a way to see things through."
Additional reporting by Martin Yip

England isn’t renowned for its weather. But just a few centuries ago, climate change–fueled conditions may have been so bad that they put children’s health at risk.
Calcium mineralization in the teeth and skeletons of people who lived in rural northern England suggests that children growing up during the height of the Little Ice Age routinely developed vitamin D deficiencies, researchers report November 5 in Frontiers in Environmental Archaeology. In the worst cases, these deficiencies developed into rickets, a bone disorder that can occur when people don’t get enough ultraviolet light.
Previous skeletal studies suggest that rickets became more common among Europeans during the 18th and 19th centuries. One culprit may have been the Industrial Revolution, when many Europeans lived in UV-poor polluted cities and often worked indoors. The unusually cold climate may have added “an extra layer of difficulty” to getting enough sunlight, says Ellen Kendall, a bioarcheologist at Durham University in England
The Little Ice Age was a period of global cooling from the 13th to 19th centuries caused by extreme solar cycles and a series of volcanic eruptions, which can cool the planet by ejecting aerosols into the atmosphere that block sunlight. In the last 200 years of the era, 18 major eruptions helped spur a temperature drop of 2 to 3 degrees Celsius over northern Europe.
Kendall and colleagues wondered how this cold climate affected health. They examined calcium deposition — how the essential mineral is incorporated into bones — in the remains of 21 people buried from 1711 to 1829 in the town of North Shields. Calcium often doesn’t fully mineralize in people with vitamin D delicacies, leaving voids in teeth as they grow.
The team found bands of failed calcium mineralization in the teeth, suggesting seasonal spates of vitamin D deficiencies. Some skeletons also showed signs of rickets. North Shields was a small rural town that hadn’t yet undergone industrialization, so these deficiencies probably weren’t due to bad air conditions.
The unusually cold weather may have changed people’s behavior during the winter, Kendall says. Residents may have kept their kids indoors or bundled them up so that little skin was exposed when they did go outside, preventing them from getting enough UV light, she says.
However, climate was still just one factor among many — including gender roles, diet and pollution — that shaped vitamin D deficiencies at the time, says Kendall. “Humans are very messy to study,” she says. “That’s one of the things that makes them so very fascinating.”

Vice-President JD Vance sent shockwaves through Washington on Wednesday by blaming his party's midterm defeat squarely on the Iran war, in what was widely interpreted as an effort to distance himself from President Donald Trump ahead of a potential 2028 White House run.
In a carefully calibrated, 600-word statement on X, the vice-president acknowledged that Trump's 2024 voters had deserted Republicans in the midterm election.
"The reason we lost is the war," he wrote. "The president himself said so last night."
In interviews late Tuesday night and Wednesday, Trump had defended the war but acknowledged that it played a factor in Democrats flipping control of the US House of Representatives and the Senate.
Vance's view on the war in Iran is an open secret in Washington. While he has repeatedly backed the conflict since the US and Israel attacked Tehran in February, he has reportedly expressed opposition in private meetings with administration officials.
But those disagreements had been kept out of the public eye - until now.
Hours after Trump and the party were handed a bruising election defeat, Vance made clear that he felt the decision to go to war was a clear political mistake.
"If you'd like to argue it was worth it, that losing the Senate for the next 6 years was worth it, then do so. Argue it was a worthwhile cost to pay. Agree or disagree, that's at least honest," Vance said.
It was a striking statement, and one with no recent precedent: it's hard to recall a similar moment in recent US political history when a sitting vice-president has so sharply broken with the president on a signature foreign policy issue.
Then came an arguably even greater surprise: Trump - who typically demands steadfast loyalty from his senior advisers - agreed with Vance that the midterms were "largely" decided by the war. He added that he would "do it again" if given the same choices.
- LIVE: Follow latest updates
- BOWEN: Trump's loss limits powers at home, but it will likely be different abroad
- THE BIG MOMENTS: Ecstatic scenes that greeted key results
- ZURCHER: Midterm carnage weakens Trump but he still wields power for now
- 'A DISASTER': Angry Republicans blame Trump for midterms defeat
It was an early sign that Trump - who has prized loyalty from his advisers - may give Vance a wide berth should he choose to launch a presidential campaign.
"I know how he feels about it. I think it was -- I think it was fine," Trump told reporters when asked about Vance's post blaming the war. "I knew that when I went in, and we stopped them from having a nuclear weapon, and they will never have a nuclear weapon."
Vance's statement seemed like "a way of separating himself from Trump," said Daniel Byman, a foreign policy expert at the Center for Strategic and International Studies.
Drawing contrasts with Trump will be a delicate balancing act if Vance seeks the presidency, Byman added.
That balance was on display in Vance's post. The vice president didn't mention Trump by name and attributed much of his election results analysis to unnamed pollsters.
Vance "put his toe in the water to see what he's going to do," Ashley Davis, a Republican strategist, told the BBC.
Beyond the Iran war criticism, Vance also offered a political roadmap that could preview a possible presidential campaign. He distilled the party's strategy to win back voters into a neat four-point gameplan: "1) End the war 2) Focus on cost of living/inflation 3) Put America First 4) Change our relationship to Israel."
The list encapsulated much of Vance's worldview since bursting onto the national political scene, and read like the core argument in a future stump speech.
The BBC has contacted Vance's office for comment.
Of course, the next presidential election is still two years away. Vance is expected to run but hasn't made an official decision, and aides insist that he's still mulling it over.
It's also up for debate exactly how much Vance broke from Trump. Vance showed the message to Trump before posting it online, according to The New York Times.
Trump, for his part, could change his mind and make clear he'll brook no dissent from Vance or anyone else.
The president has been circumspect about who he'd support to succeed him as the 2028 Republican presidential nominee. Trump has praised Vance and Secretary of State Marco Rubio on several occasions, but hasn't said when - or if â he'd make an endorsement.
The president appears to relish the guessing game of who he'd back to carry on his political movement, even in the past floating the idea that he'd continue to a third term (which is barred by the US Constitution).
Vance's midterms missive might not be that significant in the end. Or it could have been the starting gun for the 2028 race and the battle for the post-Trump Republican Party.
Nardine Saad contributed reporting.

Pope Leo XIV hosted Bob Dylan at his official residence, the Apostolic Palace, on Wednesday during the Rome stop on the singer-songwriter's Italian tour.
Dylan, 85, wore a nearly all-black outfit, including a pulled up hoodie, gloves and umbrella, starkly contrasting with the Chicago-born Pope's all-white vestments.
The meeting between the pair, who both hail from the US Midwest, was brief, according to Vatican News.
Leo presented the Nobel laureate with a rosary and Dylan gifted Leo a copy of his autobiography, Chronicles: Volume One.
The visit happened ahead of Dylan's scheduled performance on Thursday at the Palazzo dello Sport, one of several Italian stops on his Rough and Rowdy Ways tour.
Leo has previously referenced Dylan in his own work, quoting Dylan's unreleased anti-nuclear song, Go Away You Bomb, in the preface to a book titled Disarmed and Disarming: Peace Is a Gift.
"I hate you cause yer man-made and man-owned, an' man-handled," was the line quoted in the book's warning to the world against rearmament.
The song was written in 1963 amid the Cold War, but was never recorded. The typewritten lyrics were unpublished until 2013 when they were discovered and put up for auction, according to the New York Times.
It was the second time Dylan had met a pope. In 1997 Dylan was invited to perform in front of Pope John Paul II and about 300,000 young people for the 23rd National Eucharistic Congress in Bologna.
Dylan played four songs including Knockin' on Heaven's Door, and reportedly climbed the stage mid-set to greet John Paul with a handshake and exchange a few words.
The then-Pope quoted Dylan's hit Blowin' in the Wind in his sermon to the crowd.

As a blue wave washed over Election Day, ballot measures across the country showed voters strongly support environmental protection, with notable early outcomes in California and Colorado.
Democrats swept Congress on Tuesday, winning control of both houses with notable victories in Ohio, South Carolina, Texas, Michigan and Maine.
Results, which are still being tallied Wednesday, represented national disapproval of Donald Trump’s second presidency on issues like the high cost of fuel and food, an unpopular war with Iran and the proliferation of data centers, according to analysts.
The outcome of ballot measures—some of which had industry backing—on a gamut of environmental and energy issues made voter sentiment clear: they want to safeguard the environment.
With more than half of the ballots counted in California, voters appear to be rejecting a measure to fast-track construction of “essential projects” like housing, clean energy and broadband internet access by streamlining the state’s bedrock environmental law.
Proposition 45 would overhaul the California Environmental Quality Act, or CEQA, by limiting the timeline for environmental review of major projects to 365 days and requiring that legal challenges of projects based on threats to air and water quality, tribal cultural resources and other harms be resolved within 270 days.
Proponents of the measure, sponsored by California’s Chamber of Commerce, say these deadlines are needed to speed the building of much-needed housing and infrastructure in the state. But opponents, including some affordable housing advocates, say the new rules would hobble the state’s landmark environmental law by limiting the scope of review as well as the ability of communities and tribes that are not federally recognized to mitigate the harms of polluting developments on their neighborhoods or ancestral lands.
As of Wednesday afternoon, with 58 percent of the votes counted, just over 54 percent opposed the measure and about 46 percent supported it. The measure can pass with a simple majority but would need two-thirds of the Legislature to amend it.
“We’re encouraged by what we’re seeing,” said Woody Little, spokesperson for the No on Prop 45 campaign, which represents more than 550 labor, health and environmental organizations.
“We’re seeing folks show up at the polls who represent the really broad coalition that came together against this measure [and] around protecting our core environmental law here in California,” Little said.
Though it’s too early to declare the final result, Little said, “it’s very clear that millions of Californians voted to defend our core environmental protections.”
Amelia Matier, a spokesperson for Yes on Prop 45, was not immediately available to comment Wednesday. Matier previously told CalMatters that by allowing for faster, more predictable reviews, the measure would let California build housing and infrastructure at a lower cost.
Prop 45’s likely defeat is encouraging news, said Noelle Chambers, executive director of the Amah Mutsun Land Trust, an initiative to restore Indigenous knowledge and practices on the Amah Mutsun tribe’s ancestral lands, which cover parts of counties from Monterey Bay to regions southeast of Silicon Valley.
“Meaningful tribal consultation is essential to protecting ancestral lands and cultural resources, particularly for non-federally recognized tribes whose voices are too often marginalized,” Chambers said. Such consultation, she said, is fundamental to advancing the return of Indigenous stewardship to Amah Mutsun homelands.
Polling from the nonpartisan Public Policy Institute of California showed that support for Prop 45 had dropped considerably, from 73 percent to 46 percent, between July and October, as voters learned more about the measure.

If passed, the measure could cost state and local governments more than $100 million a year, partly to cover environmental damages that emerged from projects built with limited review or public input, according to the nonpartisan Legislative Analyst’s Office.
Californians are rejecting a “false choice” between addressing the affordability crisis and protecting California’s air, water, health and climate at the same time, Little said. “They’re seeing through the tens of millions of dollars of misleading advertising from some of the largest, most powerful corporations in the state,” he said. “That should really send a message to the Legislature about which side their voters are on.”
In Colorado, with 81 percent of votes tallied as of Wednesday afternoon, voters rejected Amendment 82—which would have established a constitutional right for consumers in the state to buy natural gas and for distributors and utilities to sell the fuel. The initiative was intended to prevent local and state restrictions or bans on the sale of natural gas, such as through prohibitions on gas infrastructure in new construction, and to overturn existing regulations that curtail use of the fuel.
Environmentalists worried the change would endanger Colorado’s climate goals and—as the first of its kind—set a dangerous precedent.
“It would have made Colorado the first state in the country to put one industry’s profits into the constitution,” said Kelly Nordini, CEO of environmental advocacy group Conservation Colorado.
“That would have been the opposite direction of where Colorado voters have been going for decades, which is for health and safety protections, for clean energy, and certainly not putting a preference for one industry into the constitution,” Nordini said.
Conservation Colorado organizers criticized anonymous donors for trying to convince voters the measure was sensible.

On a busy election day, the Alabama Public Service Commission requested that Alabama Power voluntarily stop billing customers, effective immediately, for television commercials and other ads it buys to promote various aspects of its business.
Alabama Power is the largest electricity provider in Alabama, with territory covering about two-thirds of the state. Though it is a monopoly, the company spends millions each year on advertising, touting its reliability, customer service and other aspects of its business.
In recent months, the company has launched a series of television commercials touting a rate freeze it announced late last year amid heavy criticism over rising electricity prices.
A state law passed earlier this year will prohibit Alabama Power from including the costs of those commercials in customers’ electric bills, meaning the powerful utility will have to find all of the dollars in corporate profits. But the new law won’t take effect until 2029.
Currently, Alabama Power is allowed to bill customers for half of its non-public safety advertising costs.
During Tuesday’s meeting, PSC President Cynthia Lee Almond moved to “request” that Alabama Power voluntarily begin excluding those costs immediately.
“I don’t see any reason why we shouldn’t go ahead and take steps now to begin that process, rather than waiting until Jan. 1, 2029,” Almond said during the meeting.
Almond then made her motion, which was not on the meeting agenda, but came after the regular report from the commission’s electricity division.
“I move that the commission request that Alabama Power consent to exclude all advertising expenses from retail rate setting until after Dec. 31, 2028, when the new law takes effect,” Almond said. “Assuming Alabama Power consents, this interim measure would be reflected in its [Rate Stabilization and Equalization] filings for 2027 and 2028.”
Commissioners Jeremy Oden and Chris Beeker IV voted yes after a brief discussion.
According to the company filings with the Federal Energy Regulatory Commission, Alabama Power spent more than $6 million in general advertising last year, roughly $4 per customer. It’s unclear from the federal filing how much of that total was passed on to customers or how much might be impacted by the new prohibition.
Alabama Power did not immediately respond to a request for comment.
Daniel Tait, executive director of Energy Alabama, said the move was a boon to Alabama Power customers, who faced some of the highest electric bills in the country in recent years.
“We are grateful for the leadership of President Almond and the full commission for acting to end customers paying for Alabama Power’s advertising,” Tait said. “Once in place, Alabama will have one of the strongest customer protections in the nation on this front.”
This will be among the last actions of the commission under its current construction before a major overhaul takes effect.
In January, the commission will expand from three members to seven. Outgoing Gov. Kay Ivey has appointed four new commissioners, who will take office in January, including the PSC’s two first-ever Black members.
Oden and Beeker will also leave the commission in January after being defeated in Republican primaries. Cullman County Sheriff Matt Gentry will take Oden’s Place 1 seat, and former state auditor and PSC Commissioner Jim Zeigler will replace Beeker in Place 2.
Zeigler, a perennial candidate in Alabama across several decades, will return to the commission 48 years after leaving the PSC. He served one term from 1975-1979, during an era of skyrocketing energy costs and protracted political battles over electric rates between Alabama Power and then-Gov. George Wallace.
Almond will be the sole remaining member of the current commission.
The new seven-member commission will be overseen by the state’s first secretary of energy, who will be selected by Gov.-elect Tommy Tuberville. The new secretary will set the commission agenda, and overruling the secretary will require a vote of five of seven commissioners.
Tuberville has not yet announced his pick for secretary of energy. The only statutory requirement is that the secretary “must have experience in utility regulation or energy policy or a related field.”
About This Story

We do not charge a subscription fee, lock our news behind a paywall, or clutter our website with ads. We make our news on climate and the environment freely available to you and anyone who wants it.

9dd23295741c.text: President Trump has conceded that the Iran war cost Republicans dearly in the midterms . Now he must decide whether to cut his losses and reach a deal — or double down and go back to bombing. Why it matters: All of Trump's options are problematic: The first is to strike. But going back to war would be highly unpopular — keeping gas prices high and probably not yielding a better military result. Another is to negotiate. But if Iranian officals refuse to make concessions — or, sensing weakness after the president's political loss, up their demands — Trump will have a hard time reaching a deal. The third is to "strangle," as aides put it. This would mean sticking with the status quo — the naval blockade coupled with crippling economic sanctions that leave the Iranian regime to "rot" — while continuing to test its appetite for a deal. This path, however, could take months to show progress. The big picture: The president has said for weeks he would end the war one way or another after the election. One of his former advisers told Axios: "It's one thing to lose the midterms. But Trump doesn't want to look like a loser twice." That's left even his closest aides unsure what he's going to do next. The intrigue: Vice President Vance, in an extraordinary statement Wednesday morning, bluntly blamed the war for the GOP's midterm drubbing. It added a new political calculation to Trump's decision. "The reason we lost is the war," Vance wrote on X . "The president himself said so last night. If you'd like to argue it was worth it, that losing the Senate for the next 6 years was worth it, then do so. ... But everyone knows why we lost. And any honest conversation about where we go from here must start there." Vance also cited the U.S. relationship with Israel as a serious liability for Republicans. Trump told reporters on Wednesday that Vance's analysis was "largely true" because the war drove gas prices up. But Trump said he'd do it again if he had to: "We had no choice. You can't let Iran have a nuclear weapon." Asked when he's going to end the war, Trump responded: "Whenever I wanted to. But it's got to be done right, because they can't have a nuclear weapon." Behind the scenes: In recent months, Vance has led a faction within Trump's inner circle advising him to reach a deal with Iran to end the war. He privately accused Israeli Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu of "being wrong on everything" regarding Iran, sources said. Vance warned that the war was highly unpopular and could cost Republicans the election, the sources said. Most senior officials around Trump have shared Vance's views. But Trump still leaned toward resuming the war. At one point, he considered launching strikes before the midterms, as Netanyahu was pressing him to do. Trump decided to wait. But against the advice of his top advisers, he still endorsed Netanyahu in Israel's election last week. State of play: The U.S. military is finishing preparations for a possible resumption of major combat operations in Iran, including sending more assets to the region, American officials say. At the same time, Qatari mediators are working to secure U.S. and Iranian support for a draft agreement to head off a return to battle and possibly resume direct talks in the coming days, regional sources say. The mediators asked White House officials before the election what Trump would do if he lost. The president's advisers couldn't vouch either way, a source with knowledge said. "We told everybody that we want to see first how the elections turn out for us," a U.S. official said. The other side: Iranian officials celebrated Trump's electoral defeat, saying it showed they're winning the war. "The Iranian nation handed Trump a strategic defeat on the battlefield and in the Hormuz — and a POLITICAL DEFEAT in Washington," Iran's Supreme National Security Council Secretary Mohsen Rezaei wrote on X. "Meanwhile, Americans got stuck with the bill for his war. Anyone who takes on Iran will pay the price — from the battlefield to their own doorstep." Diplomats involved in the mediation efforts, Trump advisers and Middle East experts said Iran's gloating could make the president more likely to return to war. "Tehran's temptation is likely to mistake Trump's political weakness for military weakness and overplay its hand, when the smarter move is to bank a deal while Washington still wants one," Ali Vaez , deputy program director for the Middle East and North Africa at the International Crisis Group, told Axios. Yes, but: Trump could opt to maintain the "no war, no deal" status quo. CIA Director John Ratcliffe, Treasury Secretary Scott Bessent and other advisers want Trump to let the naval blockade and economic pressure campaign play out longer, tightening the screws on Iran. The bottom line: There's no tidy way for Trump to "finish the job" in Iran. Go deeper: Oil prices plunge after Vance post on Iran war

The News
In Piqua, Ohio, voters on Tuesday approved a ban on large data centers and recalled the commissioners who backed Metaâs massive project there. In Trenton, less than 50 miles south, a similar ban passed. And outside Columbus, the heart of Ohioâs data center boom, voters in Ashville repealed the villageâs deal with developer EdgeConneX.
These Ohio races were part of a swell of anti-data-center sentiment that echoed across the country in dozens of ballot measures concerning bans, moratoriums, or stricter regulations and oversight. The votes were hyperlocal and often emotional in nature, but they could carry financial consequences, because some of the projects at stake were already in motion.
- Meta bought more than 600 acres in Piqua last year for about $110 million, and signed agreements with the city in January. âWe are proud of our investments in Ohio, and will work with local officials to determine the future of our investment in Piqua,â a Meta spokesperson told Semafor on Wednesday.
- Amazon had proposed a 600-acre campus on land Trenton hoped to annex; the ban effectively blocks that plan, according to local news. An Amazon spokesperson didnât directly comment on the vote but said the company is âcommitted to setting a high bar for responsible data center development in Ohio, and will continue engaging communities early as we build out this important infrastructure.â
- EdgeConneX said its development in Ashville is moving forward despite the vote, given that its permits are secured and construction is underway.
More than 40% of the USâ planned data center capacity is located in states where governors or governors-elect have pledged or already imposed a pause on new data centers, according to a Cleanview analysis. That doesnât mean the data center buildout will grind to a halt, but markets are pricing in a slowdown.
Shares of companies that are directly exposed to the physical buildout of data centers tanked Wednesday, including Modine (a maker of data center HVACs, down about 21%) and Sterling Infrastructure (site prep and electrical work, also down 21%).
Hyperscaler stocks, though, soared, with traders betting they will be forced to rein in the rapid spending that has pushed their free cash flow to negative territory. More restrictions on data center construction also means tech giantsâ compute capacity âpotentially even becomes more valuable,â Morgan Stanley US Equities Strategist Andrew Pauker told Semafor.
The View From Washington
Tech companies are also recalibrating their data center strategies in Washington as they prepare for a Democrat-controlled Congress.
One tech-focused public affairs adviser suggested companies work with Democrats to craft national rules around data center development. Incoming Democrats in the House and Senate say theyâre going into Congress with a mandate to do something about AI data centers, and Republican groups who pushed their party to listen to grassroots concerns about data centers are saying Washington Republicans can only blame themselves for the midterm losses after aligning with AI companies.
Ellen DiMauro contributed to this story.

d3612eb8ffc1.text: House Democrats channeled anti-Trump fury into a landslide victory over Republicans. Now comes the hard part: Figuring out what to do with their huge majority . Why it matters: That question is already igniting a power struggle between Democrats' ideological factions as they lay out contradictory visions for what the next two years of governing looks like. This story is based on interviews with more than a dozen sitting and incoming House Democrats from across the political spectrum. "Last night was a rebuke of the status quo," progressive Rep. Delia Ramirez (D-Ill.) told Axios, adding that "for the left it was an affirmation and a validation that we are on the right track." There is "absolutely no excuse," Ramirez said, for House Democrats not to do "the most over the next two years, and as quickly as possible." Rep. Josh Gottheimer (D-N.J.), a centrist, said Tuesday was a "gigantic night for the middle ground," and that the mandate is far more modest: "We need to crush high costs and corruption." State of play: House Democrats are on track to win more than 250 seats, which would give them a comfortable majority of dozens of votes. That blows up the plans of a cohort of incoming progressives known as the "Bloc" to demand concessions from leadership in exchange for voting with the party. The potential concessions included changes to House rules, plum committee assignments and votes to enact Medicare-for-All , defund ICE and cut off U.S. aid to Israel. What we're hearing: The left's new tactic is to try to convince the Congressional Progressive Caucus to, as one sitting House Democrat put it, "assert its authority in a way it has never done before." "That should definitely be part of the game plan," an incoming Bloc member told Axios, "we've got so many members of the CPC and I think we're adding 25 more." Said Rep. Pramila Jayapal (D-Wash.), a former CPC chair: "We have certainly used our power many times ... and we will do that again." The CPC is currently around 100 members, though not all are pugnacious ideological brawlers. The new strategy also involves aggressively recruiting incoming House Democrats from battleground districts, a group that hasn't traditionally been at the core of the CPC's membership. The left is hopefully eyeing the "Bernie Dogs": Populist candidates from working class backgrounds who won red districts with support from both progressives and centrists. They are also taking a close look at the "wave babies": Candidates who won upset victories in districts that weren't even on the party's radar and whose politics are largely unknown on Capitol Hill. What they're saying: CPC chair Greg Casar (D-Texas) argued in an interview that it may not be such a fight to pass a progressive agenda, noting that House Minority Leader Hakeem Jeffries (D-N.Y.) has called for "dramatic change." "Americans delivered a demand for bold change, and progressives are excited to deliver it," Casar said, adding that Medicare-for-All is "overwhelmingly popular" and that Democrats "should move that kind of legislation forward." Jayapal told Axios: "We will be driving an agenda that truly is big and bold and looking for [Jeffries'] leadership to make sure that is what we deliver." The former CPC chair said she is "100% down" for the items on Jeffries' 100-days agenda but "I just don't think there's any way we can stop there. ... We have to pass a living wage bill, we have to pass universal childcare." The other side: Rep. Adam Gray (D-Calif.), a leader of the centrist Blue Dog Coalition, told Axios, "The most extreme elements ... want to do messaging bills and yell and scream and point the finger." "There's time for that, let's just not make it the majority time," he continued, "and I think you're going to find a lot of people ... agree with me on this." Rep. Marc Veasey (D-Texas), an ally of Jeffries, said the results were a "victory for common sense, not any extremist ideology" and that Jeffries "understands what last night was all about and he will lead accordingly." Jeffries is being characteristically taciturn about how he will govern. "We're going to have a conversation as a caucus upon our return about what the agenda looks like," he told reporters at a press conference on Wednesday. Asked about marking up Medicare-for-All, Jeffries said House Democrats will have a "family conversation" about what health care measures to pass beyond renewing expired Affordable Care Act tax credits and reversing the GOP's cuts to Medicaid. The bottom line: "Medicare-for-All is not going to happen in the next two years and everybody knows that," said progressive Rep. Jared Huffman (D-Calif.), a co-sponsor of Medicare-for-All. "I hear all of this jockeying, and frankly I find it tedious," he told Axios. "We're going to have a huge majority to navigate these issues and it's all going to be fine. ... We're mostly on the same team here." Said another House progressive: "With this big of a majority, honestly, the Bloc has way less influence, but the good news is so do the members who buy Depends by the carton." "On balance, this is a center-left caucus," a third House Democrat said.

- Published
The Democrats have swept to victory in the US midterm elections, taking control of Congress.
While the incumbent president's party generally tends to have a bad night in these elections, the scale of the Republican defeat is being viewed as a resounding rejection of Donald Trump's two years in the White House.
From angry voters to an unpopular president, here are five reasons why the Republicans lost so many seats.
1. Soaring cost of living
From coast to coast, voters across the US have been grappling with the soaring cost of essentials. That anger was palpable on the ground in key races.
"Gas prices, grocery prices, everything's going up," one North Carolina voter told the BBC ahead of the elections, adding that she had switched her vote from Republican to Democratic this election.
Prices increased by 3.7% in the year to September, driven higher by fuel and energy prices. Average US retail diesel prices in early October were just shy of the record of $6.52 (Â£4.83) per gallon seen in September, according to government data.
Almost eight in 10 voters (79%) said inflation had caused them and their family a severe or moderate hardship in the past year, according to data from voter polls.
And more than six in 10 respondents laid the blame for that at the feet of Trump, saying they thought higher than usual prices were because of the president's policies.
2. Unpopular Iran war
A major factor in surging prices has been the war with Iran which the US and Israel launched in February.
Fuel prices then shot up after Tehran effectively closed the Strait of Hormuz in retaliation, strangling a key artery for the passage of the world's oil and liquefied natural gas (LNG).
US voters have been paying the price at the petrol pump ever since.
The war has proved broadly unpopular with most Americans. For Maga Republicans it also felt like a broken promise in Trump's America First campaign agenda in which he pledged there would be no more wars.
Around six in 10 (63%) of those asked in a voter poll said the US made the wrong decision to take military action against Iran.
Separately, three-quarters of voters (74%) said the conflict was a crucial or major factor in their vote for Congress.
The morning after the election, Trump conceded the war had played a role in the defeat but insisted in an interview on Fox that he had no choice but to intervene to stop Iran getting a nuclear weapon.

- ZURCHER: Midterm carnage weakens Trump but he still wields power for now
- RESULTS: How America voted in maps and charts
- EXPLAINER: Five reasons why Trump did so badly
- ANALYSIS: Vance walks Trump tightrope with scathing election critique blaming Iran war
- REACTION: Angry Republicans blame Trump for midterms 'disaster'
- NEWSLETTER: Sign up for Anthony Zurcher's analysis in your inbox
3. Disciplined message from Democrats
The scale and breadth of this Democratic wave was made possible by some strong candidates who came across as authentic, especially in traditional Republican heartlands.
They stuck to a disciplined message about the cost of living and healthcare access.
Former teacher James Talarico and pastor Adam Hamilton also talked about their faith in a way that struck a chord in Texas and Kansas respectively.
In South Carolina, Democrat Annie Andrews pulled off a shock upset. A former paediatrician, her focus on health care affordability resonated in a country where many see the system as broken.
Former public health official Abdul El-Sayed, who triumphed in Michigan to keep that seat Democratic, made getting "money out of politics, money in your pocket" a key slogan.
Democratic Senator Jon Ossoff, who won re-election in Georgia, made the cost of living and corruption a central message. The 39-year-old's comfortable victory in a state Trump won twice will only fuel rumours of a 2028 presidential run.
Even Trump himself praised the Democrats, telling Fox News they "did a good job".
Conversely, some Republican candidates like Ken Paxton in Texas were criticised for running poor campaigns that were not focused enough on voters' concerns.
4. Trump's unpopularity a drag on Republicans
Two of the issues voters were most unhappy with - rocketing prices and the Iran War - were directly linked to the president.
His approval ratings had even fallen among Republican voters, which made some of these states which backed him in 2024 especially vulnerable.
He urged voters to imagine he was on the ballot in an effort to galvanise his supporters.
But after more than a decade as the central figure in American politics, some see these results as evidence that the glitz may be wearing off Trump's brand.
Against a backdrop of increasing anger, making himself the focus of the Republican campaign was risky and appears to have backfired.
In the months leading up to the vote, polling indicated that many Americans wanted Trump to focus more on their concerns about rocketing prices.
In his final campaign speech on Monday in Washington DC, he talked at length about his controversial renovation project of the Reflecting Pool behind him.
5. Hispanic and black voters shift again
Two years ago a move towards Republicans among some Hispanic and black voters helped Trump secure a decisive win. That seems to have reversed in these midterms.
Democrats claimed all three House races in the overwhelmingly Hispanic congressional districts along the Texas-Mexico border.
Majority-Hispanic counties moved more than 22 percentage points against Republican Senate candidates, compared with the 2024 presidential election, according to a New York Times analysis.
The change is more than any other major demographic group in the country, data reporter Jeff Adelson said.
The shift comes amid widespread anger at immigration enforcement, with a majority (56%) of Americans saying they have an unfavourable opinion of ICE, according to the Pew Research Center.

NY-17: Last in a series on the environmental stakes behind one of the nation’s most fiercely contested congressional races.
Before midnight, and before any official body had called the race, Republican incumbent Mike Lawler conceded to Democratic challenger Cait Conley in New York’s 17th Congressional District. Conley flipped the closely watched toss-up seat, denying Lawler a third term in a district Kamala Harris won in 2024, as a nationwide blue wave promises Democrats a commanding House majority.
It was a district in which energy costs, data center development and nuclear power were central to campaign messaging. Though climate policy was seldom invoked by name, Conley pledged to fight climate change “as a national security priority.”
“When all of the votes are counted tomorrow in Westchester, it’s gonna be pretty clear that we will be short,” Lawler said during a speech to supporters Tuesday evening.
Westchester County experienced widespread problems with ballot-scanning machines on Election Day, delaying results, with concerns that the issues might discourage low-propensity voters. Still, Conley carried the county by a 34-point margin and flipped the seat by roughly 5 percentage points, according to preliminary results Wednesday. The outcome represents an approximately 11-point swing toward Democrats compared with the 2024 congressional race.
Many in the district viewed Conley’s victory as a repudiation of President Donald Trump and Lawler’s alignment with him, despite the congressman’s efforts to portray himself as a moderate. Lawler was formerly head of the New York state GOP, while Conley is a decorated Army combat veteran who served in Iraq and Afghanistan before working on the National Security Council during the Biden administration.
Trump has repeatedly endorsed Lawler, who joined him at what Trump called the 2026 Republican Midterm Convention in September in Dallas. On Tuesday, Trump urged Jewish voters in the district to re-elect Lawler, an appeal that underscored the perceived political influence of the district’s Orthodox Jewish voting bloc.
“VOTE MIKE LAWLER FOR CONGRESS — HE WILL NEVER LET YOU DOWN!” he wrote on X.
Yet Erik Lindberg, a Westchester County resident who voted for Conley, said that while Lawler “ran a really impressive constituent services shop,” he “had no significant ideological principles, other than being a member of the Republican caucus.”
“He lost because he worked in lockstep with Trump,” said Susan Shapiro, an environmental attorney and resident of the district.
William Knox, a veteran and self-described “anti-MAGA Republican” who had been undecided shortly before the election, said he voted for Democrats across the board, not necessarily because he agreed with their policies, but to give those opposing MAGA all the support he could.
A Referendum on Lawler
Throughout the campaign, Lawler sought to make rising energy costs a central issue, blaming Albany Democrats for higher utility bills. But his own record included millions of dollars in contributions from utility-related political action committees, as well as previous work as a registered lobbyist for a natural-gas advocacy group whose backers included utilities and fossil-fuel interests.
While Republicans like Lawler repeatedly sought to shift blame for rising costs onto Democrats, a majority of Americans now blame Trump’s policies for persistently high prices.
“The fact that there has been a Republican trifecta while fuel prices have hugely increased has made it clear to everyone, including the most MAGA Republicans, that this isn’t Democrats’ doing,” said Madalina Vlasceanu, a researcher at Stanford University’s Doerr School of Sustainability.
Lawler continually advocated for reopening Indian Point, the district’s shuttered nuclear power plant, and for expanding domestic oil and gas production. In addition to centering the energy debate, he capitalized on public unease surrounding artificial intelligence and data centers, regularly highlighting more than $328,000 in payments from two AI surveillance companies disclosed in Conley’s financial filings.
The result suggests Conley succeeded in distancing herself from accusations leveled throughout the campaign that she was the “AI candidate for the AI industry.”
What’s Next?
The district, in the Lower Hudson Valley, includes all of Rockland and Putnam counties, most of northern Westchester County and portions of southern Dutchess County. For many environmental advocates there, the prevailing sentiment after Conley’s victory was hope.
On her campaign website, and less consistently in campaign appearances and debates, she said she would expand federal investment in clean energy, protect open spaces, hold corporate polluters accountable and pressure the administration to rejoin the Paris climate agreement. She also opposed efforts to reopen Indian Point and pledged to tackle PFAS, better known as “forever chemicals.”
“With Democratic control of Congress, it becomes possible again to begin to reverse the assault on the environment,” said Peggy Kurtz, an environmental activist from Rockland County.

7053d16d9186.text: In our news wrap Wednesday, top officials in Iran welcomed the results of the U.S. midterm elections, Israeli President Isaac Herzog says he's accepted the results of last week’s election and will consult with party leaders on forming a new government and Ukraine's air force says Russia launched more than 300 drones overnight. Geoff Bennett: Meantime, top officials in Iran welcomed the results of last night's U.S. midterm elections, casting them as a rejection of President Trump's war. That's where we start our day's other headlines. Iran's Parliament speaker and chief negotiator said American voters sent a clear message, no to war. But Iran's supreme leader warned that anyone expecting a change in U.S. policy toward Iran is, in his words, gravely mistaken. The U.S. has carried out limited strikes on Iranian targets in recent weeks, while fears of renewed all-out war following the election have kept the region on edge. In Israel, President Isaac Herzog says he's accepted the results of last week's election and will consult with party leaders there on forming a new government. Neither Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu's party nor that of his chief challenger, former military chief Gadi Eisenkot, secured a parliamentary majority. That means Herzog must now meet with party officials and choose a candidate to form a coalition government, which would likely lead to weeks of talks. He urged all sides to work towards a compromise. Isaac Herzog, Israeli President (through interpreter): I expect the factions and the representatives to understand that, in the current reality, it is not possible to fulfill all commitments and promises. I'm not asking anyone to give up their fundamental values, but, in the current reality, in which there is no clear winner after, I'm asking for originality, creativity, boldness, and goodwill. Geoff Bennett: Earlier today, Israel's election commission said it found no evidence of voting irregularities, despite Netanyahu's attempts to cast uncertainty on the result. He's claimed without evidence that Arab-led parties, as he put it, stole that election. Ukraine's air force says Russia launched more than 300 drones overnight. Most were shot down, but one strike in Western Ukraine set a shopping center ablaze, injuring at least one person. Meantime, rescue crews are still searching for bodies after Monday's attack on a former school that was being used as a shelter in Southern Ukraine. President Zelenskyy says at least 40 people were killed, while 30 more possibly trapped beneath the rubble. It's believed to be one of the deadliest strikes of the war. In Brussels, officials from the U.S., Germany, France and other countries met to discuss Ukraine's postwar reconstruction. The E.U.'s foreign policy chief expressed cautious optimism following the U.S. election results. Kaja Kallas: U.S. voters have made their choice clear. I hope that the new Congress and the new Senate will continue supporting Ukraine and also putting more pressure on Russia. Let's see what happens now, but elections have results. Geoff Bennett: The talks in Brussels come ahead of a new round of U.S.-brokered peace talks set for next week in Abu Dhabi. A federal judge in Boston has dismissed a case against a Russian-born Harvard scientist who was accused of smuggling frog embryos into the U.S. Kseniia Petrova was arrested last year as she returned from a holiday in France with the specimens. She spent four months in detention, during which she spoke with us on this program via video call. Prosecutors agreed to drop the charges after a judge said she could seek evidence to support her claim that she had been unfairly targeted. Petrova has said she did not realize she had to declare the items. One of NASA's most successful space telescopes plunged back to Earth today. The U.S. Space Force says the Swift Observatory reentered Earth's atmosphere near Indonesia. NASA officials believe the 3,200-pound spacecraft likely burned up upon reentry, though a few components may have survived. Its demise came less than three months after a rescue mission failed. Swift was launched in 2004 to study gamma ray bursts and exploding stars and has been pulled back towards Earth ever since. The mission was meant to last for two years, but instead continued for more than two decades. Well, stocks surged on Wall Street today as investors welcomed last night's election results. The Dow Jones industrial average soared more than 1, 500 points. The Nasdaq jumped nearly 1.5 percent. The S&P 500 also ended sharply higher. And we have two passings to report tonight, starting with British celebrity hairstylist and beauty entrepreneur John Frieda. Frieda built a global hair care empire best known for products like Frizz Ease and Sheer Blonde. He started his career in London, styling some of the world's most famous figures, including Princess Diana, Jackie Kennedy Onassis, Madonna, and Sarah Jessica Parker. He opened his first salon in 1976 and later turned his expertise into a multimillion-dollar hair care business, which he sold in 2002 for a reported $450 million. His salon announced that Frieda died peacefully surrounded by family. No cause of death was disclosed. John Frieda was 75 years old. And a founding force of techno music, Juan Atkins, has died. His 1985 single "No UFOs" made "Rolling Stone"'s list of the 200 greatest dance songs of all time. The Detroit native broke out in the early 1980s, inspired by the German band Kraftwerk and George Clinton's Parliament Funkadelic. Over the years, his work as a deejay and producer helped bring techno to a global audience. Atkins is even credited with originating the name techno. His talent agents confirmed his death in Mexico City this past weekend, but did not provide a cause of death. Juan Atkins was 64 years old.
