A mother and daughter have died after a suspected grizzly bear attack in the Canadian province of British Columbia, their family has announced.
The women - identified as Jennifer Balcarras, 48, and her daughter Selah Reed, 20 -were reported missing on 1 November when they did not return from what was supposed to be a short afternoon walk, the family said.
Their remains were found in a trail area in Bella Coola, according to the BC Conservation Officer Service (BCCOS), which said evidence at the scene "suggested an animal may have been involved".
Conservation officers are working to track down any bears involved.
Balcarras' remains were found on Monday and Reed's on Tuesday during search efforts by conservation officers and the Royal Canadian Mounted Police (RCMP).
Jeff Tyre, an inspector with the BCCOS, said it was not yet clear if more than one was potentially involved in the women's deaths.
He added that any captured bear would be assessed and if it is found to have been involved in the attack "it will be dispatched in accordance with provincial human-wildlife conflict response guidelines to protect public safety".
Balcarras and Reed were "two peas in a pod" who "got along really, really well" and shared many hobbies, Balcarras' brother, Josh Balcarras, told CBC.
"When Jenny hiked, Selah was right there beside her," he said.
Balcarras had recently moved to Bella Coola to pursue a new career and begin a new chapter in her life, according to an online fundraiser to help the family with funeral costs.
Grizzly bears are listed as a species of "special concern" under federal legislation, and are an important part of the British Columbia landscape, according to Environmental Reporting BC, external.
Between 10,000 and 13,000 grizzly bears are estimated to live in the province, according to the province's Ministry of Environment, Lands and Parks, which has classified them as vulnerable.
According to the ministry, conflicts between bears and humans are "relatively rare" unless the animals are startled or protecting their cubs and food.
But there have been a number of attacks in British Columbia in recent years.
A grizzly bear injured two hikers in the McGregor Mountain area in October 2025, one of whom died later due to critical injuries. The bear was later found dead.
The following month, a bear attacked a school group - also in the Bella Coola area - injuring 11 people.
The BC Wildlife Federation (BCWF) has said that reports of grizzly-human conflicts have risen since the province introduced a ban on hunting grizzly bears for sport in 2017.
"With no hunting pressure, grizzlies and humans will increasingly occupy the same spaces with inevitable consequences," the BCWF's executive director Jesse Zeman said at the time.

8a29289b36ba.text: The results of the midterms have set up a two-year power struggle between Trump’s White House and the incoming Democratic Congress. Lisa Desjardins takes a look at the races and the potential size of the incoming Democratic majority. Geoff Bennett: Turning back now to tonight's top story, last night's midterm results have set up a two-year power struggle between Trump's White House and the incoming Democratic Congress. Amna Nawaz: Lisa Desjardins is back at the Super Screen with more on the races and the potential size of the coming Democratic majority. So, Lisa, let's start with the Senate. Democrats have so far swept the toss-up races, but it's not over yet. Where do things stand? Lisa Desjardins: That's right. Remember, this is where we started last night, a look at the toss-up races all held by Republicans right now. What's happened? Look at all these flips. This is a sweep like you seldom see in politics. And we are still waiting, of course, for results from Alaska and from Mississippi. So, just given what they have already flipped, Democrats have flipped seven seats in the Senate. They could get nine. That total, nine, is something that only comes around for either party in, say, 50 years. Either way, this is quite a tsunami that we see tonight. Now, I want to look at exactly kind of what the numbers are saying, as you see, gaining seven, and you can see all around the country. There's one that stands out here, Mississippi, which is light blue and waiting on. As you heard Liz say, we are waiting on votes because right now there's just a 65-vote difference. Mississippi has 82 counties in it. So think about that. That is fewer than one vote per county difference in this race right now. As they're waiting for provisional ballots, they also have some votes out here in Hinds County. This is a place that has 90 percent counting, and where the Democrats Scott Colom is ahead by quite a lot. We may be waiting for days or weeks on this. And, as well, we could very well be the same for Alaska, where we have a virtual tie right now as well. Geoff Bennett: So that's the Senate. Let's shift our focus now to the House. We know Democrats have claimed control of the House, but the question at this hour is the margin. How are things looking? Lisa Desjardins: That's right. I wanted to look at what the current Congress looks like. First of all, you can see it's a mostly red Congress that we have today. And then if you go to our map of where it stands now, here you can see all of this blue in the center of the country and on the side of the country, more than one blue dot in the center now. You can see Democrats at this moment have gained 28 seats. And what's interesting, as I prepared this segment, I also carefully looked at all the seats where we haven't had race calls yet. There are quite a few. And as I have been standing here, Democrats have picked up in Michigan 10 and in Michigan 4 and in Nebraska 2. The Republican has conceded, Mike Lawler, in New York 17. So remember the numbers, 28 pickups so far. This is another 23 seats where Democrats are leading and poised to flip. That is 51 seats that they could have total gain. That's the kind of number that Newt Gingrich saw in 1994, a huge shift. Amna Nawaz: So, Lisa, those are the numbers. But what do the maps tell you about who or what shifted in this election? Lisa Desjardins: Right. Let's talk about Texas there, because I think that is something historians will study for a long time. James Talarico 55 percent to Ken Paxton, that is a huge margin. Where did it come from? Again, let's compare this to 2024 and the presidential vote. You can see right here the Rio Grande Valley nice and red. I want to pick one county that I think typifies the state a little bit. That's Brewster County, where they happen to be having their famous chili cook-off right now. Happy for all of them. President Trump won this county by 13 points in 2024. What happened with James Talarico? Look at that. It's a complete flip. And this is a plurality Hispanic district. This is all Hispanic territory. I also want to point out we have a lot of close races in the House. So it may take some time to know exactly what's going on. For example, here, Arizona, we have a virtual tie right there in Arizona's Second District. And one we're watching closely, Tennessee's Fourth District right here, again, just 280 votes between Victoria Broderick and Scott DesJarlais. It's going to be a while before we know the exact margin, though we do know the general outcome. Amna Nawaz: All right, Lisa Desjardins still going strong at the Super Screen for us. Lisa, thank you. Lisa Desjardins: You're welcome.

37737cf1b6b5.text: For a deeper dive into the election data and why people voted the way they did, Geoff Bennett and Amna Nawaz spoke with Amy Walter of The Cook Political Report. Geoff Bennett: And for a deeper dive into the data and why people voted the way they did, Amy Walter of The Cook Political Report With Amy Walter is back with us. Hello, Amy Walter. Amy Walter: Hello, Geoff Bennett. I feel like I never left. Geoff Bennett: That's right. (CROSSTALK) Amy Walter: ... I didn't. Geoff Bennett: Yes, we just stayed here under the desk. (LAUGHTER) Geoff Bennett: So, look, President Trump urged voters to treat his -- this election as a referendum on him, and in many ways that's what they did. Amy Walter: Right. Geoff Bennett: The economy was a top issue for voters, as we know, with gas prices soaring amid the war in Iran. How much did voters hold the president and his party, the Republican Party, personally responsible for the economic pain they're feeling? Amy Walter: Yes, I mean, that's the real takeaway from this election. It's not just that people thought that the economy was their most salient issue. It's that they believed that it was Trump's policies that had caused the higher prices. In The Voter Poll, the exit poll, 63 percent of Americans who voted said Trump's policies are the cause of higher prices. Only 37 percent said it was for some other reason. And here's really -- the next piece of this is the priority piece. It's not just that they were frustrated about the war and its impact on gas prices and on inflation. The president has mentioned that today, as you noted, the vice president saying it's really the Iran war that's the big problem. But what voters also felt was a real sense that the president was focused much more on his priorities than he was focused on their priorities. Just 36 percent of voters said they believed that Trump has the right priorities; 64 percent said no. And when asked, well, what does he actually prioritize, 62 percent again said his priorities. Just 38 percent said the country's interests. And this, I think, was really typified, Geoff, by the fact that he ended his campaign -- we talked about this a lot going into the election -- ended it at the Reflecting Pool talking about the work he was going to do there, and then the day after the campaign, he's standing in the still-not-completed ballroom. Voters looked at that and said, I just don't understand how he could be more focused on this than on bringing down my costs. And I think the issue of betrayal overall -- it's not -- again, I don't think it's just that people are upset that their prices went up. It's that they believed that, when he came to Washington for a second time, he was not only going to fix the economy, but he was going to focus on them, and he was not, certainly not going to get the U.S. involved in overseas conflict. Amna Nawaz: Amy, let me ask you something about the redistricting push. I know we have talked a lot about the president pushed for that in a number of states over the last two years. All of that was based on the idea that Republicans could recreate the coalition that pushed him back into the White House in 2024. Amy Walter: Right. Amna Nawaz: It didn't work. Where did they fall short? Amy Walter: Yes, with almost every single piece of that coalition that Trump put together in 2024, Latinos a big piece of this, in 2024, Harris only won Latino voters by about 12 points. But Democrats this election won them by 30. Texas is a great example of the swing that we saw there. And then younger voters. Remember, we talked so much about especially younger men, younger men of color; 18-to-29-year-olds only supported Harris by three points in 2024. They gave Democrats 73 percent of the vote in this election. So the real sense, again, of the betrayal of the core promises of a Trump presidency really led to much of this backsliding with this coalition. Geoff Bennett: Amy Walter, thanks so much for your sharp insights this entire election season. Amy Walter: Thank you. Appreciate that. Geoff Bennett: We deeply appreciate it. Amy Walter: You're welcome.

Please check your inbox to confirm. The Swift Observatory's demise came less than three months after a long-shot rescue mission failed. The U.S. Space Force confirmed Swift's reentry near Indonesia after tracking its sinking orbit, the result of intense solar activity the past few years. NASA hired a private company to whip together an orbit-boosting effort, but Katalyst Space's three-armed robotic craft ran into trouble following its July launch and came crashing down in September. It was not immediately known how much of the 1 ½-ton spacecraft burned up in the atmosphere. NASA anticipated some of the denser pieces surviving. Swift rocketed into orbit in 2004 on what was expected to be a two-year study of gamma ray bursts and exploding stars. It observed thousands of them over a mission that lasted 11 times longer than planned, serving as a first responder for other telescopes that could probe deeper. WATCH: How NASA's new space telescope could help solve mysteries of dark energy and dark matter NASA is gauging industry's interest in mounting a rescue mission for another observatory whose orbit is being chipped away by solar storms: the Hubble Space Telescope. Launched in 1990, Hubble is expected to come crashing down by the mid-2030s, according to recent analyses. The space agency is looking for input from private companies on whether and how they might boost Hubble's orbit, upgrade its systems or guide it to a controlled reentry — or all three. Any such mission would need to happen by 2032. Unlike the rush job with Swift, the space agency has more time to explore options for saving Hubble, said Nicky Fox, NASA's science mission chief. "Hubble still has important science ahead of it," NASA Administrator Jared Isaacman said in a statement, "and we should be looking at every reasonable opportunity to keep it delivering for as long as possible." 0cc5efdf4d48.text: In Michigan's 7th Congressional District, progressive activist William Lawrence unseated Republican Tom Barrett in one of the year’s most competitive House races. Lawrence joined Amna Nawaz to discuss the win and what comes next. Amna Nawaz: We want to zero in now on some of the most notable results from last night's election. And we will start with Michigan's Seventh Congressional District. That's in the Lansing area. That is where progressive activistWilliam Lawrence unseated Republican Tom Barrett in one of the years' most competitive House races. Representative-elect Will Lawrence joins me now. Representative-elect, congratulations. Thanks for joining us. William Lawrence: Thank you so much. It's my pleasure to be here. Amna Nawaz: So this race was one of the most closely watched races in the entire nation, also among the most expensive House races in the country. It's a critical swing district in Michigan that Republicans really fought hard to hang on to. So how did you turn it blue? William Lawrence: It was all about the grassroots movement that we built. We knocked on more doors than any House campaign in the entire country. We have got thousands of volunteers who were out there knocking on those hundreds of thousands of doors. And I spent the last 15 months crisscrossing the district, showing up in small towns all over and here in the city of Lansing in the suburbs. And we took nothing for granted, went out to reach every single voter. And people were motivated by our campaign because I didn't take a dime of corporate PAC money, despite going up against $23 million from the other side. More money was spent trying to take me down than any other Democrat in the country. And they saw me speaking out on issues like stopping these wars, saying no to AI data centers, and investing in good housing and health care that we can actually afford. Amna Nawaz: We should mention to folks you co founded the Sunrise Movement. You are a climate activist. And, yes, AI data centers, regulating AI, those were core parts of your message. Why did they resonate so deeply where you are? William Lawrence: You know, it came to me from the bottom up. I started getting calls in the fall that we had not one, not two, but three hyperscale AI data centers proposed in different parts of my district. And in listening to people, it was clear that the pitch from these data center developers was just not persuasive. They're proposing to suck up a lot of our water, jack up our energy bills, cause all kinds of noise pollution and damage people's property values, all for the sake of generating AI, which, to hear them tell it, is going to put tens of millions of people out of work, if it doesn't kill us all by accident. So people just really responded organically in opposition to these bullies from Silicon Valley and Wall Street, and I was proud to stand alongside those residents throughout the campaign. Amna Nawaz: So you were previously endorsed by Bernie Sanders. We should note your primary opponent was actually endorsed by Michigan Senator Elissa Slotkin, who previously held this seat. She is a moderate. You are a progressive. What does your win say about this district or about the party more broadly? William Lawrence: I think all the results last night show that the American people delivered a striking rebuke to the Trump agenda and are -- have delivered a mandate for change. We have got to get the prices down. We have got to protect the Affordable Care Act and reverse the cuts to Medicaid. We have got to pass a war powers resolution to end this war in Iran. And people also want to see us stop arming Israel, stop sending money to drop more bombs around the world when our neighbors here in Michigan can't afford basic housing and health care. And I see that similar message was delivered all over the country, and I'm thrilled to be part of this huge majority, and we got to be ready to go in January to pass bills through the House and the Senate to make folks' lives easier. Amna Nawaz: I hear you saying your priorities for wanting to bring prices down, which seems to be the number one reason people voted so broadly for Democrats wanting change. On the accountability front, if I can ask you, where do you think Democrats' priority should be? Where should you go first in oversight hearings or impeachment or some other step? William Lawrence: I think there will be various ideas about how to approach it. But we've got to end this... Amna Nawaz: What is your top priority? William Lawrence: I'm interested to have conversations with my colleagues. We have to put a stop to this elite impunity. I mean, we got to get the Epstein files released. That is one top priority. So there's a bill that it was introduced by Khanna and Massie that was just one signature shy on the discharge petition from getting a vote. We definitely have to vote that bill on the House floor. And when it comes to the rest of the president's corruption and that of his administration, we have to pursue oversight and hearings and accountability and do it in a way which makes sure that we're clear that this is about defending the rule of law and putting to an end this age of elite impunity that, frankly, both parties have been complicit in. So we got to make sure to do it the right way and not allow it to distract from the economic agenda, but we got to continue to defend our economy and our democracy walking hand in hand there. Amna Nawaz: That is Representative-elect William Lawrence from Michigan's Seventh Congressional District joining us tonight. Thank you so much for your time. William Lawrence: Thank you.

15045fda0d84.text: The election led to several historic firsts. In New Hampshire, Chris Pappas became the first openly gay man to be elected to the Senate. In Georgia, Keisha Lance Bottoms will be the first Black woman governor. And in New Mexico, Deb Haaland will make history as the first Native American woman to serve as a governor. Haaland joined Geoff Bennett to discuss more. Geoff Bennett: As have been reporting, yesterday's election brought a number of historic firsts. In New Hampshire, Chris Pappas became the first openly gay man elected to the U.S. Senate. In Colorado, Melat Kiros became the first Generation Z woman elected to Congress. And, in Georgia, Keisha Lance Bottoms became the first Black woman elected governor. Among those making history is Deb Haaland, who will become the first Native American woman to serve as governor of any U.S. state. Haaland previously served as interior secretary under President Biden and was one of the first Native American women elected to Congress. Governor-elect Deb Haaland joins us now. Congratulations on your victory and welcome back to the "News Hour." Deb Haaland: Thank you so much. Thank you. Geoff Bennett: You made history, of course, but voters are also expecting results. So how will you balance the symbolism of this victory with the responsibility now of governing a state that has faced persistent challenges? So many people are dealing with the high cost of living, persistent challenges with poverty, education, access to health care. How are you planning to deliver tangible results in New Mexico? Deb Haaland: Absolutely. Thank you so much for the question and for having me. And, of course, very proud to be the first Native American woman governor in the history of our country. That wasn't why I was running, though, of course. I have so much experience, having served at the highest level of government as the secretary of the interior, where I managed a work force of 70,000, an $18 billion annual budget. And, yes, like the rest of the country, our state is facing steep Medicaid cuts; 89,000 people can be kicked off the Medicaid rolls come the beginning of the year, people losing their SNAP benefits. This is all the result of the Trump bill that passed earlier this year. And so, of course, we want to make sure that we're stepping up, the legislature and myself continuing to fill in the gaps that our governor now has worked to fill in. We know that prices are getting higher due to so many of the tariffs and the war in Iran making gas prices higher. New Mexicans are paying higher costs for everything. And so we want to put more money in the pockets of New Mexicans, enhancing the child tax credit, the working families tax credit, continuing to move our clean energy forward, which we know will lower utility costs. So there's a lot of work to do, but I'm confident that we can get there. Geoff Bennett: Democrats had a strong election night across the country. How much of your victory, in your view, was a rejection of President Trump and his approach, and how much of it was an endorsement of your own vision for New Mexico? Deb Haaland: Thank you so much. Well, we currently have a Democratic governor here in New Mexico. Generally, every eight years -- our governor is termed out the end of this year. Every eight years, the seat flips back to Republican. And New Mexicans realized that yes, we needed to keep going on the trajectory that we are going on. We have universal childcare. We have early childhood education for every child in New Mexico. And those are things that New Mexicans feel have made their lives better. And so I want to ensure that we can enhance those programs, expand them across the state, so that every New Mexico family has an opportunity to participate. Universal childcare, it's an economic driver all over New Mexico. It creates jobs and helps parents to know their kids are safe while they're at work. So it's a win-win for our state and the people of New Mexico, and we will continue down that path. Geoff Bennett: Yes. I wonder, what have you learned from your time in Washington, both in Congress and in the Cabinet, about what government gets right and what it gets wrong, and how does all of that shape your approach to governing? Deb Haaland: Well, I will tell you, I feel like I always do the right thing when I listen to stakeholders, when I have the people at the table whose lives would be affected by the decisions that I make. I did that when I was at the Interior Department, and I will do it again. The most successful projects that we got across the finish line, transmission lines, offshore wind projects, protecting millions of acres of public lands across the country, that was all done with the idea that we need to bring people to the table early, that we should act with full transparency. So I intend to be transparent as the governor of New Mexico. I intend to bring stakeholders together to tell us what they need and what is best for their communities. New Mexico is different anywhere you go. None of our communities are the same, the northeast, the northwest, the north, the south, Central New Mexico. There's so many different communities with different needs. And so we're going to make sure that we're listening and that we can do what's best for our state. Geoff Bennett: Yes. I hear you when you say that you did not run for the sole goal of making history. But you have broken barriers before, as we mentioned, the first Native American woman -- among the first Native American women elected to Congress, the first Native American Cabinet secretary. Does this victory feel different, serving as governor? Deb Haaland: Well, I mean, look, this is my first successful statewide campaign. New Mexico's the fifth largest state, hundreds and hundreds, thousands of miles of rural roads that we drove on all throughout this campaign. So I feel like I worked really, really hard for this victory. We raised the funds to hire organizers. We had them on the ground a

c6efbf1bb649.text: President Trump has sought to deflect blame for the sweeping Republican losses. But within the party, some are beginning to ask whether they have been too deferential to the president — and whether the GOP needs to rethink its identity. Amna Nawaz discussed what comes next with David Holt, the Republican mayor of Oklahoma City. Amna Nawaz: President Trump has sought to deflect blame in last night's sweeping Republican losses. But within the party, some are beginning to ask whether they have been too deferential to the president and whether the GOP needs to rethink its identity. To discuss what comes next for Republicans, we're joined by David Holt. He's the Republican mayor of Oklahoma City. Mayor Holt, welcome back to the "News Hour." Thanks for joining us. David Holt: Absolutely. Thank you. Amna Nawaz: So it was a tough night for your party. You posted on X last night this message, writing: "A political party that's morally and intellectually bankrupt deserves the rebuke of the American people." It's very strong language. So what do you think Republicans could or should have done to avoid that rebuke, to mitigate some of those losses? David Holt: Well, how much time do you have? (LAUGHTER) David Holt: We 10 years ago as a party -- I wouldn't say I was a part of this decision and that -- or that I have gone along with it -- that we as a party ultimately ceded our decision-making and our intellectual capacity to one person and really became a cult of personality, instead of what we had been, at least for the remainder of my adult life, which was a party of ideas, a conventional American political party trying to bring together enough people to win an election and build a coalition. It changed 10 years ago. And so I don't think this was a -- like something we could have messaged better in the last two weeks. I mean, I think we made a fundamental decision to really not be the Republican Party anymore, but to be this banner carrier for Trumpism, for a specific individual and his whims and desires, and to be the MAGA party. And what happened last night was such a total rejection of Trumpism and MAGA that really that party now no longer exists as a functional political movement. Amna Nawaz: We should point out your state of Oklahoma was one of the few bright spots for Republicans, right? You still control the governorship, both Senate seats, all five congressional seats. So if this was a referendum on the president, what do those results tell you about where Oklahoma is? David Holt: You're correct. I mean, the Republican nominee for governor did win in Oklahoma last night, but certainly the writing was on the wall that something was shifting even in Oklahoma, maybe not enough to shift all the way over to exchange control. But I have often pointed out, I mean, I'm a student of politics in my part of the country, and Oklahoma always follows Texas a few years later. We did in the '90s and in the 2000s, and so anyone who doesn't take pretty serious lesson from what happened last night in Texas in my neck of the woods is just living on borrowed time, because that's going to happen in Oklahoma. Oklahomans, Texans, Americans, they're ready to move into a different kind of conversation. And they still want, in my view, a center-right party, and this country needs a center-right conservative party. But people are wanting a normal party that's competent, that's talking about the real priorities that are in front of us, the real challenges and opportunities that are in front of us. And, ultimately, that's just not what was being offered. The MAGA movement had exhausted itself. Amna Nawaz: If there is one thing you want to see from your party and party leadership right now that you think could be some kind of a course correction, what's that first step? David Holt: Well, we have to return to being a political party again with a platform and ideas, and we have to be serious. I mean, too much of what you have seen from Republican governance the last few years is really seemed geared more towards entertainment. And we need -- this isn't professional wrestling. This is governance. So we have to be serious. We have to be talking about pocketbook issues, not reflecting pools and arches. We have to be meeting people where they are. I mean, I don't think this is going to be like some quick turnaround. I think this is going to be a multiyear conversation, but it finally began last night, and it needed to. And this country needs two real parties. And I think we're finally going to -- we're finally going to have that conversation that we have needed to have really for the better part of a decade. Amna Nawaz: That is the Republican mayor of Oklahoma City, David Holt, joining us tonight. Mayor Holt, thank you for your time. It's good to speak with you. David Holt: Likewise. Thank you.

2fbcaae40fad.text: A major factor in the midterm elections was the number of Latino voters who headed to the polls and supported Democrats. For perspective on this massive swing, Amna Nawaz spoke with María Teresa Kumar, CEO of Voto Latino, an organization that helps register Hispanic and Latino voters. Geoff Bennett: As we have heard tonight, a major factor in last night's victories were the number of Latino voters who headed to the polls and supported Democrats. Amna Nawaz: For perspective on this massive swing, we turn now to Maria Teresa Kumar. She's CEO of Voto Latino. That's an organization that helps register Hispanic and Latino voters. Good to see you. Thanks for being here. Maria Teresa Kumar, Founder and Executive Director, Voto Latino: Thanks for having us. Amna Nawaz: So Amy mentioned earlier, of course, that there was the shift we saw from 2024 to 2026. We should also just say, to be clear, Latinos are not a monolith. But how do you look at that and what's behind the people who backed Trump in '24 and went Democrat -- Democratic in '26? Maria Teresa Kumar: So it's -- folks are absolutely right. Latinos are not a monolith until you come for our families. And that's basically what we saw last night. It was a repudiation of the ICE raids that have been happening. I can tell you that I can go around the country and there's not a Latino, whether they work in Wall Street or they work in the fields, that don't know someone that's been caught in the dragnet. You marry that with the fact that financially they're not doing well; 36 percent of Latinas that we surveyed in April were skipping meals. All of a sudden, you realize that there is an opportunity for the Democrats to have a real conversation with them that is not talking about who is and isn't an American. What Amy was talking about, I think, is really important. I think it's something that both the Republicans and the Democrats need to take note, is that the Latino vote, because they are so young -- they're about a generation-and-a-half younger than the rest of the American voter. They are oftentimes considered very much independent, but the swingiest of swing voters because they don't have a history of voting even among their families. And so they are very issue-driven. And if you promise that you're going to basically provide for them to be able to actually stretch that dollar, then they will listen to you. But at the same time, if you start criminalizing them, then you're going to see what happened last night. Amna Nawaz: I want to talk to you about Texas in particular, basically a 30-year grip by Republicans broken last night. You have the first Latino governor in the state in Gina Hinojosa. You have the Democrat, James Talarico, winning the Senate race there. How do you look at Latino participation in those races? And generationally also, what are the trends you're seeing in Texas? Maria Teresa Kumar: So, Voto, I tell you, we started investing in Texas almost three cycles ago because we recognized that 54 percent of the kids in classrooms were young Latinos. And when you go down to the Rio Grande Valley, it is one of the poorest zip codes of people who are incredibly resilient. And when they flipped from left to right, it was because of the flood of immigrants coming across the border that was creating real chaos in their communities, and they were having a hard time stretching that dollar. So they took a chance on Trump. And what Trump did was overstep. I spent a lot of time with in the Rio Grande Valley, and I was talking to folks that were -- that voted very heavily for Trump and said, look, I'm a builder. It used to cost me $300 to do a square foot. Now it cost me $630 for a square foot because they're deporting my men. And because of the tariffs, we can't actually be able -- we can't actually try to figure out how to plan for our job, for the work that needs to happen. But I do think that the headline is, is that young Latinos showed up. And, again, when we talk about this idea of affordability versus immigration, for young Latinos, this is where we're going to see a generational shift. For young Latinos, it was absolutely to protect their parents. Amna Nawaz: When you look at this broader picture, this is the question we're asking again and again, do you feel like these votes were solely against President Trump? Or was there something also going for Democrats here? Maria Teresa Kumar: The candidate quality in Texas specifically was through the roof. Gina Hinojosa is from the Valley. Something that I -- when -- during the 2024 campaign that I often reminded the Harris campaign, neither Harris nor Biden went down to the border. Vance and Trump were there all the time. They did the retail politics so well this last week that their closing arguments were all along the Valley. If you look at who swung the most, who in Texas, when you look at the map of all the blue, it was all the southern border of Texas. And it proves the point. This was a community that has been long overlooked, but once you recognize them and you gave them something to vote for, they came out in force. Amna Nawaz: So what do you think Democrats have to do now? They have two years to try to make good on some of the promises that they made. What can they do? What should they prioritize for these voters that they have won back to make sure they don't lose them again? Maria Teresa Kumar: So, Amna, in August, we actually asked this very question, and we came up with a pothole agenda. Latino voters are looking for accountability on ICE, they're demanding for a pathway to citizenship and for the Democrats to say that out loud, and they're trying to figure out economic relief. Talk about SNAP benefits. Talk about raising the minimum wage. Talk about how you actually can identify their taxes, and, believe it or not, how do you actually create term limits for the Supreme Court? That's all top of mind. Amna Nawaz: Maria Teresa Kumar, CEO of Voto Latino, thank you so much for bein

7c90d1378b2a.text: For perspective on how both parties are responding to the historic election wins, Geoff Bennett spoke with two strategists from both sides of the political aisle. Mo Elleithee is the former spokesman for the Democratic National Committee, and Doug Heye is a former spokesman for the Republican National Committee. Amna Nawaz: Well, for perspective now on how both parties are responding to last night's historic wins, we're joined by two strategists from both sides of the political aisle. Geoff Bennett: That is Mo Elleithee, Democratic strategist and former spokesperson for the Democratic National Committee, and Doug Heye, a Republican strategist and former spokesperson for the Republican National Committee. Good to see you, gentlemen. Doug Heye: Thank you. Geoff Bennett: So, Mo, Democrats didn't just win. They won in places, in states and districts that Republicans thought were safe. What did Democrats get right in this cycle and what can they replicate in election seasons beyond this Trump era? Mo Elleithee: Yes. So we talked about this a little bit last night. My party isn't always the best at message discipline. But this cycle, boy, were they solidly on message. Candidate after candidate, the most progressive to the most moderate, from Kansas and Texas to Maine and Michigan, every Democratic candidate was talking about cost of living and corruption, and, in many cases, tying those two things together. All cycle long, Donald Trump did what Donald Trump does, just tossed out a bunch of crazy. And we usually chase it. We usually take the bait. We didn't this time. We stayed focused, and the results showed that. Geoff Bennett: And looking at the scale of the losses, was any of this avoidable for Republicans, or was the environment just too politically toxic? Doug Heye: The environment was too toxic. And, ultimately, if it were going to be avoidable, Trump would have had to be the one to avoid it by telling voters, here's what's important that we're doing for you, not here's what I'm doing that's important to me. So every time he talked about building an arch or reconstructing the East Wing or something about the Kennedy Center, all these things that voters don't really care about, especially when they're going through so much in their lives, is a real -- was a challenge to every Republican on the ballot. And I always start with my home state of North Carolina. Here's the most interesting thing to me about it, is that we have all seen the big losses, right? You have lost the General Assembly. The state Senate is still in question. So many Republican members have lost, and we're still counting ballots. But there were three constitutional amendments on the state ballot last night. All three were fairly conservative. One was voter I.D., and then two were about constitutional amendments limiting and capping taxes on property and income. Those three passed was 60 percent of the vote. So people voted for these conservative initiatives and then voted against every Republican that they could up and down the ballot to send that message to Trump. Geoff Bennett: To include Richard Hudson from North Carolina, who has the job of getting Republicans reelected across the country, congressional Republicans. He also lost his seat. Doug Heye: Sure. And the dean of the delegation, Virginia Foxx, who's the chair of the House Rules Committee, my member of Congress, right now is behind by 99 votes. They will go to a recount, but that's not an optimistic place to be in. Geoff Bennett: The vice president, J.D. Vance, was pretty blunt today. He's saying that the war in Iran was the reason Republicans lost. Here's the tweet. He says: "The reason we lost is the war. The president himself said so last night. If you would like to argue it was worth it, that losing the Senate for the next six years was worth it, then do so." What do you make of those comments? Mo Elleithee: J.D. Vance is -- has got some real challenges moving forward. The guy clearly wants to be president. He wants to be the Republican nominee. And his entire party got wiped out because of his boss and him. So he's -- really interesting to see him try to put some distance between himself and the war. And look, in fairness, J.D. Vance, it's been reported, wasn't for the war in the beginning. But I don't know that voters who repudiated this administration are going to see that, right? They're repudiating Trump/Vance. He's partly right. It's partly the war, but it is also the long litany of broken promises that both Donald Trump and J.D. Vance have made. It is, as Maria Teresa was talking about, the inhumanity that we saw in the streets. And, remember, just days ago, when Vivek Ramaswamy put out that terrible ad in Ohio that was repudiated by both parties, J.D. Vance was the first guy to go into the state and hug it and embrace it and chastise the Republicans who were complaining about it. So J.D. Vance is going to have a hard couple of weeks trying to figure out how to position himself. Geoff Bennett: And President Trump, his midterm closing argument was at the Reflecting Pool, as you mentioned. Today, the morning after his party sustained these major losses, he was at the site of his reconstructed -- or in the process of being rebuilt here, this -- this future White House ballroom. What does that choice tell you about how the president is processing these results and whether he's prepared or has a willingness to pivot? Doug Heye: Well, it's not where we would want him to be consistent with his messaging, but he's been consistent that what is important to him as a priority of building things is somehow going to be important to voters throughout the country, and it just hasn't been. And if we were having this conversation and there were no Iran war, or we're having it the day before it started, what would we be talking about? Grocery prices. We would be talking about gas prices, that everything is too expensive. So was the war in Iran a contributor? Absolute

87ffc4a0a839.text: Republicans woke up "in shock" Wednesday morning after they got hit with the biggest midterms wave in 50 years. Within hours, that shock was turning into rage. Why it matters: The battle for control of what's left of the Republican conference — headlined by Majority Leader Steve Scalise (R-La.) and Judiciary Chair Jim Jordan (R-Oho) — is the first salvo in a quest to bring GOP lawmakers back from the political wilderness. Johnson set the tone Wednesday morning, when he took himself out of the running for leader, citing the toll the job has taken on his family. A key outstanding question is the extent to which Republican finger-pointing leads to a wholesale shake-up of the party's leadership ranks, versus a slight readjustment. Driving the news: The intra-party blame game quickly hit a fever pitch. "Dear Republican Senate and House "Leadership," No, the polls were not wrong. You were. Even with record amounts of money at your disposal, you managed to get absolutely annihilated," Rep. Greg Steube (R-Fla.) wrote on X Wednesday morning. "Please do us all a favor and step aside so new leadership can take a truly conservative direction," Steube added. "When you have the worst defeat in modern history, you need a new playbook," another GOP lawmaker told Axios. State of play: The fallout is rippling across the entire House GOP leadership team, with every top position facing a contested race. Minority leader: Scalise and Jordan are squaring off in a rematch of their bitter 2023 battle for the speakership. Minority whip: Tom Emmer faces a challenge from Rep. August Pfluger (R-Texas). NRCC Chair: Rudy Yakym and Brian Jack will face off for the post. Current NRCC Chairman Richard Hudson (R-N.C.) is on track to lose his own reelection bid. Zoom in: Behind the leadership infighting, Republicans are reckoning with what went so disastrously wrong on Election Day, with some blaming the Trump administration's policies for their losses. "Iran, Iran, Iran ... we should have never done the war before the midterms," one GOP lawmaker told Axios. Another pointed to "Iran, ICE, inflation, fuel prices, lack of focus on pocketbook issues" as factors in the defeat. "Iran and the vanity of putting your name on things like the Kennedy Center," another GOP lawmaker said. What's next: House Republicans are scheduled to elect their next leadership team this coming Tuesday. The winner needs a majority of House Republicans in a secret-ballot vote.

Six people have died after a large fire broke out in a residential building in Brooklyn, New York City, officials say.
Several others were hurt in the blaze, which occurred early on Thursday morning, the New York City Fire Department (FDNY) said in a statement.
More than 230 fire and emergency medical personnel were sent to the scene near Sunset Park after the fire was first reported at around 01:40 local time (06:40 GMT).
Mayor Zohran Mamdani said he was "heartbroken" by the deaths, and has asked New Yorkers to "take a moment to pray for the full recovery of those who were injured".
The cause of the blaze is being investigated.
A crew specialising in hazardous materials was sent to the scene because of the presence of a lithium-ion battery, although it was not clear whether this was linked to the blaze.
The emergency responders reportedly discovered on their arrival that the building's first and second floors had been engulfed by flames.
Four individuals were pronounced dead at the scene, according to the FDNY.
A male and female were also taken to the hospital, where they were pronounced dead, the New York City Police Department (NYPD) said.
Six other civilians were injured, two of them critically, along with three firefighters, the FDNY said.

A investigation is underway after "a major fish kill" in a County Down river, the Department for Agriculture, Environment and Rural Affairs (Daera) has confirmed.
The pollution caused the death of brown and migratory sea trout in the Gransha, Ballystockart and Inler (also known as Enler) Rivers.
Glenn McKibbin, the secretary of Inler Angling Club, said about 1,000 fish were killed in the incident and it "could not have happened in a worse location on the river or at a worse time".
The Northern Ireland Environment Agency (NIEA) and Daera Inland Fisheries are working to "identify the source of the pollution and to finalise the numbers of fish killed".
The Department said the incident was reported by a member of the public on Tuesday at 09:30 GMT.
Fish stocks 'obliterated'
McKibbin said that "current and future fish stocks obliterated for years to come".
He added that resident and non-resident migratory fish, which only return at this of year to spawn, have been impacted.
"Knock-on effects for other wildlife such as resident kingfishers, herons & otters unavoidable.
"For our members and volunteers who work tirelessly in a bid to improve the river this is soul-destroying, particularly as the river was still in recovery from major pollution incidents / fish kills in 2013 and 2015," McKibbin said.
"Waterways up and down the country continue to be treated like sewers.
"The paltry fines that usually follow incidents of this nature are not a deterrent and the current 'system' is broken."
Many migratory fish, such as trout and salmon, swim up smaller tributaries to lay their eggs in cleaner, gravel-bottomed, or cooler waters away from larger predators in the main river.
A tributary is a smaller river that flows into a larger mainstem river where many migratory fish, such as trout and salmon, swim up to lay their eggs away from larger predators in the main river.
Inler Angling Club Chairperson David Pyper said: "For those who dedicate so much time and effort to caring for the river, witnessing the sheer loss of fish in circumstances such as these is particularly disappointing.
"The club hopes that the forthcoming investigations will establish the cause of this latest incident and help ensure appropriate steps are taken to protect the river and its wildlife."
The club has encouraged local representatives and authorities to continue to prioritise rivers and direct resources towards improving water quality and preventing further incidents.

Protests are taking place across France after five unions launched a national day of strike action, joining high school students and demonstrators criticising the rising cost of living.
More than 250,000 people had taken to the streets in almost 70 towns and cities by 13:00 (12:00 GMT) on Thursday, and that was "just the start", said Sophie Binet of the CGT union.
The unions have vowed to take the wave of protests that began in September over poor conditions and resources at lycÃ©es (high schools) "to the next level".
They have since spread to include workers and the so-called "yellow-vest" movement against high prices.
Interior Minister Laurent NuÃ±ez said 70,000 police were being deployed, vowing "an extremely firm response" to any potential outbreaks of violence.
Some unrest has been reported in the cities of Lyon and Rennes.
A car was set alight near the Gallieni bridge over the RhÃ´ne river in central Lyon, as hundreds of people belonging to the radical left-wing "black bloc" clashed with police.
Meanwhile, there were clashes in the north-western city of Rennes, where the local prefect said a "hostile group of masked individuals" had gathered in front of the main union march.
The five unions have combined forces across the public and private sector, announcing more than 250 separate actions as part of their campaign for higher wages to combat the cost of living and protect public services.
Binet told reporters at the start of a march in central Paris that protesters had "just reached a new level in their mobilisation" and were demanding immediate answers.
Disruption was reported in schools, hospitals and public transport, and the Eiffel Tower and some exhibition rooms at the Louvre museum in Paris had to close.
Workers were also asked to halt production at oil refineries and France was expected to import more electricity than it produced on Thursday because of disruption at nuclear plants.
A coalition of unions has urged workers, pensioners and young people to join Thursday's day of strikes to intensify pressure on the government. In particular they are seeking a rise in the minimum wage, or Smic, which is currently â¬12.31 (Â£10) an hour.
The head of the CFDT union, Marylise LÃ©on, complained that it was not just the minimum wage that needed to increase: "We are asking for a net increase of â¬100 a month."
The government has sought to appease public anger over rising prices, bringing down the cost of fuel by releasing 10 million barrels of diesel from strategic reserves. Ministers have also promised school students to reform the unpopular Parcoursup university admissions platform and eventually replace it by 2028.
The education ministry said that 16% of teachers had gone on strike, and the unions said disruption had affected more than one in four lycÃ©es, which cater for 15-18 year-olds, as well as the vast majority of universities.
Large numbers are expected on the streets, especially in the capital, and the CFDT leader said she would be happy if 800,000 people turned out.
Meanwhile, a revived gilets jaunes (yellow-vest) movement that staged a revolt against the high cost of living several years ago has called for further blockades and protests on Friday and Saturday too.
Union leaders have complained that recent marches have been kept away from the centre of Paris, because of violence that broke out in towns and cities on 17 October and led to more than 2,000 stores being looted and historic buildings being set on fire.
Thursday's march was eventually allowed in central Paris, although not along the route proposed by the unions between Place de la Bastille and Place de la Concorde, which would have taken protesters near the National Assembly, the ÃlysÃ©e Palace, and the prime minister's residence at HÃ´tel Matignon.
Instead, the march was set to follow another central route from Place de la RÃ©publique to Place de la Nation. The CFDT union complained that getting court approval for the route only on Wednesday evening made organising the march more difficult.
The last big mobilisation at the weekend passed off with relatively little violence, and the interior minister said the police deployment would be on a similar scale on Thursday. NuÃ±ez has spoken of three potential risks on Thursday, from radical left "black blocs" groups and looting to wildcat marches without union authorisation.

AI companies are racing to lock down clients in the oil industry. A deal announced Monday between ADNOC and OpenAI was the highest-profile example in a broader push at ADIPEC by tech companies to pitch bespoke, AI-driven tools to help operate drilling rigs, refineries, and other oil assets.
Thanks to the breakneck evolution of frontier AI models, âWeâre now really seeing the technology mature to the level where it will make a significant change in the operating processes within the sector,â said Dan Jeavons, president of UK-based Applied Computing. The company, which counts numerous veterans of Shell and other producers on its staff, uses AI to process millions of data points coming from sensors inside oil infrastructure and help the operator work more efficiently, identify malfunctions faster, and reduce emissions. Competition in this space is heating up; last week Honeywell Technologies launched an AI platform at the new Dangote refinery in Nigeria.

After months of war-related belt-tightening by global oil and gas companies, the makers of bolts, pumps, and other widgets for the industry are beginning to see sales pick up. ADIPEC is first and foremost a trade show, with hundreds of vendors selling every imaginable tool and piece of equipment, from simple screwdrivers to entire offshore drilling platforms. Even when oil prices surged, oilfield equipment vendors â which constitute a $250 billion global market â didnât often benefit, since most production companies moved to defend their balance sheets rather than rush to drill more.
Now business is looking up again: âIn the past month or two, thereâs been a surge in orders, and all of them are very urgent,â said Deleen Laxamana, an administrator for hardware producer PressBolt. âPeople are spending money again,â added Shawn Sharp, vice president of Texas International, which manufactures giant wrenches used for manipulating pipes. One hot new product flying off the shelves: drones, which oil companies are snapping up to monitor equipment and deliver supplies offshore.

Democrat Scott Colom and Republican incumbent Cindy Hyde-Smith are locked in a tight race for a US Senate seat in Mississippi, a state that has not elected a Democratic candidate to the upper chamber in more than 40 years.
With 96% of votes counted as of Thursday morning, Colom was leading by just over 1,000 votes.
Hyde-Smith, the first woman to represent Mississippi in the US Congress, was elected in 2018 and has been endorsed by Donald Trump. The president won the state by more than 22 points in 2024.
If Colom wins the race, he would be the first black US senator elected in Mississippi since 1875.
Both campaigns projected confidence as the count continued.
"We remain confident that when every legally cast vote is fully and accurately counted, Mississippians will have reelected Cindy Hyde-Smith," the incumbent's campaign said in a statement.
The Democrat's campaign had an "army of lawyers" working to ensure the count continued "ensure the process is followed according to the law," Colom said on Wednesday.
"I am very happy with where we stand," Colom said. "I'm confident once the process plays out, where we are, where the ballots are, we're gonna win."
Counting continues in the Mississippi race after Democrats won control of both chambers of Congress, scoring victories in deep red states such as South Carolina, Texas and Kansas, which had not elected Democratic senators in decades.
The Democratic Party had sent extra funding to the Mississippi race in recent weeks, seeing an unexpected opportunity to flip the seat.
Senate Minority Leader Chuck Schumer has dispatched extra legal and campaign resources to the state as the count continues, Punchbowl news reported.
Hyde-Smith led the race early on with about 30% of votes counted, but as more ballots were processed, Colom started to gain a small edge over his opponent.
Mississippi does not have automatic recounts for tight races or allow candidates to request recounts. The state also allows mail-in ballots to be counted if they are postmarked by Election Day and received within five business days later.
About 3,600 absentee ballots remained outstanding as of Wednesday, Mississippi Secretary of State Michael Watson said in a statement.
Several thousand affidavit ballots also remained outstanding, according to Colom. Voters can cast these ballots at polling sites if they say they are eligible but do not appear on the rolls or there is another issue. Election officials then set them aside for extra verification.
That means the race is very likely not to be called until at least 10 November, said Julie Wronski, an associate professor of political science at the University of Mississippi.
"Because the difference between the two candidates is so narrow, really, we're going to have to wait for every single vote received in any capacity to be counted," Wronski said.
On the campaign trail, Colom, a district attorney, focused his message on his Christian faith and plans to address economic concerns. He took aim at Trump's policies including the war in Iran and the rising cost of living in the US.
Wronski said Hyde-Smith, who was appointed to the role in 2018 to fill a vacancy, ran a mostly lacklustre campaign, relying on the state's reliably conservative base to deliver.
"The lack of public appearances was quite striking," Wronski added.
Trump campaigned alongside Hyde-Smith last month, saying he was there "because Cindy's doing great, but I just got to make sure. I can't take a chance".
Mississippi is a state home to the largest percentage of African Americans in the US, at nearly 40%, a group that overwhelmingly votes Democratic and reportedly showed up in large numbers this election.
Charles Taylor, director of the NAACP's Mississippi branch, told the BBC his organisation saw a huge swell in black voter participation leading into Election Day.
"We saw long lines for absentee voting," Taylor said. "We saw long lines in person yesterday. Folks everywhere were motivated across the state."
"So, when the data comes back, I think it's going to tell a story that black voters turned out and turned out big."
Colom told the Washington Post, external in October that Democrats had not typically done well in Mississippi because large wins from Republicans in recent years led them to direct resources elsewhere.
In 2020, Democrats threw their support behind Mike Espy, a former US secretary of agriculture who they believed had captured momentum, but he lost to Hyde-Smith by a wide margin.
National Democrats are "conditioned not to care about Mississippi", Colom told the outlet. "To me, you can't be a party that cares about working people if you don't care about working rural people in Mississippi who are struggling."

Tuesdayâs Democratic sweep shook the energy stock market, boosting clean energy company shares on the expectation of a more renewables-friendly Congress and casting a pall on oil.
Solar companies First Solar and SunRun both rose around 8%; wind companies Orsted and Vestas, and the EV makers Lucid and Rivian also rallied. Chevron and ExxonMobil fell, meanwhile, weighed by the prospect of lower oil prices if Democrats push for a quicker end to the war in Iran. And the likelihood that new state and local-level Democratic leaders could impose restrictions on data center development weighed on companies riding the AI energy demand boom, including fuel cell battery maker Bloom Energy and gas turbine maker GE Vernova.
A Democrat-led Congress is likely to push to resurface tax benefits for renewables, and to push to reinstate other forms of Congressionally allocated clean energy funding. Still, the initial market reactions may overstate how much will change under a split government, TD Cowenâs John Miller told Semafor: Democratic infighting could impede the passage of permitting reform legislation, and pro-renewables legislation is vulnerable to Trumpâs veto.

958acc1e845a.text:
Before Tuesday’s election, Republicans held more governorships and state legislative seats than Democrats, along with an advantage in state trifectas—unified control of the governor’s office and both chambers of the legislature.
That advantage has disappeared, clearing the path for more climate and clean energy legislation, according to analysts and advocates.
Democrats swept the vast majority of competitive races at the state level, flipping control of governors’ offices from Republicans in Georgia, Iowa, Ohio, Nevada and Texas.
Democrats have a 29-19 edge in governorships, with Kansas too close to call and Alaska likely to take a while to declare a winner.
The party is on track for a net gain of hundreds of legislative seats, potentially giving it control of more nationwide than Republicans for the first time in more than a decade. Going into the election, Republicans had 4,072 seats and Democrats held 3,257, according to MultiState, a research and lobbying firm. Democrats had a net gain of more than 350 seats on Tuesday and are likely to add several hundred more as results continue to be tabulated, according to MultiState.
Democrats won five new trifectas: Michigan, Minnesota, Nevada, Pennsylvania and Wisconsin, with Arizona likely to be the sixth once officials finish counting. Those additions would give the party 22 trifectas, with Republicans holding unified control in 18 states and nine with split control. Kansas is yet to be determined.
Republicans lost trifectas in Iowa, Georgia, Texas, New Hampshire and Ohio. Before the election, Republicans had trifectas in 23 states, Democrats had 16 and 11 were under split control.
The implications for climate and energy policy are likely to be profound, said Caroline Spears, executive director of Climate Cabinet, an advocacy group.
“In the states, we had a generational political window shift to make people’s lives better, to lower costs and to lower climate pollution at the same time,” she said in a conference call.
This was the “affordability election” with concerns about inflation and high energy prices, she said.
Newly elected lawmakers will enter office with energy policy proposals to address voter concerns, she said. She noted that renewable energy is less expensive than fossil fuels and can be developed quickly, promising rapid benefits for consumers. The growth of electric transportation reduces greenhouse gas emissions and shields consumers from the volatility of gasoline and diesel, she said.
Jay Inslee, former Democratic governor of Washington and a prominent advocate for climate and clean energy policies, urged lawmakers to seize this opportunity.
Inslee took a jab at President Donald Trump, calling him the election’s clear loser, even though he wasn’t on the ballot.
“The chief climate denier got his head handed to him,” Inslee said.
John Farrell, co-director of the Institute for Local Self-Reliance, a research and advocacy nonprofit, said in an interview that he is excited to see what comes next with the new trifectas.
“There is this growing sense that more accountability measures are needed in order to rein in [utility] rates, and that utility companies are central to that problem,” he said.
Farrell sees an opportunity for Wisconsin to catch up with neighboring states that have already established climate and clean energy agendas. He’s pleased that Democrats’ legislative majorities in Minnesota are large enough to give the party leeway to propose more ambitious policies. In Michigan, he is encouraged by residents calling for publicly owned utilities and pushing back against the influence of large utilities.
This story is funded by readers like you.
Our nonprofit newsroom provides award-winning climate coverage free of charge and advertising. We rely on donations from readers like you to keep going. Please donate now to support our work.
Donate Now
In the past, Farrell might have worried that utilities would stave off consumer-friendly policies by showering newly elected Democrats with campaign donations. But he thinks scenarios like this are less likely now because the public is wary of candidates they view as puppets for large companies. And some candidates have shown it’s possible to win without accepting money from utilities.
“We’re in a moment right now where there is enough scrutiny to make it harder for that sort of check-writing strategy to be successful,” he said.
More on the six states that attained trifectas or are on track to do so:
Arizona: Democratic Gov. Katie Hobbs cruised to re-election and her party was on track to win majorities in the state House and Senate, although officials are still counting ballots in many races. Analysts said a Democratic trifecta is likely based on available results.
Michigan: Democrat Jocelyn Benson, Michigan’s secretary of state, won the governor’s race. Democrats expanded their majority in the state Senate and gained a majority in the state House, with some races still being counted.
Minnesota: Democratic U.S. Sen. Amy Klobuchar was elected governor by a wide margin. The party expanded its majority in the state Senate and turned an even split with Republicans in the state House into a comfortable majority, with counting still underway.
Nevada: Democrat Aaron Ford, the state attorney general, defeated the incumbent Republican governor, Joe Lombardo. Democrats also retained control of the state House and Senate.
Wisconsin: Democrat David Crowley, the Milwaukee County executive, was elected governor. Democrats flipped control of both chambers of the Legislature, with an 18-15 majority in the state Senate and a 53-46 majority in the state House.
Pennsylvania: Democratic Gov. Josh Shapiro easily won re-election. His party gained a 26-24 majority in the state Senate and expanded its majority in the state House to 111-88, with four races still being counted.

eb38cf964cb2.text: Democrats' blowout win further complicates the fraught path to passing a permitting deal in the lame duck. Why it matters: Cutting hurdles for projects is a top priority for fossil fuels and renewables sectors. But critics argue the Senate plan unacceptably weakens environmental protections and tribal input. The big picture: Dems' looming control of Congress "worsens the outlook" for the bill this year, the advisory firm Capstone said in a note. The firm sees Democrats as "further emboldened" to punt the bill into 2027. President "Trump is likely to put pressure on House Republicans to support the package, but with his standing diminished in the wake of the midterms, his political capital may be limited," it states. Analysts with Jefferies also see reduced odds of lame duck support for a package that makes it easier to build gas pipelines. Yes, but: The bipartisan bill's Democratic co-authors argued on Wednesday that now remains the time, with Sen. Sheldon Whitehouse (D-R.I.) calling it a "bird in the hand" and saying "we'd be fools not to take it." "Democrats ran and won on affordability, and this bill lowers costs for families and will allow us to start delivering on our election promises," he said in a statement. State of play: Rapidan Energy Group now sees a 20%-25% chance in the lame duck, down from 30% pre-election. Yet Rapidan's rather bullish on a permitting deal with Trump in 2027-2028. That challenges the view of many bill supporters who see a fleeting opening right now. Rapidan's logic: Trump struck first-term deals with Dems on the debt limit, government funding and more — at times against the will of GOP congressional leaders. "Democrats need only five or six Republican votes to reach 60 on a bill Republicans helped write, and Trump's first-term precedent ... suggests he may be willing to make deals with Democrats to reduce the veto risk," their note states. Catch up quick: TD Cowen analysts quickly dropped their assessment of lame duck passage from 40% to 25%, while the firm ClearView Energy Partners also argues that Dems' bicameral win could weaken the prospects. What they're saying: American Clean Power Association head Jason Grumet told reporters on Wednesday the bill reflects voters' interest in cheaper energy. "I think that the understanding in Congress is that this is a really unique opportunity, and if you don't move forward in the next three or four weeks, it's hard to imagine a bipartisan effort over the next couple of years," said Grumet, whose group represents renewables, storage and transmission companies. The other side: Rep. Jared Huffman (D-Calif.), who is likely to helm the Natural Resources Committee, is arguing that Democrats should show that the days of Trump's "supplicant Senate" are over. Huffman, who wants to wait until next year, said Dems should demand hearings and amendments on the bill he currently opposes. The bottom line: The White House is still pushing for lame duck action, but did not directly say whether it would be open to a deal on an altered bill next year. "The White House supports the bipartisan deal worked out between Republicans and Democrats and agrees that the time to get permitting reform done is now," a White House official said. Amy Harder contributed reporting. Sign up here for Axios' Future of Energy newsletter.

HPâs new chief executive, Emma Walmsley, is the latest in a parade of CEOs who have done the job before. Nearly 30% of incoming S&P 500 CEOs over the past year had already been a chief executive, double the historical average, according to data from Russell Reynolds.
Many are switching industries, too, as companies favor experience over expertise. Walmsley spent nearly nine years running drugmaker GSK before HP tapped her to steer the PC maker through a memory-chip crunch. She fills the seat Enrique Lores vacated in February to run PayPal, whose longtime boss Dan Schulman now runs Verizon. Lucid poached Silvio Napoli from elevator maker Schindler.
Chalk it up to a contagious case of retired-CEO-itis, perhaps, but the job itself has also changed. Sector expertise matters less than outward-facing skills: navigating tariffs, export controls, and an unpredictable Washington. âSomeone whoâs âbeen-there-done-thatâ gives boards a sense of security, regardless of the industry,â Constantine Alexandrakis, who runs CEO search firm Russell Reynolds, tells Semafor.

39d9b210e83f.text:
Matthewâs view
For decades, Gulf oil and gas companies boasted of their reliability. But recent deals point to a new recognition: The region can no longer guarantee energy security for the world. Instead, Gulf producers will spend the next decade investing internationally, enmeshing themselves in global energy supply chains so the region is ready when the next disruptions hit.
In the early days of the Iran conflict, as oil shipments through the Strait of Hormuz virtually ground to a halt, their focus was on rerouting. New pipelines, railways, and ports were discussed as ways to get around the chokepoint.
Saudi Arabiaâs East-West pipeline proved to be a crucial lifeline, both for energy markets and the kingdomâs financial health, as did Abu Dhabiâs pipeline to Fujairah. Both are now being expanded. But as Houthi attacks on the Saudi pipeline have shown, Plan B isnât enough. The problem isnât just a couple of narrow waterways, itâs the inability to ensure the security of Gulf energy facilities in a crisis.
This yearâs conflict has shown the relative ease with which cheap drones can slip past some of the worldâs most expensive air defense systems and hit pipelines, ports, and ships. Pouring billions more into new pipelines may achieve little more than creating a longer target list and spreading defensive systems more thinly. The outcome of the US midterms makes it more likely the Iran conflict remains unresolved from the Gulfâs perspective â with President Donald Trump possibly facing constraints on his ability to pursue âfinish-the-jobâ strikes and a track record of failed diplomacy that may not get any better faced with Iranâs famously tough negotiators. That ensures fundamental animosity in the region will continue to fester.
But even if the Iran war is settled today â bringing to an end Houthi threats to shipping through the Bab el-Mandeb Strait and Iranian attacks on shipping through the Strait of Hormuz â the Gulfâs reputation as a reliable supplier of oil and gas has been irreparably damaged.
To avoid losing market share, the Gulf is readying itself for when instability next hits.
QatarEnergy is buying up international LNG shipments as a hedge against any future closure of the Strait of Hormuz. Abu Dhabi had already launched an international investment plan before the war and is now accelerating its ambitions.
Saudi Arabiaâs latest deal, to store oil in underground caves in Singapore, may not be big enough to sway global markets. But it, too, is a statement of intent â in this case to build reserve capabilities around the world, ready for a worst-case scenario.
Expect to see many more similar deals in the months ahead. Unable to ensure the security of domestic infrastructure, Gulf energy companies will increasingly hedge by going global.

2db34d5b79cb.text:
Jihadâs view
Resilience or luck? At the recent IMF-World Bank Annual Meetings in Bangkok, this question was on every policymakerâs mind. There were good reasons for relief: despite a succession of shocks, the global economy had held up better than many feared. So too has the Middle East and North Africa.
When hostilities erupted in the Gulf at the end of February, provoking the largest oil and energy shock in history, many feared the regionâs economies would be overwhelmed: Shipping lanes would close, energy prices would soar, and the more vulnerable economies would struggle to stay afloat. Eight months later, those worst fears have not materialized. Activity has slowed sharply in some places, but it has not collapsed. In many economies, it has continued to expand.
Economies have adjusted, while existing buffers and policy responses have helped absorb the shock. But pressures are building, particularly in import-dependent, low-income, and fragile states.
The IMFâs latest Regional Economic Outlook for the Middle East and Central Asia projects output in the Middle East and North Africa to contract by 1.3% in 2026, 2.7 percentage points below our April forecast. Yet that headline figure conceals considerable differences in a region that spans more than 20 countries.
Several Gulf economies face deep contractions this year as disrupted energy production and trade take their toll. A sharp rebound is expected in 2027, assuming the conflict abates and trade gradually normalizes. But it will not erase the losses: Gulf output is projected to remain below pre-conflict expectations in the medium term.
Major oil importers like Egypt, Jordan, and Morocco have shown surprising resilience, with growth expected to exceed 4% this year. Remittances, tourism, investment, and favorable financial conditions have helped sustain growth, while policy measures have cushioned households from higher food and energy costs. But pressures are building, with inflation expected to decline more slowly than forecast in the spring.
The risks will grow the longer conflict-related disruptions persist. Low inventories and tight spare capacity could magnify further energy price spikes. Prolonged uncertainty could weigh on investment, tourism, and trade. The poorest economies are especially vulnerable: food accounts for a large share of household spending, and declining aid leaves less room to cushion another shock. A global market correction, whether prompted by a reassessment of AI-driven gains or interest rates remaining higher for longer, would add to the strain, particularly where financing needs are already large.
For MENA policymakers, the consensus in Bangkok was clear: In times of turbulence, preserving macroeconomic stability remains the immediate policy priority. As one finance minister put it, âthe policy frameworks and buffers built in good times decide how much room we have in the bad times.â
Policies should focus on containing inflation, preserving fiscal sustainability, and protecting the vulnerable. With food, energy, and transport costs rising, central banks need to guard against renewed inflation. Meanwhile, governments should protect vulnerable households while keeping debt manageable and pursuing the investment and reforms needed for future growth. That means mobilizing revenue, prioritizing spending, and ensuring support is targeted and temporary. Countries with stronger buffers have more room to support recovery and reconstruction. Those with less will face tougher choices to avoid adding to their debt.
But managing this shock is only part of the task. Regional economies need to prepare for the next crisis. Diversifying trade and production would reduce reliance on narrow export baskets and vulnerable transport routes. Better infrastructure and deeper regional integration would cut rerouting costs and strengthen supply chains. Investment in renewable energy would limit exposure to volatile fuel markets.
At the same time, the region needs new engines of growth. Digital technologies, including AI, offer opportunities as Gulf economies invest in data centers and digital infrastructure. Turning that investment into broader prosperity will require better education and skills, stronger governance and competition, and deeper links to global markets.
The experience of the past eight months suggests that resilience has been earned, through adjustment, stronger policy frameworks, and buffers built before the conflict. But resilience is a process. If the Middle East conflict persists and buffers are steadily depleted, todayâs delayed effects could become tomorrowâs larger adjustment.
Governments have an opportunity to act. In an era of recurring shocks, the economies that prepare before the next disruption will be best placed not just to endure it, but to emerge stronger.
Jihad Azour is the IMFâs Director for the Middle East and Central Asia Department

Global oil markets have shifted to a supply surplus, despite months of disruption caused by the war in the Middle East. JPMorgan estimated supply exceeded demand by 1.4 million barrels a day last month, driven largely by Middle Eastern exports returning to prewar levels, while HSBC forecast Saudi output will jump in the fourth quarter as exports recover faster than expected.
Soaring output in Latin America â which is producing around 1.5 million more barrels a day than last year â also contributed to the global glut. The surplus and the US midterm results have pushed crude prices down 20% from this yearâs peak, putting Americans âdays away from enjoying the cheapest retail gasoline since March,â a leading Bloomberg columnist wrote.
