Timâs view
One of the many ironies of Tuesdayâs Democratic sweep of Congress was that for Big Oil, the same bull energy market that delivered one of its most profitable years ever also returned power to the party thatâs often bent on bringing the industry to heel.
Still, Mike Sommers, who as president of the American Petroleum Institute is the countryâs top oil lobbyist, told me heâs not particularly worried about a green backlash. Thatâs in part because the blue wave carried many more affordability-minded moderates than climate-focused progressives: âI think we just elected a lot of Joe Manchins and Mary Landrieus,â he said, referring to a pair of well-known former Democratic senators who advocated for the industry.
Sommers said itâs possible that the Trump administrationâs oil deal with Venezuela becomes a target for oversight hearings. Democrats, while not able to directly control US national security strategy, can also flex their powers over the budget and personnel confirmations to pressure US President Donald Trump on a deal with Iran, which would push oil prices down.
But apart from that, in practice thereâs not a whole lot that Congress can do to hurt the oil industry; the more tangible actions tend to come from the executive branch, like former US President Joe Bidenâs freeze on LNG terminals. Between an ongoing refinery crunch and the AI power rush, any legislative or budget proposal that appears to take molecules off the market isnât likely to go far, and industry leaders appear ready to swallow their pride: âWeâre here to serve,â Hunter Hunt, CEO of Texas driller Hunt Energy, told me in Abu Dhabi. âWeâll adjust as best we can.â
Sommers is anxious to see the permitting reform bill currently awaiting approval in the Senate, which would give a major boost to energy projects of all stripes, passed before Democrats take their majority seats in January. The Senate is due to vote on Monday about whether to bring it to the floor for passage, a vote that some progressives may try to undermine, targeting a more renewables-friendly deal. But the toxic relationship between Democratic leaders and the White House, as my colleagues reported, means the more likely outcome is no deal at all.
Meanwhile, executives from âLittle Oilâ companies on the tradeshow floor at ADIPEC this week werenât thrilled by the election outcome, but not really sweating it either. âOil will survive,â said Tom Inman, whose Houston company Dragon Products makes pumps and other fracking gear. âDemocrats have tried to shut us down before. But itâs still very easy to sell oil.â

b40ff4a9db30.text: By — Hannah Fingerhut, Associated Press Hannah Fingerhut, Associated Press Share Copy URL https://www.pbs.org/newshour/nation/3-people-injured-in-iowa-post-office-shooting Email Facebook Twitter LinkedIn Pinterest Tumblr Share on Facebook Share on Twitter 3 people injured in Iowa post office shooting Nation Nov 5, 2026 1:25 PM EST DES MOINES, Iowa (AP) — Two people were shot at the main post office in Iowa's capital Thursday, and a third person was injured trying to escape before the shooter was taken into custody, authorities said. None of the injuries were believed to be life-threatening, police said. "They're all at the hospital. They are being cared for right now," Des Moines police Sgt. Paul Parizek said of the victims. Parizek said officers responded within three minutes and quickly captured the suspect, who was found just east of the post office. The shooting happened on the second floor of the facility, and reports started coming in around 9:10 a.m. The post office is just north of downtown Des Moines and across the street from one of the city's main hospitals. The building is a four-story regional sorting facility with a walk-in service counter accessible to the public. It was not immediately clear whether the victims were employees or members of the public. Gov. Kim Reynolds said she's in contact with the Department of Public Safety regarding the shooting. "We are monitoring the situation and our prayers are with everyone involved," she posted online. "Grateful for the immediate response by law enforcement." Des Moines Public Schools said the district's nearby elementary school, welcome center and nutrition center went into a secure status after police notified the district of the shooting at 9:20 a.m., meaning no one was allowed in or out of the buildings. That status was lifted after police notified them at 10 a.m. that a suspect was in custody. A free press is a cornerstone of a healthy democracy. Support trusted journalism and civil dialogue. 06e3d0fa64e1.text: President Trump won historic levels of support from Black men in 2024. Two years later, those gains appeared to evaporate as Republicans suffered their worst midterm defeat in 50 years. Why it matters: Democrats feared the Supreme Court's decision weakening the Voting Rights Act would threaten their political future in the South. Instead, Black voters helped deliver historic Democratic victories in Texas and Georgia, with a potential upset brewing in Mississippi. By the numbers: Roughly nine in 10 Black voters backed Democratic House candidates Tuesday, according to the AP Voter Poll . Only about one in 10 Black men backed Republicans. Roughly one-quarter supported Trump in the 2024 presidential election, according to AP's analysis. For context, a separate 2024 national House exit poll found Black voters favored Democrats 84%–14%. Black men split 75%–24%, while Black women backed Democrats 90%–8%. State of play: Two Democrats who faced questions about their support among Black voters won crucial Senate races. Michigan: Progressive Democrat Abdul El-Sayed defeated Republican Mike Rogers , becoming the nation's first Muslim senator. A late-October poll showed El-Sayed drawing 87% support among likely Black voters. Texas: Democrat James Talarico defeated Republican Ken Paxton after courting Black voters who overwhelmingly backed Rep. Jasmine Crockett in the Democratic primary. An August Texas Southern University poll showed Talarico leading Paxton 79%–12% among likely Black voters. Zoom in: Talarico built commanding margins in Harris County, home to Houston, and Dallas County, both home to large Black electorates, according to AP county-level returns . Zoom out: Black voters helped elect former Atlanta Mayor Keisha Lance Bottoms as the first Black woman governor in U.S. history . About nine in 10 Black men voted for Bottoms, compared with roughly three-quarters who supported Kamala Harris in Georgia in 2024, according to the AP Voter Poll . Black women's support remained around 90%. In majority-Black Clayton County, Bottoms received nearly 86,000 votes — about 13,600 more than Democrat Stacey Abrams received in the 2022 governor's race, AP reported . In Mississippi's U.S. Senate election , Democrat Scott Colom built commanding leads over Republican incumbent Sen. Cindy Hyde-Smith in heavily Black Hinds County, home to Jackson, and majority-Black Claiborne and Jefferson counties, according to unofficial overnight returns . Colom held a narrow statewide lead Thursday morning, with thousands of ballots outstanding and the race still uncalled . The intrigue: Florida Republican Byron Donalds became the state's first Black governor, but most Black voters backed Democrat David Jolly. About one-quarter of Black men voted for Donalds, compared with just one in 10 Black women, according to the AP Voter Poll . Between the lines: Election returns don't prove a nationwide surge in Black turnout or establish that anger over civil rights rollbacks motivated voters. But early voting offered signs of heightened Black participation in Georgia. Black voters accounted for 32.4% of Georgia's early ballots, up from 30.2% in 2022, according to an Atlanta Journal-Constitution analysis . The figures don't establish whether the overall Black turnout rate increased. Voting rights concerns may also have motivated some Black voters. A Democratic-aligned August Data for Progress survey in Mississippi found 43% of Black voters more enthusiastic than usual about the midterms, compared with 31% of white voters. Another 53% of Black voters said politicians making voting harder, gerrymandering and spreading false election claims made participation feel more important. Worth noting: Yolanda Renee King , the 18-year-old granddaughter of Martin Luther King Jr., cast her first ballot Tuesday in Atlanta. The bottom line: Democrats needed Black voters to win. Tuesday's results suggest they held together a coalition that looked vulnerable after 2024 — potentially giving Black voters more leverage heading into 2028.

9da50dae2c83.text: Young voters swung so hard toward Democrats in Tuesday's midterms that it raises new doubts about whether Republicans can build a lasting coalition among Americans under 30. Why it matters: Trump's success with Gen Z voters, especially young men , fueled talk of a generational shift toward Republicans. Tuesday's results tell a different story. By the numbers: An estimated 66% of voters ages 18–29 backed Democratic House candidates Tuesday, compared with 31% for Republicans, according to Tufts University's CIRCLE , which analyzed preliminary data from the NORC Civic Health & Elections Project. That's a 35-point Democratic advantage, compared with 14 points in the 2024 national House exit poll , when young voters favored Democrats 56%–42%. Democratic support among men under 30 rose from 51% in 2024 to 59% in 2026. Among young women, it climbed from 61% to 70%, according to 2024 exit polling by Edison Research and CIRCLE's updated 2026 analysis of NORC data. Young white voters favored Democrats 63%–34% in the SSRS survey, after splitting 50%–48% in 2024. State of play: Polls flashed warning signs for Republicans in the final weeks before Election Day. An October Harvard Youth Poll found voters ages 18–29 who said they would definitely vote favored Democrats 63%–26%. Just 9% of young Americans said the country was headed in the right direction. Zoom in: Democrats drew overwhelming support from young voters in major statewide races, according to preliminary SSRS polling. In Texas, 76% of voters under 30 supported Democratic Senate candidate James Talarico, while 73% backed Democratic gubernatorial candidate Gina Hinojosa, according to CIRCLE's state analysis . In Georgia, 70% backed Democratic gubernatorial candidate Keisha Lance Bottoms. More than 60% favored Democratic candidates for Senate and governor in Ohio. In Iowa, where young voters backed Trump in 2024, Republican Senate candidate Ashley Hinson lost significant ground with the group, according to AP Voter Poll data . Democrat Josh Turek won the Senate seat, while Rob Sand captured the governorship. What they're saying: "Gen Z voters are proving that they have the power not just to decide races, but to be the decisive factor in flipping both chambers of Congress," Santiago Mayer, executive director of the Gen Z-led voter outreach organization Voters of Tomorrow, said in a statement. The group credited its youth outreach in Iowa with helping Democrats Christina Bohannan, Lindsay James and Sarah Trone Garriott win their U.S. House races. Zoom out: CIRCLE found 79% of young Black voters and 71% of young Latino voters backed Democratic House candidates. Caveat: Young voters accounted for an estimated 11% of Tuesday's electorate, compared with 12% in the 2022 midterms, according to CIRCLE's analysis of NORC data. That smaller share doesn't tell us whether turnout among eligible young voters rose or fell. Their numbers could have grown even as a larger overall electorate reduced their share. Different polling methods in 2024 and 2026 also complicate precise comparisons. The NORC and SSRS surveys produced different estimates of Democratic support. Yes, but: Republicans haven't necessarily lost the young conservatives who helped Trump win in 2024. An earlier More in Common study identified a faction of younger Trump supporters embracing more hard-line views on gender roles and religion. The bottom line: The surveys can't tell us whether those voters switched parties or a different mix of young Americans showed up Tuesday.

241618de9c4c.text: By — Tales Azzoni, Associated Press Tales Azzoni, Associated Press Share Copy URL https://www.pbs.org/newshour/nation/cristiano-ronaldo-announces-his-international-retirement-from-portugal Email Facebook Twitter LinkedIn Pinterest Tumblr Share on Facebook Share on Twitter Cristiano Ronaldo announces his international retirement from Portugal Nation Nov 5, 2026 1:03 PM EST Cristiano Ronaldo won't play for Portugal anymore, ending on Thursday a career that spanned six World Cups and included a European title and the men's all-time international scoring record. His announcement marked the end of a lauded career that began more than two decades ago before Euro 2004 and finished with him walking out on the national team after falling out with coach Jorge Jesus. READ MORE: Goals, technology and hydration breaks: How the biggest World Cup in history will be remembered "To the Portuguese people, the day has come for me to hand back the No. 7 shirt of our national team," the 41-year-old Ronaldo said in a long video message on social media. "I never felt it belonged to me alone but for 23 years I had the privilege and the responsibility of wearing it, defending it and carrying it with me into stadiums all around the world. "Today the time has come to pass it on to the future. It was not an easy decision because some decisions are not made with the mind alone. They are also made with the heart. A journey that began in August 2003 and changed my life forever has come to an end." Ronaldo will keep playing at club level, which he is expected to finish at the end of this season with Al-Nassr in Saudi Arabia. READ MORE: Spanish police investigating after soccer player dies following on-field collision He is in pursuit of his 1,000th career goal and sits on 985. Of those, a record 146 goals came in 234 appearances with Portugal. Portugal plans tribute to 'greatest of all time' While long-time peer Lionel Messi finished his career with Argentina last month after a much anticipated farewell match, Ronaldo's final appearance with Portugal has ended up being on Sept. 24 in a 1-0 home win over Wales in the Nations League. Jesus kept him on the bench for the following match and said he didn't plan to start him in the next one, so Ronaldo decided to leave the team's training camp. Jesus later said Ronaldo would be welcome back and the decision to return was up to him. The Portuguese soccer federation released a statement expressing "deep gratitude and immense admiration" for Ronaldo's service to the country. READ MORE: Cristiano Ronaldo's World Cup career ends after Mikel Merino's late goal sends Spain to quarterfinals "Cristiano Ronaldo has raised Portugal's profile and inspired generations of young people who dream of following in his footsteps; for many of us, he is the greatest player of all time!" the federation said. It said it intends to organize a tribute to Ronaldo "in which the fans and the country can one more time applaud and celebrate a player who has given us so much." Ronaldo helps Portugal reach new level Before Ronaldo debuted for Portugal by replacing Luís Figo in a 2003 friendly against Kazakhstan, Portugal had never won any major trophies. Then he and successive generations of talented teammates made Portugal a regular presence at major tournaments. Portugal won its first major title at Euro 2016, and the Nations League in 2019 and 2025. READ MORE: Ronaldo hush-money settlement faces fresh scrutiny in U.S. appeals court "Throughout my entire career with the national team, I always pushed myself beyond my limits," Ronaldo said. "I wanted to win. I wanted to be better. I wanted to make history. "I always demanded the most of myself. I always wanted more. I always believed we could go further. And I gave everything I had for this shirt." Portugal qualified for the World Cup only three times before Ronaldo's time — 1966, 1986 and 2002. On his watch, Portugal qualified every single time. The same was true for the Euros, which Portugal had played only three times before Ronaldo — 1984, 1996 and 2000. After he arrived it played in the tournament every time. Portugal was runner-up in Ronaldo's Euro debut in 2004 at home. At the World Cup, Portugal went as far as fourth place with Ronaldo, in his tournament debut in 2006. Paraguay's President Santiago PeÃ±a has announced his resignation following a political crisis sparked by the collapse of a bank linked to him.
"I want to apologise to the people if at any point I failed," he said in a video message on social media. "It was never my intention to betray the trust you placed in me."
The crisis erupted after Ueno Bank entered an insolvency process, which froze all operations. Lawmakers accused PeÃ±a, who was a shareholder until last year in the company that owned the bank, of conflicts of interest and misconduct.
PeÃ±a has rejected suggestions of impropriety. His resignation comes after Paraguay's lower house of congress voted in favour of pursuing an impeachment trial.
In his video message posted on X, PeÃ±a said his resignation was to protect stability, social peace and democratic institutions.
Ueno Bank has said it has about three million customers, equivalent to about 60% of Paraguay's adult population.
It held pensions and some other public funds and, after its collapse earlier this week, millions could not access their accounts.
The central bank seized the digital lender, and people took to the streets protesting and demanding PeÃ±a's resignation.
A new president of the Central Bank of Paraguay has been appointed and Congress has approved a process to pay depositors.
PeÃ±a won election in 2023 representing Paraguay's ruling conservative Colorado Party, beating a centre-left challenger.

At least 21 aircraft and several airports across Europe have been targeted by bomb threats in the second such incident this week, with the UK calling it a "malicious hoax".
Flights to Austria, Belgium, Bulgaria, the Czech Republic, France, Italy, Poland and Romania were affected. An Aer Lingus plane from Dublin to Rome was diverted to an air base in France and Italian fighter jets escorted Finnair's Helsinki-Rome flight.
EasyJet said its flights from Newcastle and Glasgow were met by police in Prague as a precaution. London Heathrow and Birmingham airports received threats that were assessed as not credible.
No explosives have been found during searches, and it is not clear if the incidents, some claimed by a little known group, are related.
The airport authorities in Italy's capital Rome said the hoax threat against two inbound flights received on Thursday had come by email.
The warnings were signed on behalf of a group or individual calling themselves "Fighters of the Male State", claiming to be targeting a "feminist regime" and wanting to "make our mark on history".
They threatened to "turn the skies red" with explosions.
These details were first reported by Italian media and then confirmed to the BBC by Aeroporti di Roma, which manages both of the city airports.
"Fighters of the Male State" likely refers to the Russian group "Muzhskoi Legion" ( "Male Legion") - an ultra-right group with such extreme views it was banned by a Moscow court in 2021. Yet it retained tens of thousands of online followers as it cheered on the full-scale Russian invasion of Ukraine in the following year.
But that email, even if genuine, is unlikely to provide the leads that police and airport authorities need to pin down who is generating these hoaxes and why.
UK Transport Secretary Heidi Alexander described Thursday's incidents as "malicious hoax threats."
She said the government was taking "these threats seriously", stressing that there were "established processes for dealing with hoax and malicious threats".
A UK government spokesperson later said the threats reported "in the early hours" of the day had been "resolved", without giving any further details.
Heathrow later said in a statement it had received a threat earlier in the day which was "deemed not credible", adding there was "no risk to passengers, colleagues or the aircraft".
"There are robust UK aviation security standards in place to assess and safely manage these types of situations," the statement said.
Meanwhile, a Birmingham Airport spokesperson told the BBC it had received a threat, after which "processes were immediately initiated in conjunction with emergency services and partners".
The following flights were targeted by threats on Thursday:
- Aer Lingus said its flight from Dublin to Rome diverted to Normandy, landing safely. The company added that it was working to "re-accommodate customers to their final destination as soon as possible".
- Two Finnair flights from Helsinki landed at their destinations as normal, the airline said. One was escorted into Rome's Fiumicino airport by Italian Air Force fighter jets, Aeroporti di Roma told the BBC, while the other landed in Vienna, Austria
- Wizz Air said two flights which departed Milan were affected - one was heading to Warsaw, before being diverting to Vienna; the other landed safely in Bucharest, with teams inspecting the aircraft
- Polish airline LOT said its flight from Warsaw to Brussels landed as planned, and "no suspicious items were found". Another LOT flight from Warsaw to Paris was stopped before take-off and the plane and baggage underwent a security screening, with no hazardous items found
- Three Ryanair flights landed in Bulgaria, according to Bulgarian media - one from Copenhagen and another from Madrid landed in the capital Sofia, while a third coming from London bound for Sofia landed in Plovdiv. The flights were escorted by Bulgarian air force fighter jets
- No explosives were found on four flights which landed in Prague, Czech police said. EasyJet later said its flights from Newcastle and Glasgow were among those affected. "Passengers on both flights disembarked normally," the company said
- Aegean Airlines said it "was informed of a bomb threat" concerning two of its flights from Thessaloniki in Greece to Milan, and also from Athens to Vienna. It said threat was "unfounded", and both flights departed from the respective airports"
- A Ryanair flight from Porto in Portugal landed safely in Milan as planned, with bomb disposal experts checking them on arrival, Italy's Ansa news agency reported
- Spain's airport authority said it had received bomb threats affecting three flights at Madrid airport, but any threat was ruled out following inspections. Iberia later said two of its flights - Milan-Madrid and Rome-Madrid - were affected. It was not clear whether the third plane was the above reported Ryanair Madrid to Sofia flight
- Air Serbia said its flight from Belgrade to Bucharest "landed safely at its destination airport", and after checks, a reported bomb threat was "assessed as unfounded"
Emily Noble, who was aboard the diverted Aer Lingus plane from Dublin to Rome, said she was about an hour into her flight to attend a friend's wedding in the Italian capital when passengers were told about a "technical" problem.
Later, as the Aer Lingus plane began circling for an unplanned landing in France, the pilot said there was a "security" issue, the 26-year-old from Dublin told BBC Verify.
On board it was "an odd experience," Noble said. "It was worrying because we didn't know what was going on, but we were all trying to be as calm as we could."

27af678533ff.text: By — Becky Bohrer, Associated Press Becky Bohrer, Associated Press Share Copy URL https://www.pbs.org/newshour/politics/alaskans-are-waiting-for-more-votes-in-senate-and-governors-races-both-could-go-to-ranked-tabulations Email Facebook Twitter LinkedIn Pinterest Tumblr Share on Facebook Share on Twitter Alaskans are waiting for more votes in Senate and governor's races. Both could go to ranked tabulations Politics Nov 5, 2026 12:11 PM EST JUNEAU, Alaska (AP) — Alaskans settled in Wednesday to await more results from key races on the general election ballot, including a bitterly fought U.S. Senate campaign and an open seat for governor. A ballot measure seeking to repeal Alaska's unique system of open primaries and ranked vote general elections also was too early to call. LIVE RESULTS: Alaska Senate midterm election If no candidate wins more than 50% of first-choice votes, rankings will come into play. Alaska accepts ballots from overseas voters for up to 15 days after the election, making Nov. 18 the date targeted by state elections officials to tabulate under the ranked vote system. Stand with free and independent journalism. Join Press Pass from PBS News The major candidates in the Senate race are two-term Republican Sen. Dan Sullivan and Democratic former Rep. Mary Peltola. READ MORE: Will ranked choice voting affect timing of Maine and Alaska's Senate race results? Here's what we know In the governor's race, former state lawmaker Jonathan Kreiss-Tomkins is trying to become the first Democrat elected to the office in a generation. He faces three other Republicans, including business owner Bernadette Wilson, who was endorsed by President Donald Trump. Litigation and allegations of partisan tricks rocked the Senate race The contest dominated headlines ahead of Tuesday's election and attracted the attention of the U.S. Department of Justice. With less than two weeks before Election Day, the agency sued at President Donald Trump's direction seeking to block certification of the race if Sullivan loses. The lawsuit cited potential confusion with another Sullivan on the ballot, retired teacher Dan J. Sullivan. A federal judge dismissed the lawsuit, but the department has appealed. READ MORE: Justice Department sent target letters in Alaska Senate criminal probe. Here's what that means Suspicions long held by the senator and his supporters that the lesser-known Sullivan was running to sow confusion gained new life last week, when The New York Times reported that top political aides to Peltola appeared to be involved in recruiting him. The report was based on interviews with a former Peltola campaign manager, who was fired shortly before the August primary. It also cited text messages and campaign finance documents indicating that an operative trying to recruit candidates was paid by a group backing Peltola. Federal authorities have confirmed the existence of a criminal investigation in the matter. Peltola denied any involvement. Dan J. Sullivan, who has denied running at the behest of Democrats, has not responded to messages seeking comment in the last week. The senator elevated the issue in his closing argument to voters and questioned Peltola's denials. On Wednesday his campaign expressed confidence in Sullivan's chances, "despite the biggest election cheating scandal in the history of Alaska" and "despite a bloodbath for Republicans everywhere else in the country." Sullivan and Peltola say the vote count will take time Both campaigns urged patience as the ballot count continues. Peltola addressed supporters Tuesday night after news broke that Democrats had won enough seats to gain control of the Senate. She was joyful — even taking a selfie with the crowd — but said it will take time for the state to count ballots. Alaska allows up to 10 days to receive absentee ballots sent from within the U.S., a timeline that can be critical for ballots from rural Alaska communities that are often accessible only by air or water and rely on air service for mail delivery. "It's going to take a long time to make sure we're counting every vote from every far-flung hinterland community, from every tiny outpost, from all of our service members serving overseas, our young people going to colleges," Peltola said. Democrat seeks to reclaim governor's office Kreiss-Tomkins expressed excitement about the early vote results when speaking to supporters on election night, saying, "What a night this is for the future of our state." He cast himself as a consensus builder in the race to succeed term-limited Republican Gov. Mike Dunleavy and said he would work across party lines to address the state's challenges. State Republican leaders urged their voters to rank the three GOP candidates in the race to maximize the party's chances of success. But Trump, speaking at a rally in support of Republican candidates including Sullivan and Wilson last month in Wasilla, called ranked voting a "scam." And he railed on social media against the other two Republican gubernatorial candidates, former Anchorage Mayor Dave Bronson and former state Attorney General Treg Taylor. Wilson said in a statement Wednesday that she was "cautiously optimistic for the days ahead." Alaska's last Democratic governor was Tony Knowles, who had back-to-back terms from 1994 to 2002. The state had an independent governor from 2014 to 2018. Ballot measure seeks to repeal unique elections process Alaskans were asked to decide for the second time in two years on a ballot measure seeking to repeal the open primary and ranked vote general election system. Voters approved the system in 2020, and it took effect for elections in 2022. Voters narrowly rejected a repeal effort two years ago. A free press is a cornerstone of a healthy democracy. Support trusted journalism and civil dialogue. Donate now By — Becky Bohrer, Associated Press Becky Bohrer, Associated Press

a10de408ae53.text: Democrats won the midterms on voter frustration with high prices . Now they face the same problem that sank Republicans: Americans want lower prices, and there is little that policymakers can do to deliver them quickly. Why it matters: Prices for necessities like groceries and gas can fall in a healthy economy. But the kind of broad price declines that would reverse years of price gains would likely come with job losses and falling incomes, leaving households worse off than before. It sets up an early test for the incoming Democratic-controlled Congress and Democrats in statehouses across the country: delivering relief that voters can actually feel in their household budgets. What they're saying: "Can you bring prices back to 2019 levels? No," Brendan Duke, senior director for federal budget policy at the Center on Budget and Policy Priorities, tells Axios. "But a lot of the price shocks are policy-induced, so there are ways that policy can reverse them." Duke points to reversing food assistance cuts, restoring health insurance subsidies and ending the Iran war as possible sources of relief, with the "big, fat asterisk" that President Trump might not sign off. Other economic problems — a potential rise in unemployment or the AI bubble bursting — could overshadow affordability without solving it, Duke says. The big picture: Democrats have limited power over sources of pressure on household budgets. Their midterm sweep helped lower oil prices through market expectations. But Trump still controls the next steps in the war, and further relief heavily depends on his next moves. Congress could vote to repeal tariffs, potentially reducing costs for imported goods and American manufacturers. But Trump could simply veto that legislation (and more generally, there is no guarantee that businesses would pass all the savings on to consumers). Plans to restore expired Affordable Care Act subsidies or reverse Medicaid cuts could hit a wall because of internal divisions or Trump's veto power. The intrigue: Democrats who won big Senate races campaigned on bringing down prices, including proposals targeting groceries and gasoline. James Talarico in Texas promised to lower grocery prices by rolling back tariffs and boosting competition. In North Carolina, Roy Cooper pledged to "make stuff cost less," while incoming Annie Andrews in South Carolina proposed suspending the federal gas tax. Democratic victories in governors' races could produce a patchwork of state-level relief, including directly giving voters money: The governor-elect of Texas, Gina Hinojosa, for instance, has proposed $1,500 rebate checks . The other side: "'Affordability' seems to be the mandate for the new Democrat majority. So they need to either find a 'magic wand' to bring prices down quickly, or they need to ... give money to people (so the high prices are made 'affordable') yet again. Only causing more inflation," Jeff Gundlach, the billionaire investor and CEO of bond giant DoubleLine Capital, wrote on X on Wednesday. What to watch: Prices don't have to return to their old levels for Americans to recover their purchasing power. That can come through a slower, less politically sexy process: wages growing faster than prices for a sustained stretch. But that bets on the possibility that there won't be another inflationary shock. And it has been a tough decade so far for such a bet. Reality check: For all the Democrats' Congressional gains, they do not control the executive branch, will not have veto-proof majorities and it's generally the president, not Congress, who takes the blame when people are unsatisfied with the economy. Still, as Democrats look to win back the White House in 2028 and maintain congressional majorities, it would be nice to point to concrete action to help affordability.

The White House has denied rumours that Defence Secretary Pete Hegseth and Secretary of State Marco Rubio might leave their jobs in a post-election shakeup of the Trump administration.
US media have reported there are calls to replace Hegseth - in particular over his handling of the Iran war, which is being blamed for heavy Republican election losses.
One outgoing congressional Republican has threatened to force an impeachment vote against Hegseth as early as next week. The defense secretary posted a video statement defending his record and denouncing the effort.
"You see, they attack me. They attack us because we are effective," he said. "It's not going to work. We will not back down."
Meanwhile, Rubio is denying reports he is considering leaving his post ahead of a 2028 presidential run.
Working for Trump until the end of his term has "always been my plan," Rubio told The New York Times in an interview.
"I love the work I'm doing," Rubio said. "And plus I always laugh when they say he's going to leave his job. I go, 'Which one?'"
Both the White House and US State Department also shut down reports that Rubio might be leaving after this week's midterm losses, with both calling it "fake news".
The defence secretary, though, faces a more uncertain political future.
Trump and Vice-President JD Vance have both blamed the Iran war for Republican losses that allowed Democrats full control of the US House of Representatives and the Senate.
In a telephone interview with ABC News, Trump said that he had received "calls about" Hegseth, but added that he had "every intention" of keeping him.
Later on Thursday, he told reporters at the White House that "Pete Hegseth has done a fantastic job", and went on to list what he sees are some of his achievements, including the arrest of Venezuelan leader NicolÃ¡s Maduro in January and the Iran war, now into its ninth month.
The Washington Post reported on Thursday that Trump might be, however, considering ousting General Dan Caine, the chairman of the Joint Chiefs of Staff, or Centcom chief Admiral Brad Cooper. Both played significant roles in offering guidance on the war, which started eight months ago.
Meanwhile, Republican Representative Thomas Massie, a frequent critic of Trump, has said he will push ahead with plans to push for Hegseth's impeachment.
He told news site Politico that he will trigger his resolution to impeach the defence secretary early next week.
And on X, he warned that the president should replace Hegseth before a new Democratic-controlled Congress forms in January.
"He should do it while he can still get the replacements confirmed in the Senate," Massie wrote on X.
Hegseth has also been rumoured to be interested in running for an open Tennessee Senate seat.
In his video statement, Hegseth denounced the "sham articles of impeachment" effort against him from a "disgruntled, defeated congressman, along with all his Democrat allies", and listed ways the department has fulfilled Trump's America First agenda under his leadership.
That includes, he said, reviving military recruitment, rebuilding the defense industrial base, and rooting out diversity initiatives.
Of the Democrats, he said: "Their policies don't work. So their obsession with political theatre disguised as power drives them to try to destroy their opponents. It's all about the politics of personal destruction."

Democratic socialist Nithya Raman has toppled incumbent Karen Bass in the race for mayor of Los Angeles.
Raman's win stunned political watchers in California after she entered the race as a long-shot candidate against Bass, a political heavyweight who previously served in Congress and had never lost a race for political office.
Raman has frequently been compared to New York City Mayor Zohran Mamdani. Both are democratic socialists and ran on progressive platforms.
Her win solidifies that America's two biggest cities will now be led by democratic socialists, which include some of the most high-profile politicians in the US, such as Mamdani and Alexandria Ocasio-Cortez.
Los Angeles was always likely to have a Democratic mayor but the question in the city - the second most populous city in the US - was just how left voters would be willing to go.
Bass, also Democrat, announced that she had called and conceded to Raman in a post on social media on Thursday, writing "while this is not the outcome we hoped for, the people of Los Angeles have spoken."
"Moving this city forward is what Los Angeles needs from all of us," Bass wrote. "I love Los Angeles. I believe in Los Angeles. And I will continue to ensure the promise of a better life belongs to all of us."
Raman, a member of city council and Indian immigrant, ran on a platform of change and fixing the "broken status quo and the politicians who failed them over and over again".
She ran on cutting homelessness, increasing housing in the city, saving Hollywood jobs from continued cuts and protecting residents from immigration enforcement efforts. Raman also vowed to fix the city's many issues, including helping beautification efforts, fixing roads and even helping bring back nightlife in the city.
The major issue in the race, however, was the LA fires, which killed dozens of people and razed neighbourhoods across the area in 2025. Bass faced intense political fallout over her absence during the emergency and the city's response to the disaster.
The next mayor in LA will oversee hosting the Super Bowl in 2027 and the 2028 Summer Olympics.
Raman entered the race as a long-shot candidate but slowly shored up support, especially from younger voters, before besting reality star Spencer Pratt in the primary race earlier this year.
Raman's win over Bass has all the appearances of echoing voter sentiment across the US as part of sweeping Democratic wins, including in deep-Republican country that hadn't seen liberal leaders in decades.
Washington DC also elected democratic socialist Janeese Lewis George as its new mayor, furthering progressive leadership in another major US city.
US President Donald Trump was asked at the White House about the wins by politicians on the left flank of the Democratic Party and said, "If you go by history, it's going to be a disaster".
Such candidates have become a focal point of attacks by Republicans.
Bass had been a prominent member of Congress before becoming LA's first black female mayor. Her roots are closely tied to LA and its history, even working as a community organiser during the violent 1992 riots over police brutality in the beating of Rodney King, who was black.

High above the Arctic, powerful winds usually circle the North Pole each winter, helping trap some of the coldest air on Earth.
But this circulation, known as the polar vortex, has weakened and shifted position in recent days.
While such disruptions can occur during winter, scientists say an event this early in November is unprecedented in modern observations.
Similar disruptions in past years have sometimes been followed by colder weather affecting parts of Europe and North America.
However, as this is happening so early in the season, there are few historical examples to compare with and it could throw current winter forecasts into even more uncertainty.
What is the polar vortex?
The polar vortex develops every autumn as temperatures fall in the Arctic.
Strong westerly winds form in the stratosphere, roughly 10 to 30 miles (15-50km) above Earth's surface, locking the coldest air near the pole.
Atmospheric disturbances can cause the air high up to start warming which then makes the vortex winds weaken. This sudden stratospheric warming (SSW) can eventually lead to the strong westerlies reversing into easterly winds.
In the following days and weeks these changes can alter the position of the jet stream, increasing the chance of a blocked weather pattern where it can become drier with a colder northerly or easterly wind bringing Arctic air in.
It can also boost the possibility of snow, especially in eastern UK.
Unknown territory
Most SSW events tend to occur from mid-winter but we are currently witnessing a dramatic weakening of the strong winds with some forecasts even showing a reversal of the polar vortex winds by mid-November.
Due to this weakening, the vortex has stretched and briefly split into two smaller circulations around the Arctic.
If the winds continue to weaken and end up reversing as forecast, this will be known as a major SSW event.
Jeff Knight, lead climate scientist from the Met Office, told the BBC: "It would appear to be the earliest on record looking back over the 75 years we've been observingâ¦with most experts agreeing this is a very unusual event."
The current earliest major SSW event occurred on 28 November in 1969 and 2025.
Reasons for why we're seeing such an early event is not clear. It could be just part of the variability of our weather patterns.
But we also know in a "normal" El NiÃ±o year, this can typically bring a weakening of the polar vortex towards the end of winter.
While the warmer waters of the Pacific in an El NiÃ±o directly disrupt the weather around tropical areas, pulses of energy in the atmosphere, known as planetary waves, can cause disturbances even at polar regions.
These waves can push the polar vortex out of position and break the circulation up.
With the current record El NiÃ±o taking us into uncharted territory in terms of disruption to worldwide weather patterns, Knight suggested it could have "helped load the dice for this SSW event. However, because this is so rare, there's not enough evidence".
A link between a strong El NiÃ±o and early onset of a SSW event is unclear and will need further research.
Will the UK see snow?
Long-range forecasts issued by the Met Office show that the UK was more likely to see a stormy start to winter, followed by a colder spell to end winter. This is consistent with expectations from an El NiÃ±o pattern.
However, this unusually early SSW event was not widely expected.
Professor Andrew Perez-Charlton, meteorologist at the University of Reading, said: "The typical response to a SSW is for colder and drier conditions over Europe and the UK."
"Because we haven't seen a SSW event quite like this before, it is harder to anticipate a cold spell at the moment."
One reason is the timing.
The Arctic is not yet as cold as it becomes later in winter, with the polar vortex itself having only recently developed.
Any influence it may have on weather patterns could be weaker than during a mid-winter disruption.
And because the air isn't at mid-winter temperatures yet it means cold and snowy weather for the UK is far from guaranteed.
Continuation of drought conditions "more concerning"
Long-term forecasts are based on large-scale climate signals and how they have affected weather patterns in previous years.
Much of the forecast for this autumn and winter has been focused around the influence of the exceptionally strong El NiÃ±o, pointing to a stormier start to winter, with the potential to be followed by colder and drier conditions from January.
But this unusually early disruption of the polar vortex and SSW presents meteorologists with a situation for which there are few modern comparisons.
For Perez-Charlton, the "concerning thing would be if this event ends up bringing the typical drier weather pattern and lack of rain" associated with a sudden stratospheric warming over the coming months.
With most of England and Wales still in drought, we need to rely on a wetter winter to fill up extremely low reservoirs.
For now, experts stress that it is too early to know whether recent changes in the polar vortex will change the winter outlook.

US President Donald Trump has signed an executive order that he says will prevent future presidents from making certain changes to the White House Oval Office.
Trump, a former real estate mogul, has altered the president's official office during his second term, most notably by adding many gold features to its walls.
"So we're making it a national monument, and it will not be allowed to be touched by anybody, destroyed, ripped down by stupid people, in order to build something in a slightly different shape," Trump told reporters on Thursday.
American presidents currently have the power to make some changes to the White House but large projects require the permission of Congress.
Thursday's executive order declares the Oval Office to be a national monument, along with some of its surrounding rooms.
The document also says that it does not "restrict the President's authority to redecorate the monument, select furnishings, or make ordinary operational and security modifications that do not substantially impair the monument's historic structure or architectural character".
"We like the Oval Office, and it's a symbol like the White House itself. It's a symbol of our country and the greatness of our country," Trump said.
The president has the power to create national monuments, which are similar to national parks.
Trump's order calls on the office to be maintained by the National Park Service "in a manner that protects its historic character, architectural integrity, and association with the Presidency".
The entire building is already designated as a National Historic Landmark, which is intended to prevent against sudden changes to the building.
Trump's proclamation notes the existing protection, but says "nonetheless, the Oval Office merits specific recognition and protective management as a discrete historic structure of national significance".
Congress has carved out an exemption to the National Historic Preservation Act, in order to allow presidents to make needed changes. The current Oval Office has existed since the early 1930s, after its conception by President Franklin D Roosevelt.
Greg Werkheiser, from the law firm Cultural Heritage Partners, which specialises in historic preservation, says that temporary alterations like "furniture and decor is completely up to the president's discretion".
"As long as they're not damaging the permanent art and architecture, they can generally do whatever they want," he tells BBC News.
Werkheiser argues that the Trump administration has shown extreme disregard for other historic sites in Washington, and through lawsuits has attempted to undermine the laws that require preservation.
Trump has undertaken a massive beautification project in Washington and has held three events in the past week to boast of the construction, even as his Republican party was trounced by Democrats in the midterm elections.
"The hypocrisy is that on the one hand he's talking about the importance of preserving the Oval Office - which is legally meaningless because he can't do it - and on the other hand he is absolutely taking an axe to the law that allows us to preserve other historic sites."
Werkheiser notes Trump's efforts to renovate the Kennedy Center in Washington DC, to build a new triumphal arch in the city, and to paint the granite exterior of the historic executive office building. His firm has filed lawsuits to block two of the projects.
In October, the president suggested in an interview with Time, external magazine that the Oval Office would need to be torn down due to security concerns from the US Secret Service.
"I said, 'My ass, you can't build a new one. This is a special place,'" Trump said at the time.
During the midterm election campaign Democrats criticised Trump's redesigns, with former President Barack Obama saying that his golden tweaks have "got the White House looking like Saddam Hussein opened a Cheesecake Factory".

93ab760674bd.text: Nvidia CEO Jensen Huang has been asked by three House Republican committee chairs to brief Congress behind closed doors about his reported ties to a woman accused of spying for China. Why it matters: The request escalates the scrutiny of the Nvidia CEO over his alleged relationship with Alice Huang, a businesswoman accused of spying for China. Catch up quick: Jensen Huang and Alice Huang purportedly had a "close" relationship, per reporting from The New York Times . The Times also reported that President Trump was briefed by intelligence officials about their relationship and the allegations that Alice Huang was a spy, but chose not to act. The Wall Street Journal subsequently reported that officials in at least three countries had concerns that Alice Huang was passing information to the Chinese government, potentially including sensitive details on Nvidia chips. Nvidia has denied the allegations, saying Jensen Huang and Alice Huang's contacts were just routine business interactions. The Chinese government previously called the allegations it was spying on Nvidia "groundless speculation." Zoom out: Reps. Brian J. Mast (R-Fla.), John Moolenaar (R-Mich.) and Rick Crawford (R-Ark.) sent a letter to Jensen Huang Thursday, requesting he sit for a joint briefing with the respective House committees that they chair: Foreign Affairs, the Select Committee on the Chinese Communist Party and the Select Committee on Intelligence. They are seeking answers on Nvidia's protocols to protect itself from foreign adversaries and his interactions with Alice Huang, according to the letter. "Recent reports raise significant national security concerns regarding the [People's Republic of China] access to sensitive U.S. technology and information," the letter reads. "The issue of PRC infiltration and access to cutting-edge U.S. technology is core to the investigative work of our three committees this Congress. It is vital that Congress determines the extent to which U.S. national security has been placed at risk," the letter continues. The other side: "Meetings with customers are part of a CEO's job; Jensen talks with thousands of customer executives every year," Nvidia said in a statement. "Our regional cloud customers receive ordinary business information—not sensitive NVIDIA trade secrets—and zero information relevant to national security," the company said. "We're confident that if the U.S. government believes that any person is a threat to American industry, it would let us know," it added. Editor's note: This story has been updated with a statement from Nvidia.

fe8f3288ecce.text: By — Kim Chandler, Associated Press Kim Chandler, Associated Press By — David Fischer, Associated Press David Fischer, Associated Press Share Copy URL https://www.pbs.org/newshour/nation/alabama-executes-man-for-1991-killings-in-last-of-3-u-s-executions-carried-out-the-same-day Email Facebook Twitter LinkedIn Pinterest Tumblr Share on Facebook Share on Twitter Alabama executes man for 1991 killings in last of 3 U.S. executions carried out the same day Nation Nov 5, 2026 7:49 PM EST Florida carried out a record-tying 19th execution of the year in an unusual instance of three states administering the death penalty on the same day. Jesse Guardado was pronounced dead at 6:13 p.m. following a three-drug injection at a state prison in Starke. He had pleaded guilty to fatally stabbing 75-year-old Jackie Malone inside her Walton County home in 2004 before stealing her jewelry box, $80 and other valuables to buy drugs. The woman had helped him get a job and housing. Hours earlier, Indiana executed a man for killing two children in a house fire in 2010, and in Alabama, a man received the last lethal injection of the day for his conviction in the killing of an elderly man and woman in a home robbery. The executions were taking place the same day California Gov. Gavin Newsom announced he will commute all 548 death sentences in his state, saying he believes "state-sanctioned killing is incompatible with California's values." WATCH: Newsom plans to commute all of California's death sentences That was in sharp contrast to Florida's outgoing governor, Republican Ron DeSantis, who has made aggressive use of the death penalty like few other governors. His state has carried out more than half of the 35 executions so far this year in the U.S., where capital punishment has come under renewed scrutiny following Tennessee's failed execution of Christa Pike in September. It is the second time since August that three states had conducted executions on a single day, although it remains unusual. Prior to this year, the last time it happened was 2010. Florida inmate apologized before receiving lethal injection Guardado, 64, was already strapped to a gurney with an IV in his arm when the death chamber curtain went up promptly at 6:00 p.m. Asked if he had a last statement, he replied, "I would like to once again apologize for the pain and suffering I've caused to the victim's family and my own family as well." The drugs began flowing immediately afterward. About a minute later, Guardado began breathing heavily, followed by some sputtering and twitching. As the twitching subsided, a warden shook Guardado and shouted his name, but got no response. A medic soon after pronounced him dead. DeSantis, who leaves office in January, has said he wants to bring justice to victims' families who have often waited decades for death sentences to be carried out. He signed the death warrants that led to a state record of 19 executions in 2025. The state will set a new record if two more executions are carried out as planned later this year. The victim's son, Patrick Malone, spoke briefly to media witnesses after the execution. Instead of discussing his mother or her murder, he questioned those who oppose the death penalty. "Do such people ever think about what happened to the victim or consider the unending aftermath the victim's family endures and relives every time that terrible event comes up?" Malone said. Alabama man drew the death penalty for a double killing In neighboring Alabama, Michael Taylor, 54, received a lethal injection and was pronounced dead at 6:10 p.m. local time. The execution got underway shortly before 6 p.m. as Taylor replied "no sir" when asked if he had any final words. He appeared to mouth "thank you" toward his attorneys seated in the witness room. Taylor's spiritual adviser approached and prayed with him, and he then closed his eyes, never opening them again. In 1991, Taylor, then 19, fatally beat two people, ages 83 and 79, with a metal bar during a robbery in their Gadsden, Alabama, home. Police arrested him with the victims' Cadillac an hour away in Birmingham. Death penalty opponents had urged Republican Gov. Kay Ivey to reduce Taylor's sentence to life in prison, noting his age and immaturity at the time. She declined. Ivey issued a statement immediately afterward calling his actions "reprehensible" and saying, "35 years ago yesterday, Ivan and Lucille Moore kindly opened their home to Michael Taylor. Mr. Taylor repaid the Moores by beating them to death with a metal bar, all to rob them for money to buy clothing and jewelry." The state changed the execution method after a judge declared a nitrogen gas method unconstitutional. Taylor's attorneys had objected to the last-minute switch to lethal injection since he selected nitrogen gas as his method years ago, but a judge ruled against Taylor. Lawyers had asked for a life sentence for Indiana man In Indiana, Jeffrey Weisheit, 50, was pronounced dead at 12:45 a.m. at the state prison in Michigan City, said Noelle Russell, spokesperson at the Department of Correction. He had no final words. Weisheit had publicly acknowledged killing his girlfriend's two children in a house fire in the Evansville area in 2010 but had hoped Gov. Mike Braun would grant clemency and change his sentence to life in prison. Braun declined. Lawyers failed to persuade Braun, a Republican, to allow Weisheit to undergo brain scans in an effort to reinforce their argument that he has a history of head injuries and mental health problems that should prevent execution. Weisheit's last objection centered on the state's planned use of lethal drugs purchased from a pharmacy that is facing a disciplinary hearing next week at the Indiana Pharmacy Board. The Indiana Supreme Court declined to intervene Wednesday night, though two of the five justices wanted a 10-day stay for more information about the drugs' expiration and storage. f698c8b9d564.text: Tuesday's blue tsunami is poised to sweep an unusually large cohort of House Democrats into office who are virtually unknown outside of their districts. Why it matters: Obscure though these incoming lawmakers may be on Capitol Hill, they are poised to play a major role in determining the direction of the Democratic Party. House Democrats' progressive and centrist wings are both looking to recruit as many of these so-called "wave babies" as possible to grow their strength for the ideological fights ahead, Axios reported on Wednesday . Rep. Pramila Jayapal (D-Wash.), a co-chair of the Congressional Progressive Caucus' PAC, told Axios some of these candidates applied for her group's endorsement but didn't get it because "honestly.... the districts looked so tough." "We will definitely be reaching out to them," she said. What we're hearing: Several Democratic operatives told Axios they had to Google many of the candidates who won upset victories in North Carolina, Tennessee and elsewhere on Election Day. "Never heard of them," a senior House Democrat, who was involved in battleground House races, told Axios. Said another House Democrat: "I don't think they were on my radar, and they were not on any of the DCCC's targeted lists from what I am aware." Tennessee 4th: Victoria Broderick Photo courtesy of the Victoria Broderick campaign Perhaps the most stunning result of the night was Broderick's upset over longtime Rep. Scott DesJarlais in a seat President Trump carried by 24 percentage points in 2024. Broderick leads DesJarlais by just 280 votes but told Axios in an interview she is "100% confident" of victory and is "ready to be a representative." "There's a little shock, and there's almost a beauty in that. It's beautiful, it's poetic, for the district," said Broderick, a local activist and tech support worker. DesJarlais had regularly won in landslides since he was first elected in 2010, despite a history of scandals . GOP state legislators drew Republican voters out of his Trump+43 district this year and replaced them with Democrats to make neighboring seats more favorable. That opened the door for Broderick, who previously lost to DesJarlais by more than 40 points when she challenged him in 2024. Broderick had spent just $90,000 to DesJarlais' $500,000 as of Oct. 14, according to Federal Election Commission filings. Neither national party spent on the race. "I'm a progressive," Broderick told Axios. "I ran the most progressive race they've ever had in that district. ... I ran on safety, affordability, freedom and equity." Broderick said she supports universal health care and that "every working person deserves affordable living." Asked if she would vote for House Minority Leader Hakeem Jeffries (D-N.Y.) as speaker, she said: "We are still waiting to get our feet wet and understand where we're going with everything, so I am not going to say 'yes' or 'no' to that question." North Carolina 5th: Chuck Hubbard Photo: Al Drago/Bloomberg via Getty Images Like several others , Hubbard benefited from a combination of a Republican "dummy-mander" and strong coattails from Democratic Senate candidate Roy Cooper. The retired local newspaper journalist and publisher has declared victory over Rep. Virginia Foxx, the chair of the powerful House Rules Committee. Hubbard leads by 100 votes in a district Trump carried by 17 points in 2024. (AP has not called this race, and there are provisional ballots still to be counted.) The seat was made less Republican-leaning in 2024 when GOP legislators redrew North Carolina's maps to turn their evenly split U.S. House delegation into a 10-4 Republican one. Now it's likely to be 10-4 Democratic. Like Broderick, Hubbard previously challenged Foxx in 2024 but lost by 19 percentage points. Foxx had a more than 2-to-1 spending advantage this year, with $1.6 million in disbursements as of Oct. 14 to Hubbard's $700,000, per FEC filings. The only national party ad spending was $175,000 from the Democratic group American Bridge, according to AdImpact. Cook Political Report rated the race as "likely Republican." "I know it wasn't on anybody's radar, but that's not required to win the race," Hubbard said in an interview. "The person who has to believe in winning the race is me." Hubbard described himself as "probably center-left," saying he "might rate conservative, even, financially" but that "when it comes to social issues, I probably skew to the left." On health care: "I'm in favor of public choice in health care. You can call it universal health care, you can call it Medicare-for-All." On Israel aid: "We're going to have to find a way to exert some control on Netanyahu." On voting for Jeffries as speaker: "I have nothing against Hakeem Jeffries at all, but I think it's unwise to say ... before talking to him." North Carolina 6th: Cyril Jefferson Photo courtesy of the Cyril Jefferson campaign Another beneficiary of Cooper's performance and 2024 redistricting, Jefferson unseated freshman Rep. Addison McDowell in a district Trump carried by 16 points. Jefferson, the mayor of High Point, N.C., spent just $225,000 to McDowell's $1.3 million, per FEC filings. Neither national party invested in this race. The only ads were from McDowell, who launched a $230,000 campaign ad buy and spent another $40,000 on franked ads , according to AdImpact. "What they kept saying was, 'Your seat's just nowhere on our radar, we don't think it's going to get on our radar until something happens,'" Jefferson said of his meetings with national groups to solicit their support. Jefferson said they consistently laid out three criteria that he needed to meet to be taken seriously: Strong fundraising, competitive polling, and grassroots enthusiasm on the ground. "I'll tell you, the fundraising part is really tough," he said, telling Axios his de facto campaign manager used to be one of his students when he was a high school teacher. "There are examples where me and progressives may not be on the same sid

5d973da28a69.text: By — Sarah El Deeb, Associated Press Sarah El Deeb, Associated Press Share Copy URL https://www.pbs.org/newshour/politics/jd-habibi-arabs-celebrate-el-sayeds-use-of-a-term-of-affection-in-his-victory-speech Email Facebook Twitter LinkedIn Pinterest Tumblr Share on Facebook Share on Twitter 'JD, habibi.' Arabs celebrate El-Sayed's use of a term of affection in his victory speech Politics Nov 5, 2026 7:42 PM EST BEIRUT (AP) — From Michigan to the Middle East, Arabs are celebrating Abdul El-Sayed's Senate win and delighting in his introduction of Arabic terms like "habibi" and "inshallah" to the American political lexicon. After being the target of Islamophobic rhetoric on the campaign trail, the rising political star who will be the first Muslim American U.S. senator has mocked his critics on the right while championing the Palestinian cause and leaning into his faith and Egyptian heritage. READ MORE: The election brought a wave of historic firsts. Here are some groundbreaking winners "JD, habibi," El-Sayed said in his victory speech, addressing U.S. Vice President JD Vance, who had warned that the candidate would lead rioters in burning down Detroit. "There is this delicious irony in the fact that you're constitutionally obligated to swear me in in January." 'Habibi' is a term of affection "Habibi" literally translates to "my beloved" and is peppered through Arab pop songs. In everyday speech, it often means "buddy," "pal," or "bro." El-Sayed's supporters have sported shirts reading "Habibi for Abdul." El-Sayed, the son of Egyptian immigrants, said his campaign had turned "inshallah" — "God willing" — into "hamdulillah," which means "thank God." Arabs thrilled to the gentle ribbing of the vice president, with many posting music video clips featuring "habibi" to social media. It was a rare outpouring of joy in a region traumatized by past and present conflicts — which have also fueled negative stereotypes in the West. One user on X posted a video of Egyptian diva Shireen Abd El-Wahab dancing to one of her most popular songs, joking that El-Sayed would make it the new national anthem. Egyptians are renowned in the Arab world for their sense of humor and are known for cracking jokes in the face of life's difficulties, a spirit that has been popularized in films and by famous comedic actors. Riffing off El-Sayed's victory speech, some shared a meme from an Egyptian film in which a man attends a funeral while high and is unable to stop laughing. "I came here to crack jokes," read the caption, quoting a line from the film. An Egyptian academic, Khalil al-Anani, praised El-Sayed on X, saying: "'Habibi' is the sweetest word." He thanked the senator-elect for bringing joy to Egyptians. Signs of change after decades of prejudice Arab and Muslim Americans have faced prejudice for decades, with popular films depicting them as terrorists and politicians on the right fanning baseless fears about the imposition of sharia, or Islamic law. During the campaign, U.S. President Donald Trump referred to El-Sayed as a "jihadist," evoked the Sept. 11 attacks and deliberately misstated the candidate's name. On social media, users responded to such attacks by posting light-hearted videos, including of Lebanese diva Haifa Wehbe belly dancing and young veiled women breakdancing in the streets. "Donald, look, I know you've struggled with my name," El-Sayed said in his victory speech. "So after JD swears me in in January, you can just go on and call me 'senator.'" 39072f0f45d9.text:
Republicans in Florida narrowly held off a nationwide repudiation Tuesday of their party and President Donald Trump, eking out slim victories in statewide races. But the GOP failed to flip congressional seats Democrats held and lost seats in the Legislature.
Voters elected Republican Byron Donalds as governor over Democrat David Jolly by a margin of a little over 1 percentage point and Republican Ashley Moody for the U.S. Senate over Democrat Angie Nixon by less than 3 percentage points. Both GOP candidates raised significantly more money than their Democratic challengers. Republicans also held onto three cabinet positions in similarly close races.
“Mr. President, I want you to hear from Florida that we are still red!” Donalds, a Trump-endorsed congressman representing the 19th district in southwest Florida, announced Tuesday night to cheering supporters gathered to celebrate his victory. Donalds is the first Black governor elected in Florida and first Black Republican governor in the nation.
It was possible but perhaps unlikely Republicans might take a more moderate approach on issues such as climate change after Democrats’ gains in Florida, said Aubrey Jewett, associate director of the School of Politics, Security and International Affairs at the University of Central Florida.
“They didn’t win, and so that stings. But on another level I think it gives perhaps Democrats a little bit of hope after all, because it really seemed that Florida had become a red state to such a degree that Democrats just didn’t really have any hope,” he said. “I emphasize though, a loss is a loss, and it stings. And I’m sure they’re disappointed that they lost, and they don’t have control of the executive branch. And they actually, in some ways, they came so close and didn’t win, it perhaps stings a little more.”
Democrats did maintain seats in four congressional districts where the boundaries were redrawn to favor Republicans, as part of a controversial redistricting effort this spring directed by Gov. Ron DeSantis, a term-limited Republican, and the GOP-controlled Legislature. Among the winning Democrats were Rep. Darren Soto, whose Hispanic-majority district in central Florida was redrawn to include conservative-leaning areas as far south as Lake Okeechobee.
Susannah Randolph, director of the Florida chapter of the Sierra Club, said the redistricting effort failed.
“That was very inspiring,” she said. “I think folks kind of saw through that scheme.”
Democrats also made gains in the Legislature, where Republicans maintained majorities in the Senate and House but lost super-majorities in both chambers, Jewett said. Democrats now will wield more influence as bills are shaped and voted on.
“Still the big picture is the Republicans have the majority, and they are in charge,” he said.
Republicans benefited from an infusion of campaign contributions and boast 1.5 million more registered voters in the state than Democrats. But for many years Florida was a must-win swing state, opting six times in a row for the prevailing presidential candidate, from Bill Clinton in 1996 to Trump in 2016. For much of the 20th century Democrats ruled the state. Randolph said Tuesday’s results suggest Florida could be a swing state again.
“That’s kind of up to the Florida Democratic Party,” she said. “If I were them I would be looking at the fact that Angie [Nixon] and Jolly got wildly outspent and had just hardly any resources and came as close as they did with a giant voter registration gap.”
DeSantis as governor dismissed the role of climate change in intensifying hurricanes and flooding and did little to address the emissions exacerbating the problem or hold polluters accountable. He focused his environmental policy instead on the Everglades and water quality.
Some voting locations in Florida were closed early this week because of heavy rain and flooding. Rachel Cleetus, climate program director for the Union of Concerned Scientists, said the situation demonstrated the urgency of the issue of climate change in the state.
“Florida is almost one of the most acute manifestations of this fossil fuel energy crisis affecting costs, as well as climate change is causing so much damage and the threats are growing for the state,” she said. “It’s just unmistakable that these issues are top-of-mind for voters.”

41fe8ea2b5fb.text: President Trump said Thursday night that voters had themselves to blame for the stock market's historic sell-off . Why it matters: Two days after Republicans lost the midterm elections in historic fashion, the president is lashing out at the voters who rejected his candidates and message. Driving the news: Stocks plunged Thursday, with the tech-heavy Nasdaq sinking more than 5% as AI-linked stocks sold off. Investors are skittish about the future for AI development — and the data centers that power the technology — after Tuesday's blue wave ushered in candidates who campaigned on restricting AI. What he's saying: " The Stock Market crashed today because the Dumocrats had a big Tuesday — So sad to see, you only have yourselves to blame!" Trump posted to Truth Social. The intrigue: Thursday's plunge was an unusually delayed reaction — the market actually had a massive rally Wednesday as the initial election results became apparent. Trump was quick to claim credit at the time for the conditions that led to those market highs. What to watch: Stock futures were down again in pre-market trading late Thursday, and Asian markets were broadly lower as well, pointing to the potential for another rough day Friday.

86a37e45b7f9.text: By — David McHugh, Associated Press David McHugh, Associated Press By — Paul Wiseman, Associated Press Paul Wiseman, Associated Press Share Copy URL https://www.pbs.org/newshour/world/tankers-carrying-russian-diesel-change-course-raising-doubts-about-shipments-to-u-s Email Facebook Twitter LinkedIn Pinterest Tumblr Share on Facebook Share on Twitter Tankers carrying Russian diesel change course, raising doubts about shipments to U.S. World Nov 5, 2026 7:17 PM EST FRANKFURT, Germany (AP) — President Donald Trump's plan to allow imports of Russian diesel appeared to falter this week after state and federal officials warned that handling any shipments could bring legal consequences and two tankers initially bound for the United States changed course. Trump announced an agreement with Russian President Vladimir Putin on Oct. 9 to make more than 300,000 metric tons of Russia's diesel available immediately to U.S. and global markets, with larger shipments to follow. The U.S. banned Russian energy imports after the 2022 invasion of Ukraine, and the deal angered some lawmakers and foreign allies. WATCH: First lady Melania Trump hosted Russian and Ukrainian officials. Trump met with Putin's envoy The arrangement has yet to produce a confirmed U.S. delivery. Analysts have said the imports were unlikely to do much to lower U.S. diesel prices, which have reached record highs during the U.S. war with Iran. Two sanctioned tankers that departed from the Baltic Sea port of Primorsk last month originally declared their destinations as the U.S. East Coast. As of Thursday, both had changed course, one toward Brazil and the other into the Mediterranean, according to marine data company Kpler and vessel traffic site MarineTraffic.com. A third vessel was still in the North Atlantic headed toward the U.S. but changed its destination from New York to "for orders," which leaves the unloading point open. Neither the White House nor the Kremlin have disclosed whether the agreement was put in writing or revealed the price, payment terms or participating companies. Although the Treasury Department temporarily authorized Russian diesel transactions that would ordinarily be subject to U.S. sanctions, New Jersey Gov. Mikie Sherrill advised port and terminal operators in her state to turn away ships carrying the fuel, warning in a letter dated Monday that "any effort to profit from the illegal trade in Russian fuel will be met with harsh penalties." Sherrill argued that the Trump administration lacked authority to override the import ban enacted by Congress more than four years ago and said New Jersey would use its legal and regulatory powers to prevent state facilities and companies from handling Russian fuel. A bipartisan group of senators has urged Trump to negate the deal, saying the U.S. "should not provide Putin with a financial lifeline." Lawmakers also have warned major banks, port authorities and fuel distributors that facilitating the imports could expose companies to civil or criminal liability and future congressional investigations. The administration maintains its authorization was lawful, and no court has ruled on the dispute. In response to a request for comment Thursday, the Treasury Department issued a statement saying the sanctions exemption its Office of Foreign Assets Control issued for the sale, delivery, unloading and importing of Russian diesel until April 7 was consistent with previous actions and "in compliance with all applicable laws." A Trump administration official who was not authorized to comment publicly and spoke on condition of anonymity said en route Russian diesel shipments would reduce price pressures for Americans. The official said increasing shipments was in keeping with Putin and Trump's agreement but did not specify whether any Russian fuel would reach the U.S. directly. Expensive diesel can have wide-ranging economic effects, including on consumer prices, since the trucking industry and many farmers use the fuel to produce and transport goods. Trump has tried blaming Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelenskyy for this year's diesel spikes. He has pressed Ukraine to halt drone attacks that damaged Russian refineries and curbed production of the fuel. The Financial Times first reported the diverted courses of the two sanctioned vessels, the Russian tanker Talisman and the Sierra Leone-flagged Leruo. Kpler analyst Matt Smith said it was not clear if Russian diesel shipments had U.S. buyers yet and that the third tanker in the North Atlantic also might change course. "Because of regulatory, sanctions concerns, we may not see this cargo discharge on the U.S. Atlantic coast," Smith said. "It's clear there's hesitancy here in bringing these barrels onshore just because of the implications of doing so." Kremlin spokesman Dmitry Peskov said details were not available about commercial shipments but that "all the diesel will find its buyers." Putin's special envoy, Kirill Dmitriev, dismissed the Financial Times report. "Fake. Tankers destined for the US continue on course," Dmitriev posted on X. Wiseman reported from Washington.
