A US midterms voter poll has suggested data centres were a highly motivating issue for many Americans, leading some to argue public backlash against the artificial intelligence (AI) infrastructure construction boom might have helped shape the election outcome.
BBC Verify has looked at its role in the campaign and examined the potential consequences for the AI industry.
What did the voter poll suggest?
The poll for AP and a consortium of news organisations found 56% of surveyed voters said data centres were a "crucial or major" factor in their vote, while 76% said they would oppose the construction of a new data centre in their community.
The hostile sentiment was considerably stronger among those who said they voted Democrat at this election.
This follows other recent Pew Research polling, external which suggested about half of Americans think data centres are "mostly bad" for the environment, home energy costs and quality of life, a big deterioration in favourability since January.
The congressional voter poll results certainly suggest a remarkable degree of salience for a subject which likely would not have been on most Americans' radar five years ago.
However, it is some way behind several key issues people considered a "crucial or major factor" in their vote, including government corruption (90%) and the cost of living (89%).
Did the AI backlash affect Senate races?
Three of the Senate seats flipped by the Democrats have significantly more data centres, external, Texas (595), Ohio (258) and Iowa (117), than the median of 55 across all 50 states.
And Texas alone has 31 ongoing data centre construction projects, the most of any state, external.
But other factors would also have been motivating voters in these states, as elsewhere.
BBC Verify analysis of state-level voter polling for Senate elections suggests states which swung to the Democrats either followed the national trend over data centre concerns, or seemed less concerned.
So we can't say how many votes or Senate seats were directly delivered by data centre opposition.
But it's notable that three key states in the US AI build-out, Texas, Georgia and Ohio, all elected Democrats as senators and governors who called for tighter regulation on data centres in one form or another.
These proposals include:
- temporary bans on construction
- ending tax breaks
- requirements to fully cover their own energy and water infrastructure costs
- mandates to use unionised construction workers
- stricter environmental and transparency safeguards
- local rights to veto
What could the election results mean for the future of the AI boom?
The US economy has been heavily supported in recent years by massive corporate investments in AI, external, including for data centre construction.
Official data, external shows inflation-adjusted monthly spending on building data centres, excluding the IT hardware to go into them, in August 2026 was $5bn (Â£4.2bn) - five times higher than in 2023.
Analysis by Columbia Business School, external suggests AI infrastructure investment in the US is currently larger as a share of the overall economy than spending on new railways was at the height of that boom in the 19th Century.
Cori Crider, executive director of the Future of Tech Institute, a European think tank, told BBC Verify the industry should anticipate that new state leaders will put conditions on or "even stop runaway data centre build".
Seema Shah, from global investment firm Principal Asset Management, said requirements for developers to pay for additional investment in the electricity grid, meet tougher standards over their usage of resources like water, or give up tax incentives could "raise development costs and slow new supply".
However, Heather West from the Eurasia Group consultancy said temporary bans on construction and new regulations might delay the data centre roll out, but would not stop it entirely.
She said "projects already permitted or under construction will largely proceed", but delays would affect the "next wave" of building through "local fights, slower permitting, and pressure to make data centres pay for their own power".
Analysts from the consultancy Oxford Economics have said there are also strong economic incentives for politicians to avoid policies that would severely disrupt data centre construction, pointing to tax revenue and construction jobs they bring.
Deepak Surana of the Futurum Group, a technology research firm, said he expected there would ultimately be "a negotiation, not a moratorium" from Texas state leaders on data centres to ensure no negative impact on residents' energy and water bills.
OpenAI, which has a data centre in Texas and under-construction projects in Ohio, pledged to ensure it fully paid for its own electricity on Thursday, external - one day after the midterm results.
Additional reporting by Nicholas Barrett, Rob England and Christine Jeavans

Relatives of Britons killed in this summer's wildfires in Spain have told the BBC they are disgusted, after regional politicians blocked an official inquiry into the disaster.
Nine British nationals were among the 15 people who died when fire ripped through the hillside village of BÃ©dar, in the province of AlmerÃa in south-eastern Spain, on 9 July.
Families have criticised the authorities' actions, including the decision not to send an emergency alert to mobile phones as the flames closed in.
"If that evacuation warning had come through in time, my father would still be alive," says Duncan Chard, who blames failures by officials on the day for a number of the deaths.
He lost his father Michael and his dad's partner Christine.
The governing People's Party (PP) and far-right Vox in the Andalusian parliament have rejected a request for a commission of inquiry made by the opposition Socialist party to which Prime Minister Pedro SÃ¡nchez belongs.
The PP and Vox argued that an ongoing criminal investigation would provide the necessary answers.
The Andalusian government, PP and Vox have been approached for comment.
Families of those killed say there must be a public and transparent probe.
"It's just outrageous. It's an injustice. As family members, we're absolutely disgusted. This is an insult," says Duncan Chard.
The families also say their grief has been made worse by how police have handled their loved ones' remains and belongings since the fire.
'Issue the damned alert!'
Michael Chard built his house in BÃ©dar from scratch. "He called it Casa Micas," his son said. "It was his place in the sun, it was his little paradise."
On the morning of the fire, Michael's partner Christine had met friends and was due to go to the hairdresser. "Then everything changed... the whole world changed for them," he said.
Duncan Chard said his father, who had two artificial knees and walked with a stick, left his house with Christine as soon as they saw the flames. They left their phones and passports behind and tried to escape by car, but the road was blocked.
"This is an action of a brave person who was fighting to the end," he said.
Andalusia's emergencies chief, Antonio Sanz, has said the region decided not to use the system that sends emergency alerts to mobile phones because it could not be tailored to specific communities.
Officials have said some residents needed to evacuate while others were safer staying in their homes. They also argued an alert could have caused panic and traffic jams.
The families reject that.
"Issue the damned alert!" said Chard. "Ring the bells, send the police guy out with his horn, go door to door, do everything."
Thomas-Wolf Verdonckt, a Belgian virologist whose father Stanislas, 63, died, was on the phone to him as the flames approached.
He says the victims "never received advice on what they should do, and certainly not warnings that they were in danger", and that the authorities' claim that everyone in the area was given adequate warning is not true.
"The only contact that the government managed to make with the victims was a couple of minutes before the flames engulfed everyone. One police car drove by with the sirens on. There was no talking, there was no messaging."
BÃ©dar's emergency plan was last approved in 2019, and regional officials say it was in the process of being updated. The municipality is classified by the Andalusian government as being at risk from wildfires.
Of the 15 people who died in BÃ©dar, 14 were foreign nationals: nine British citizens, three Belgian, one French and one American. The other victim was Spanish.
In the days after the fire, Sanz faced a backlash for appearing to blame the victims. He said some people who made the decision to leave "at the last minute, took the wrong path".
Verdonckt has been trying to find answers ever since the blaze.
"The morning afterwards, the Spanish officials brought out... a version of events which was simply the complete opposite of what I experienced," he said.
He also believes a public inquiry is needed to prevent a similar disaster happening in Spain in the future.
"They are putting the safety of citizens in second place. That's simply not okay."
'A huge hole in our lives'
Danni Gillam-Kirton, an assistant headteacher from Nottinghamshire, lost her parents Pete and Fran in the fire.
They had lived in BÃ©dar since 2018. Fran, a former headteacher, ran a quiz night that raised money for the local school and church.
"They were fantastic parents, my biggest champions and cheerleaders," said Danni. "They leave a huge, huge hole in our lives."
She says her mother texted her at about 19:00 to say they had packed in case they had to leave.
"They were waiting for instructions, and those instructions didn't come," she said.
Her parents died on the part of BÃ©dar known as English Hill, one of the places where, families say, the authorities' only contact came minutes before the flames arrived.
Gillam-Kirton says her grief has been made worse by the way the Spanish authorities have behaved since.
Local police had told the family that Pete and Fran's car had been "meticulously searched" by forensic specialists and that she would find nothing.
But in August, a month afterwards, Gillam-Kirton and her husband found what appeared to be human bones in the burnt-out car in which her father died. "I picked up what I recognised to be... part of a pelvis or a hip joint," she said.
Gillam-Kirton fears they were her father's remains.
Within minutes they also found her parents' mobile phones, jewellery, house keys and money. Police had earlier told the family that no personal belongings had survived.
Spain's Guardia Civil police have been approached for comment.
The fragments were eventually sent to Madrid for testing. The family says police have now told them no DNA was recovered and that the bones were those of an animal.
But Gillam-Kirton says experts, including a forensic anthropologist who worked on the Grenfell Tower

7ce978363f46.text: A federal judge temporarily blocked construction of President Trump's much-contested triumphal arch near Arlington National Cemetery, hours after the project received final planning approval. Why it matters: The 14-day order halts the Trump administration's plans to begin work immediately on the 250-foot arch as the court considers lawsuits challenging the project's legality. Driving the news: U.S. District Judge Tanya Chutkan issued a temporary restraining order early Friday barring construction of the arch for 14 days in response to a lawsuit brought by D.C. and Virginia. The order prohibits construction, excavation, land disturbance, utility installation and road closures related to the arch. The administration must certify its compliance to the court by Monday, Nov. 9. The backdrop: The ruling came hours after the National Capital Planning Commission — stacked with Trump loyalists — gave the project final approval Thursday during a packed virtual hearing that saw over 100 people testify and stretched over nine hours. Opposing speakers included the D.C. Preservation League's executive director, military veterans and some of the family members of those buried at Arlington Cemetery. Zoom in: The judge is considering separate legal challenges to the arch: One from D.C. and Virginia , and another from veterans. The lawsuits argue that the administration lacks the necessary congressional authorization and has failed to comply with federal requirements. The same judge earlier this week ordered that the government must notify the court within 30 minutes of beginning any activity related to arch construction. The government has said that Maryland-based Grunley Construction Company might already be preparing to start construction in anticipation of sign-off. The big picture: The proposed 250-foot arch has also been the source of fierce public objection and protests . Critics have accused the administration of sidestepping necessary federal historic-preservation reviews and congressional sign-off, among other concerns. Meanwhile, some Democratic lawmakers have suggested they'll make it harder for Trump to push his D.C. projects through once they assume Congressional control come January. Between the lines: Critics of the project say it would overshadow and dishonor nearby Arlington Cemetery, snarl traffic during construction, hurt the local environment and create airspace safety issues at DCA, among other issues. Building the project would take two to three years, with crews working 20 hours a day, per the administration. What they're saying: The Trump administration has argued that the arch would improve the Arlington Cemetery visitor experience, as well as improve national security by containing drones and snipers, although final plans submitted to the NCPC didn't show these elements. Trump earlier this week called the project "one of the great things we've ever done." Representatives for the White House did not immediately respond to Axios' request for comment early Friday. Editor's note: This story has been updated to reflect U.S. District Judge Tanya Chutkan's ruling.

39cd81521109.text:
- Published
A federal judge has temporarily blocked construction of US President Donald Trump's "triumphal arch" in Washington.
US District Judge Tanya Chutkan ruled that there should be a 14-day pause before any work can start on the arch which the Trump administration had said could begin this week.
Earlier on Thursday the National Capital Planning Commission (NCPC) voted 8-4 to allow construction of the planned 250ft (72m) arch.
Trump appointees on the board said the arch would be a fitting tribute to US history and to veterans but opponents have argued it would block the view of Arlington National Cemetery, the resting place of thousands of US soldiers and service people.
The so-called Arc de Trump - a play on the name of the famous arch in Paris, the Arc de Triomphe - is one of the US president's efforts to remake the capital city in his style and is meant to commemorate the country's 250th anniversary.
The approval on Thursday evening came after nearly nine hours of public comment.
It is not yet clear when construction of the arch could start, as a number of lawsuits are seeking to block it.
A rendering of the project's design from earlier this year includes a golden, winged Lady Liberty statue on the top of the arch, flanked by two gold eagles. The phrases "One Nation Under God" and "Liberty and Justice for All" are inscribed in gold on either side of the structure.
The Trump administration has said the arch would double as a complex to store military equipment - complete with the ability to deploy snipers and drones.
"There will be no facility like this anywhere in the World," Trump previously wrote on his Truth Social platform. He added that out of "the 59 top cities and Capitals", Washington is "the only one in the world that does not have a triumphal arch". He did not specify to which cities he was referring.
Mark Paoletta, the chairman of the NCPC and one of the Trump appointees, said at Thursday's meeting that the president understood "it's important to our national identity to display who we are through grand monuments".
He and other commissioners said the structure fulfils a 100-year plan to build a monumental work on Columbia Island, just as Congress and various commissions intended.
Paoletta added that the arch would honour the nation, its veterans and "provide the sacred ground of Arlington National Cemetery with the monumental gateway it deserves".
Opponents have strongly disagreed.
Anne Wright, who spent 29 years in the US military and also worked in the diplomatic service, told the BBC she would try to stop the construction.
"We'll tie ourselves to the bulldozer, we've got veterans in wheelchairs and we'll chain the wheelchairs to these things," she said.
Wright referenced this week's midterm elections, in which Trump's Republican Party lost control of Congress, saying: "[Trump's] policy of war, of ego â they've been rejected."
Fellow veteran John Pomeroy - who served in the Air Force for six years, including during the Vietnam War, and whose parents are buried at Arlington - said the arch "would lessen the solemn nature of a visit to the cemetery".
He described Trump's suggestion that the arch could store military equipment as "silly" and a "half-baked idea", arguing it would be a target for terrorist attacks.
Like Wright, Pomeroy said he would "impede construction workers as much as I can" if they came to the site to begin work.
Democratic Congressman Jared Huffman argued in his statement to the commission that the arch would disrupt sightlines not just of Arlington but of the Lincoln Memorial, fracturing "a view meant to underscore the unity and sacrifice of the American people, and doing that with a structure we often associate with emperors or kings who built grand arches as tributes to themselves".
"This is a tribute to Donald Trump," Huffman added.
Lawsuits have been filed against the plans, raising concerns about the environment, traffic congestion and safety. There is also a disagreement over whether congressional approval is needed to build the arch.
It is one of several construction projects Trump has proposed for the US capital. That includes at the White House, where he is facing legal challenges over the construction of a ballroom, which is estimated to cost $400m (Â£300m).
His plans to renovate a 106-year-old golf course, which he has dubbed "trash island", is also being challenged in the courts.

- Published
Nigeria's Federal High Court has sacked the leadership of the opposition African Democratic Congress (ADC) party - and also ruled that the nomination of its presidential candidate, former Vice-President Atiku Abubakar, is invalid.
A statement from the ADC said the ruling was another desperate attempt to cripple the opposition.
Presidential elections are scheduled to take place on 16 January when President Bola Tinubu's main challengers are again expected to be Abubakar and former Anambra State Governor Peter Obi.
What is the row about?
Several high-profile politicians joined the ADC in 2025 - disillusioned by the factional infighting in the once powerful Peoples Democratic Party (PDP).
Among them were Abubakar - who had served as vice-president between 1999 and 2007 when the PDP was in power - and former Senate president David Mark.
As accommodations were made for the line-up of political heavyweights, Mark took over as its interim chairman.
But Nafiu Bala Gombe, a former ADC national deputy chairman, argued before the court that this was not lawful as Mark and others had not been elected at a national convention.
Instead, he said, he himself should have taken over the party's leadership following the resignation of the ADC's former chairman in 2025.
This is not first time the Federal High Court in the capital, Abuja, has ruled on the leadership of the party.
In July, judge Musa Liman said Mark had been chosen in accordance with the country's laws and the party's constitution - in a case brought by another former ADC member.
Abubakar said the latest case raised serious legal concerns: "Why, after that judgment, was another case filed to reopen the same dispute?"
In a statement, the ADC added that Thursday's judgement by Justice Peter Lifu was aimed at stifling the opposition momentum and "was a calculated attempt to weaken the ADC and frustrate" Abubakar's candidacy.
What happens next?
The ADC says it will challenge the ruling at the Court of Appeal.
In a statement on X, Abubakar, 79, said it showed the "panic was real" by those who felt threatened by his candidacy, external.
He said the timing of the judgment was telling as it came "barely a day after a mammoth crowd turned out in Sokoto [northern Nigeria] to welcome him" at the launch of his campaign.
"The people of Sokoto came out in their thousands because they are hungry for change and believe in our promise to make life affordable again. What we witnessed in Sokoto is only the beginning."
Political parties in Nigeria have increasingly been taking internal issues to court.
But as it stands, the electoral commission has issued its final list of candidates, external - and Abubakar is on the ticket for the ADC with former Rivers State Governor Rotimi Amaechi as his running mate.
Will the latest ruling affect the opposition?
The ADC is seen as the most powerful opposition to President Tinubu. Many influential politicians opposed to the ruling All Progressives Congress (APC) have already defected to the party.
The legal saga could complicate things - it may cause uncertainty for hundreds of ADC candidates as well as raise questions over who has the authority to represent them.
But Abubakar, who is running for the presidency for a seventh time, is confident the matter will be resolved and called on his supporters not to be distracted.
"Nigerians deserve relief from this crushing cost-of-living crisis. We urge our supporters to remain resolute, take our message from house to house and door to door, and stay peaceful and focused," the 79-year-old said.
Peter Obi - the other main presidential candidate, who is on the ballot for a second time - has said he is shocked by Thursday's high court ruling.
He released a statement on X with the heading, external: "Do not undermine democracy".
The 65-year-old went on to say: "My concern is that three months before a general election, it is in the public interest to have certainty.
Obi had briefly joined the ADC before leaving earlier this year to join the Nigeria Democratic Congress (NDC) - in part because of the legal challenges within the ADC.
"The sustenance of democracy in Nigeria, in the midst of encroaching military rule in West Africa, should strengthen our resolve to protect opposition politics and not stamp out opposition parties," he said.
The NDC's candidate said that, as president, he would ensure that the existence of opposition parties would be respected.
"This is a time to strengthen our democracy by allowing the opposition to thrive."
Additional reporting by Chris Ewokor in Abuja

500da05091f7.text: By — Derek Gatopoulos, Associated Press Derek Gatopoulos, Associated Press Share Copy URL https://www.pbs.org/newshour/world/zelenskyy-pushes-for-clear-postwar-security-guarantees-in-ukraine Email Facebook Twitter LinkedIn Pinterest Tumblr Share on Facebook Share on Twitter Zelenskyy pushes for 'clear' postwar security guarantees in Ukraine World Nov 6, 2026 12:49 PM EST KYIV, Ukraine (AP) — Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelenskyy says his government is seeking specific guarantees from Western allies on how post-war security support would function when the nearly five-year war sparked by Russia's full-scale invasion of his nation finally ends. Zelenskyy's comments in an interview aired late Thursday followed two days of discussions among allies in Brussels that focused on postwar security and reconstruction. They also came before planned three-way talks next week in Abu Dhabi between Ukraine, Russia and the United States, the first trilateral peace discussions since February. While talks on the contours of peace continue, the grim reality of war remained front and center Friday in Ukraine, with more Russian drone attacks and a rising death toll from Moscow's guided bomb strike Monday on a former school operating as a humanitarian aid distribution center. Russian overnight drone strikes caused extensive power outages in several regions, including the Kyiv area, while Bulgarian authorities found what they identified as a Russian drone in the Black Sea. Zelenskyy seeks security guarantees for Ukraine Two days of talks in Brussels discussed postwar reconstruction, funding for 2027 and security guarantees backed by the Ukrainian government's Western allies. The meetings brought together officials from the U.S., U.K., France, Germany and the European Union, along with representatives from the World Bank and the U.S. investment group BlackRock, Ukrainian lead negotiator Rustem Umerov wrote in an online post. "We separately discussed the threats from Russia to Ukraine and all of Europe, as well as joint steps to counter them," Umerov wrote. In his television interview, Zelenskyy said he wanted to see tangible results. "What matters is that it's clear on paper," Zelenskyy said in an interview with Ukraine's private 1+1 television broadcast late Thursday. "The question isn't dozens of points, but simply an understanding of the outcome: If Russia starts (attacking) again, what will happen? Who will do what, with what means, and when?" Zelenskyy said it was important to maintain bipartisan support for Kyiv in the United States but acknowledged Democrats' sweeping victories in this week's midterm elections could have a positive effect on U.S. assistance, including the faster delivery of Patriot missile interceptors that Kyiv says are vital to fend off Russian airstrikes. "I believe our chances of getting additional assistance from the United States may now grow," he said. Trump met a Russian envoy in Washington President Donald Trump met Thursday with Moscow envoy Kirill Dmitriev but declined to give details of what they discussed. "There's going to be an agreement, it's going to be a big agreement and it's going to involve more than Ukraine," Trump said, adding that it might include all of Europe. Trump's son-in-law and envoy Jared Kushner said in a social media message that the goal of the Brussels talks was to "develop practical arrangements that address the security concerns of all sides, reduce the risk of future conflict and create a more stable and predictable security environment." European Union is skeptical The European Union played down expectations for an agreement anytime soon. "We look forward to seeing it materialize, but there's a lot of work that needs to go into it," European Commission spokesperson Paula Pinho said. The commission hosted the first day of talks Wednesday at its Brussels headquarters. "Above all, there needs to be a willingness on the side of the one who first started the war, the one who aggressed," she told reporters, in a reference to Russia. "There's a very long way to go there because we haven't seen much movement on that side." Moscow awaits details on possible deal flagged by Trump The Kremlin on Friday did not comment on Trump's remarks about a possible deal. "There are no details," Kremlin spokesman Dmitry Peskov told reporters. Peskov said Russia had received no ideas from Europe on security guarantees, but added that any discussion of security between Russia and Ukraine would at some point be "impossible" without Europe's involvement. The Kremlin spokesman accused the European side of "persistent indecisiveness and a lack of readiness," adding that European leaders "haven't even managed to decide who is authorized to speak on their behalf." Death toll climbs above 50 following Russian attack on aid location The death toll from a Russian bomb attack this week on a shelter and a former school now being used as an aid distribution center rose to 53 after more bodies were recovered from the rubble, Mykhailo Semikin, acting head of the region's military administration, said in an online post. Ten powerful guided bombs destroyed the facility at Komyshuvakha, a village in southeast Ukraine. Several dozen people are still believed to be missing after what was one of the deadliest attacks in the region in nearly five years of fighting. Relentless drone war continues Russian strikes on Ukraine's energy infrastructure caused extensive power outages in seven regions of the country overnight and Friday morning, the Energy Ministry said. The Kyiv region was hardest hit, with damage forcing continued grid restrictions and crews working on day and night shifts to restore power. Zelenskyy said the electricity outages and resulting water cuts were worst in the Kyiv area, where "the challenges are very serious" for the capital's residents and industry. Ukraine's air force said Russia launched 227 attack drones, including 86 jet-powered ones, with strikes reported at 14 locat

6c30c0edf9a5.text:
Reedâs view
The marketâs freakout, driven by AI-related stocks, suggests a US midterm election that spells disaster for the tech industry. Thatâs not the full story.
For one, many of the 40 local and state anti-data center measures that passed this week wonât halt construction altogether and certainly wonât affect compute coming online until 2029, at the earliest. What they mainly do is require tech companies to offer concessions and guarantees that a lot of the hyperscalers and data-center builders were already moving toward anyway, such as by offering cheap power, school funding, or distributing stock to help spread the wealth.
Despite the fair amount of mudslinging at data centers and Big Tech from a number of victorious Democratic candidates, many of the tech executives Iâve spoken to this week see the vote as a rejection of the fringes on both the right and the left â and theyâre relieved about that. A move to the center may mean more productive relations between government officials and the tech industry, they say, and neither side wants to screw it up. Democrats also donât want to cause a recession, and they know tech is the economyâs bright spot.
Sure, a lot of tech leaders made tactical blunders over the last couple of years when it comes to politics. Supporting a single candidate or a single party is always a bad move in the long term. Companies that took money from the presidentâs family or got sweetheart government contracts are going to face real scrutiny. We all can agree that Metaâs Mark Zuckerberg went further than he needed to in bending the knee to President Donald Trump, and got little for it.
But companies like Microsoft, Apple, and Alphabet, which have mostly played the long game politically, wonât have to change much â they stayed close to both parties. They get that the political landscape is always changing, sometimes very quickly and drastically. And when that happens, you want as many friends as you can get.

c1aea0b9f216.text:
For all the talk about how nothing can displace Silicon Valley as the epicenter of tech, it turns out New Yorkâs tech scene is growing faster than San Franciscoâs.
Tech jobs are up 32% in the last decade, according to a new report from Tech:NYC shared first with Semafor. Thatâs more than twice the rate of the Bay Area.
âIncreasingly, tech is just woven into everything about the cityâs economy,â said Julie Samuels, Tech:NYCâs president and CEO. All it takes is one subway ride to see that firsthand: Ads from tech startups offering AI tools to banks, law firms, and insurers have shot up. Thinking Machines Lab and Cohere opened their first New York offices this year, and Anthropic leased a 16-story Hudson Square building.
Software developers accounted for the most new tech jobs at non-tech companies, a sign we still need engineers and canât yet vibe code our way to an AI future.
With 452,000 jobs, New Yorkâs tech workforce remains far smaller than the Bay Areaâs 804,000, but its more diverse economy makes it more insulated from the boom-and-bust cycles that have hit Silicon Valley, Samuels said.
âWhen I spend time talking to my friends in the Valleyâ¦ they are talking about AI safety and some of the risks associated with this technology all the time,â she added. In New York, âthe conversation is much more about implementation of the technology. Whoâs using it? Whoâs paying for it? How is it changing businesses?â

Former Intel CEO Pat Gelsinger had some pointed words for the semiconductor industry this week at a private gathering of industry leaders: Namely, they arenât âparanoidâ enough.
According to a PowerPoint presentation reviewed by Semafor, Gelsinger said the industry has grown too complacent and is failing to innovate on new technologies that could create exponential performance gains.
While the AI boom has created record demand for every part of the semiconductor stack, current technologies are being stretched to their limits, he said. Everything from the lithography used to imprint circuits on chips to the technology that connects chips to one another, to the cooling systems in server racks, is beginning to run into the boundaries of the laws of physics.
One slide in the presentation was labeled: âStop waiting for the physics to break.â
Gelsinger was speaking in front of an audience represented by most of the leading semiconductor companies at the International Trade Partners Conference organized by SEMI, a chip industry trade association.
Gelsinger pointed to several new breakthroughs in areas like optics, power management, and cooling that the industry has yet to adopt. He named several new companies, including some in the portfolio of Playground Global, the venture capital firm he now works for.
âWe need AI to be 10,000X better,â the presentation said. âThatâs the opportunity. Not a better chip, but an entirely new kind of system.â

f5737d165f08.text: By — Alanna Durkin Richer, Associated Press Alanna Durkin Richer, Associated Press By — Eric Tucker, Associated Press Eric Tucker, Associated Press Share Copy URL https://www.pbs.org/newshour/politics/harmeet-dhillon-resigns-after-radical-reshape-of-justice-departments-civil-rights-division Email Facebook Twitter LinkedIn Pinterest Tumblr Share on Facebook Share on Twitter Harmeet Dhillon resigns after radical reshape of Justice Department's Civil Rights Division Politics Nov 6, 2026 12:32 PM EST WASHINGTON (AP) — Harmeet Dhillon, a conservative attorney who oversaw a radical reshaping of the Justice Department's Civil Rights Division, celebrated the mass departures of career lawyers and spearheaded sweeping investigations into elite universities, said Thursday that she had resigned from her post. Dhillon had been a powerful and divisive figure inside President Donald Trump's Justice Department since her confirmation last year as assistant attorney general, where she dramatically changed the direction of a division created during the country's Civil Rights Movement to protect the rights of minorities. "We ushered in the downfall of illegal DEI, we fought to protect women and girls' sports, and so much more," Dhillon said in a social media post announcing her departure, using the acronym for diversity, equity and inclusion. She called serving in the position "the honor of a lifetime." Though the resignation was announced on the heels of midterm elections in which Democrats swept the House and Senate in a startling rebuke of Trump, Dhillon said in an interview with Fox News Digital that she had made the decision to depart weeks earlier but was asked by the White House to remain in her post until after the elections. She said she wanted to return to the private sector and had not been asked to resign. "My decision, my choice," she said. As leader of the division, Dhillon drew fierce criticism from former Justice Department attorneys who accused her of abandoning its traditional civil rights enforcement mission in favor of conservative causes. More than three quarters of the unit's workforce at the beginning of Trump's second term have left — a move Dhillon has called the "biggest single personnel self-purge in DOJ history." She accused the past administration of pursuing a misguided liberal agenda and welcomed the departures of attorneys not aligned with the Trump administration's priorities, saying in an interview last year with conservative pundit Glenn Beck that "the job here is to enforce the federal civil rights laws — not woke ideology." During her tenure, the Civil Rights Division scrapped police reform settlements and investigations and launched probes into universities the Trump administration saw as improperly prioritizing diversity and inclusion, discriminating against white applicants in the admissions process and failing to crack down on antisemitic conduct on campus. Her pressure campaign against schools led to numerous settlements, and in one case, the resignation of the president of the University of Virginia. She also led an effort to pressure states to turn over detailed voter records despite repeated court losses. Attorney General Todd Blanche wrote in a social media post announcing Dhillon's departure that she had led the division with "conviction" and "defended the civil liberties of every American and enforced the law without fear or favor." "The Department is grateful for her dedicated public service, and we wish her every success in her future endeavors," Blanche wrote. But Stacey Young, a former Civil Rights Division attorney who now leads a network of Justice Department alumni, called her "the most destructive, lawless and hateful" head of the division in department history. "Americans' civil rights don't enforce themselves. For almost 70 years, the Civil Rights Division brought to fruition the civil rights laws that Americans demanded," Young said in an emailed statement Thursday. "Dhillon decimated it." Dhillon, who was born in India and immigrated with her Sikh family to the United States as a child, was a prominent figure in conservative legal and political circles well before being tapped to her Justice Department position. As a California lawyer, she was involved in numerous high-profile causes and legal fights, including challenging that state's stay-at-home order during the coronavirus pandemic and filing a lawsuit that accused the state of failing to verify citizenship for voter registration. She launched a bid to become chair of the Republican National Committee but lost in January 2023 to Ronna McDaniel in a race that exposed fierce internal divisions in the party. Dhillon and her law firm also represented Trump himself as a House committee investigating the Jan. 6, 2021 attack on the U.S. Capitol issued a subpoena for his testimony. The panel ultimately abandoned that effort and wrapped up its work without forcing the issue, prompting Dhillon to boast on the social media platform X that the committee had "waved the white flag." Raman's rise came in a year that saw Democratic divisions across the country, with insurgent left-wing candidates challenging establishment rivals. Raman is promising to oust the police chief, whom she views as too accommodating with federal immigration authorities. She also wants to improve basic services that have deteriorated for years and left neighborhoods with dirty, pothole-ridden streets, buckled sidewalks and broken streetlights. She said her plans could reduce the number of people sleeping in tents and encampments by at least half by 2028, when the city will host the Olympic Games. However, the problem has long proved intractable, despite billions spent in the region. The News
Catherine Cortez Masto was one of just three senators in the Democratic caucus to oppose last yearâs government shutdown. She clashed openly with her own Democratic colleague over police grants. She seemed, at times, like a lonely centrist.
Not anymore.
Democratic victories deep in red territory this week did more than power the party back to the Senate majority. They gave Cortez Masto reinforcements; the influx of red-state members next year will dramatically reshape the Senate Democratic Caucus. Self-styled moderate senators-elect like Iowan Josh Turek and Kansan Adam Hamilton could be joined by Mississippi and Alaska Democrats by the time the next Congress begins.
Progressives like Michigan Sen.-elect Abdul El-Sayed grabbed more headlines than centrists like North Carolina Sen.-elect Roy Cooper this year. But Cortez Masto, who supported an inordinate number of moderates this cycle, expects something striking to happen in 2027: the center and the left will align on the bread-and-butter priorities of the party.
âWe are going to be united about restoring the [Obamacare] tax credits, or getting rid of the harmful tariffs, or reining in Trumpâs ability to wage this war, and standing strong against a completely out of control ICE thatâs killed American citizens,â the Nevada Democrat said in an interview this week.
There will be a natural divergence, too, on some high-profile issues. It might not fully show up until a Democratic president gets elected, but voters should not expect Texas Sen.-elect James Talarico to vote with the rest of the party on energy issues.
âIf someone goes after the hundreds of thousands of oil and gas jobs in Texas and Alaska, I would expect those senators to stand up for that. Just like if somebody is going after the thousands of good-paying union jobs in mining in Nevada or my gaming industry, Iâm going to stand up for it,â Cortez Masto said.
Turek told Semafor last month that heâs a proud moderate who would have supported the Laken Riley Act and its stricter penalties for noncitizens accused of crimes â a bill Cortez Masto also backed. The Iowan also said he would have voted with Republicans on farm and data center legislation that most Democrats opposed.
His comments are a preview of how hungry some new senators will be for bipartisanship, despite a Democratic base that wants to use new majorities to fight the Trump White House.
âOne of the things Iâm the most proud of in my time in the legislature, is Iâm independently recognized as one of the most bipartisan and one of the most effective. 700 times I voted with Republicans,â Turek said.
As chair of the centrist ModSquad group, Cortez Masto worked behind the scenes to elect moderate candidates, raising $4 million for Democrats, hosting fundraisers for Turek, Peltola, New Hampshire Democratic Sen.-elect Chris Pappas, Mississippi Democrat Scott Colom and Illinois Sen.-elect Juliana Stratton.
The associated PAC spent $18 million across the country, including $3.5 million in Iowa, $2 million in New Hampshire, $1.5 million in Texas, $1 million in North Carolina, $385,000 in Alaska and nearly $5 million backing incumbent centrists in Virginia and Colorado, according to details provided to Semafor.
The group also spent for Reps. Angie Craig, D-Minn., and Haley Stevens, D-Mich., both of whom lost their Senate primaries to more progressive candidates. El-Sayed will have company on the left in the new class, joined by Sens.-elect Peggy Flanagan of Minnesota, Troy Jackson of Maine, and Stratton.
Cortez Masto still predicts Democrats will hang together.
âModerates are united in really seriously tackling the affordability crisis, just like our progressive colleagues,â she said.
Whatâs next
The new senators wonât be sworn in until next year, but big decisions for Democrats await in the lame duck. Next week the Senate will vote on a bipartisan permitting reform bill that is being criticized by environmental groups.
That bill will need support from senators like Cortez Masto, who said âthereâs some good, positive things in there for the state of Nevadaâ but that sheâs working on protecting tribal lands in the bill before she can commit to supporting it. Democrats will also have major leverage on a potential year-end government funding deal.
Next yearâs new Democratic majorities will debate how much energy to spend on working with Trump, who likes cutting deals but often struggles to get negotiations done. Cortez Masto said the Congress needs to focus on sending him bipartisan legislation like this yearâs housing bill, which became law without Trumpâs signature.
âThereâs many things we can do in a bipartisan way for him to sign. The question is whether heâs willing to do it,â she said.
Trump has sounded some conciliatory notes after the election, saying that heâll âget along, probably, with the Democrats unless they want to be destructive.â
That period of divided government will play a major role in the 2028 campaign as voters watch whether the Democratic majorities can be effective. Cortez Masto is up for reelection in Nevada; though she didnât explicitly commit to running for a third term, she said âIâm not done fighting. Iâm going to continue to be in this.â
Asked if she was genuinely undecided on running again, she replied: âNo, Iâm just telling you right now, my focus is on putting a plan in place to address affordability and accountability.â
Burgessâs view
Red- and purple-state Democrats are the majority makers of the Senate, and most of them skew toward the center. Their priorities will be critical for incoming Majority Leader Chuck Schumer, who could compete for a filibuster-proof majority in 2028 if he plays his cards right.

5a98ada8c8bd.text: By — Associated Press Associated Press Share Copy URL https://www.pbs.org/newshour/world/what-to-know-about-pope-leo-xivs-trip-to-uruguay-argentina-and-peru Email Facebook Twitter LinkedIn Pinterest Tumblr Share on Facebook Share on Twitter What to know about Pope Leo XIV's trip to Uruguay, Argentina and Peru World Nov 6, 2026 12:13 PM EST VATICAN CITY (AP) — Pope Leo XIV is returning home to the continent where he spent two decades as a missionary priest and learned to be a pastor, visiting Uruguay, Argentina and his second homeland of Peru. The Nov. 6-17 trip marks the longest and farthest of his papacy and is coming just three weeks after Leo underwent surgery Oct. 13 to remove a cancerous tumor from his right lung. Doctors nevertheless gave him the green light to make the trip. READ MORE: Pope Leo XIV welcomes Bob Dylan to the Vatican in a brief visit Latin America still is home to around 40% of the world's 1.4 billion Catholics, but the Catholic proportion of the region's population has shrunk in recent year s and the decreases are especially notable in the countries Leo will visit. Uruguay: Nov. 6-8 The trip begins in Uruguay, whose secular identity and separation of church and state are so deeply entrenched that Christmas is officially "Family Day" and Holy Week is "Tourism Week." According to Vatican statistics, nearly 77% of Uruguay's 3.5 million people are baptized Catholics. But more than half of all Uruguayans identify as religiously unaffiliated — the highest portion in Latin America – and only a fraction of those who identify as Catholic actually go to Mass regularly. READ MORE: Leo XIV has become the first pope in history to vote in a U.S. general election Leo's itinerary includes a stop at a parish in Casavalle, a poor neighborhood on the outskirts of Montevideo plagued by drug trafficking and gang violence. The church works with national and municipal authorities on support initiatives, including housing construction and addiction recovery programs. Leo will also celebrate Mass in Paysandú, some 375 kilometers (230 miles) from the capital and chosen because of its accessibility to those living north of the Río Negro, a river that crosses the country, and proximity to the Argentine city of Colón. The visit begins with a welcome ceremony at the Plaza Independencia in the center of Montevideo, a symbol of Uruguay's national identity and history. The plaza features a monument to independence hero José Gervasio Artigas. But most significantly, Leo will mark an important Catholic feast day Nov. 8, which commemorates the Virgin of the Thirty-three, the patron of Uruguay and an icon deeply rooted in the country's history and patriotism. According to tradition, 33 independence patriots acquired the small, wooden Guaraní statue and had it with them when independence was declared from the Brazilian empire in the Uruguayan city of Florida on Aug. 25, 1825. It was to the virgin that the insurgents entrusted their faith. By celebrating the feast day, paying homage to Artigas and celebrating Uruguay's independence, Leo is expected to emphasize that Uruguay's secular nationhood is intrinsically connected to its Catholic heritage. The goal is to suggest that there is still a place for faith today in even the most secular of countries. Argentina: Nov. 8-11 A pedestrian walks past a mural depicting Pope Leo, before his trip to Argentina from Nov. 8 to 11, in the outskirts of Buenos Aires, Argentina, Nov. 4, 2026. Photo by Agustin Marcarian/ Reuters Pope Francis' refusal to return home to Argentina during his pontificate, and his polarizing tenure as both archbishop and pope, left a conflicted legacy that will dog Leo's visit. But the American pope will formally honor his predecessor when he visits Buenos Aires' cathedral and in a more symbolic way when he visits the federal prison where then-Cardinal Jorge Mario Bergoglio ministered to inmates. In the capital, Leo will also meet with libertarian President Javier Milei, who once called Francis "the representative of evil on Earth." Milei later apologized. Milei's sweeping spending cuts, though, have strained relations with Argentine church leaders, who have criticized his government for cuts to disability funding and for putting economic orthodoxy ahead of the needs of the poor. That flashpoint will be on display when Leo visits the Don Orione care home in Claypole, south of Buenos Aires, a Catholic institution that houses more than 400 people with disabilities. The institution has reported facing extreme economic problems due to the spending cuts, outdated rates, inflation, and state payment delays. READ MORE: South Americans pray for Pope Leo's recovery as uncertainty hangs over his visit Leo will also hear of economic woes when he meets with business leaders, trade unions, workers and social representatives at the Argentine Catholic University. Union leaders have said they intend to brief him on the crisis, including rising unemployment, poverty, and the erosion of household purchasing power. According to official data, poverty in Argentina reached 32.3% of the population during the first half of 2026, representing about 15 million people. Another possible flashpoint between Milei and Leo could come over artificial intelligence. Milei, a Trump ally, has courted AI investment and data centers with promises of limited regulation, while Leo has warned about the threats to humanity and the environment of the AI race and called for strict, internationally policed safeguards on its development. Leo will celebrate his first Mass in Argentina at Buenos Aires' Monumento de los Españoles, where St. John Paul II led prayers for peace on June 12, 1982, during Argentina's war with Britain over the Falkland Islands. John Paul, who also came in 1987, was the first and last pope to visit. When Francis was elected, around 71% of Argentina's population identified as Catholic, according to the Pew Research Center. That percentage has fallen to 58% in 2024.

Shares in artificial intelligence and technology firms have been climbing following an enormous sell-off that wiped trillions of dollars off stock values.
The tech-heavy Nasdaq stock index opened higher following a market rout that began in the US on Thursday before spilling over to Asian and European markets into Friday.
Investors had been selling off tech shares in part due to concerns the Democrat victory in the midterm elections would mean slower artificial intelligence development.
However the latest US employment figures added to a mixed picture for American markets on Friday morning, with an unexpectedly strong 165,000 jobs added to the economy in September.
On Thursday, businesses closely linked to artificial intelligence development took a hammering on stock markets, particularly chip and semiconductor makers.
But the Nasdaq Composite opened up on Friday and flattened out around 1.7% higher by lunchtime, reversing some of its 5.5% fall.
The S&P 500, which tracks the share prices of the largest publicly-traded US companies, was around 0.9% higher by lunchtime. The Dow Jones Industrial Average opened a little down before nudging into positive territory.
Nvidia, which shed hundreds of billions in market value on Thursday after shares slid more than 9%, began Friday up more than 6% but settled around 4% higher as trading continued.
SpaceX and Tesla shares, which were also hammered on Thursday, saw more mixed gains, up more than 6% and nearly 5% respectively.
Chipmakers AMD and Micron both dropped by more than 17% on Thursday, but AMD shares had risen by about 12% on Friday while Micron was up more than 8%.
However, stock markets in Asia and Europe fared worse on Friday.
The Kospi in South Korea closed down 6% on Friday, with shares in chipmaker SK Hynix plunging more than 10%. European markets also fell, with the main indexes in Germany, France and Spain ending the day down.
In the UK, the FTSE 100, which tracks the largest companies on the London Stock Exchange, declined 1.01%.
In addition to the recent market volatility, UK traders were also digesting the latest Bank of England decision to raise interest rates and the signal that another rate rise could be on the cards to curb rising prices.
Dan Coatsworth, head of markets at AJ Bell, said it had been a brutal week for markets, and the key question was whether the jump in the S&P 500 and Nasdaq would be sustained.
"While no-one knows what happens next, it's clear that we've just seen a significant shift in market sentiment," he said.
"Once investors have had the weekend to catch their breath, next week could give a clearer indication of whether the tech trade is going down the pan or fighting back."
The market fluctuations come after the sweeping Democrat victory in the midterm elections.
A number of Democrats campaigned for new rules and regulations for artificial intelligence (AI) and data centres, and the party has since won control of both houses of congress as well as key contests in states that have been part of the AI data centre race.
US President Donald Trump on Friday reiterated his supported for what he calls "super intelligence", saying only "foolish leadership" would "say no to the riches they bring".
However, there have also been concerns over whether the enormous amounts of money being spent on AI will pay off.
Russ Shaw, founder of global tech advocacy firm Tech London Advocates, said the election result was sending a message that a rethink was needed on AI.
"The incoming Congress is going to really focus on AI in a very dramatic way," he told the BBC's Business Today.
"I'm a big fan of AI, but I'm watching what these companies are doing, and they're not communicating effectively at all, particularly in the US, about what the benefits of AI are all about."
He said people were watching firms come into their communities and build data centres while their own energy costs were going up, and those companies "have to be better neighbours".
Strong jobs figures could ease market fears
As well as the fallout of the midterms and the plunge in artificial intelligence stocks, US traders will also be digesting the latest jobs figures.
And those numbers were better than expected: US employers added 165,000 new jobs in October, well above the average monthly increase and more than double what analysts had expected.
Overall the unemployment rate, which counts the number of people who are out of work but actively looking for a job, eased slightly to 4.1% from 4.2% in September.
The Bureau of Labor Statistics (BLS) said the unemployment rate has remained in the narrow range of 4.1% to 4.3% since March.
Neil Birrell, chief investment officer at investment firm Premier Miton, said while the jobs figures may feel like second billing to the market movements they were still important.
"The US economy is running hard which may mean the risks the markets are worrying about at the moment are not such a risk to the real economy as is being feared," he said.

More than two dozen Democrats are eyeing runs for the White House in 2028, following their party's success in the US midterm elections this week, according to the man behind Barack Obama's successful re-election bid.
Jim Messina, who led Obama's 2012 campaign, said that since Democrats saw major victories in congressional races as well as state elections, he's spoken to "over two dozen campaigns" that are actively considering running in 2028 and have begun the financing process and hiring staff.
"I think you're going to start having Democrats announce exploratory committees next week or the next couple of weeks, probably after Thanksgiving", Messina told the BBC's Americast podcast.
He said he already knows someone relocating to work on a governor's presidential campaign.
He also predicted that the number could shrink as candidates faced pressure to raise large sums needed for the primary contests that will decide the party's nominee.
Messina gave some insight into the conversations he's had, saying: "When I sit down with candidates or their campaigns, I say to them, 'Tell me your economic vision for the future of this country. What are you going to do on AI?'"
Then there's another factor: the outgoing president, Donald Trump, who will still be in office during the campaign season.
"And so, do the Democrats take the bait and talk about Donald Trump every day, or do you stay focused on your message?" he said.
"It's going be the most interesting presidential [election] since 2008."
Messina, who went on to become Obama's deputy chief of staff at the White House, said the party's success in the US midterm elections was down to their ability to stay focused on the economy and the effect of Donald Trump's tariffs, which were "devastating to rural voters".
"When you're a farmer and you're paying $7 for a gallon of diesel to put in your tractor, the economics just don't work, and at the same time you're paying more for everything," he said.
Staying on message about the economy helped them flip seats in traditionally strong Republican states like Iowa, Kansas, and Texas, he said.
"The common criticism of Democrats is that we can't stick to one message. And for the first time in a very long time, Democrats stuck to the economy. They didn't take the bait on the social wars," he said.
Messina cautioned Democrats that success in this year's midterm elections was not a ringing endorsement of the party and that "the MVP of the election for the Democrats was Donald Trump".
The hard part will now be bringing the party's progressive and centrist wings together in Congress, he said.

Many extreme weather events are becoming more common and more intense around the world, fuelled by human activities such as the burning of fossil fuels.
Here are four ways that rising temperatures are affecting weather extremes.
1. Hotter, longer heatwaves
Even a small increase in average temperatures makes a big difference to heat extremes.
As the range of daily temperatures shifts to warmer levels, hotter days become more likely and more intense.
Scientists use computer models to simulate how individual extreme weather events unfold in two scenarios:
- today's world with about 1.4C, external of human-caused warming
- a hypothetical world without human influence on the climate
That way, they can estimate, external how much a particular heatwave, storm or drought was affected by climate change.
The UK experienced its hottest summer on record in 2026, which the Met Office said was made 130 times more likely by climate change.
Five widespread heatwaves affected the country, resulting in 40 days of temperatures above 30C (86F).
Head of Climate Attribution at the Met Office, Dr Mark McCarthy, described summer 2026 as "remarkable" and warned that extreme heat events would only become more common as the world warms.
Climate change has also intensified multiple heatwaves across the world this year, according to scientists at the World Weather Attribution group (WWA).
Examples include Australia's worst heatwave in six years in January, the 45C that India experienced in April and Europe's deadly June temperatures.
Heatwaves can happen as a result of heat domes, external, which are created when an area of high pressure stays over the same area for days or weeks, trapping hot air underneath.
Higher temperatures in the Arctic - which has warmed nearly four times faster than the global average, external - may be affecting the fast band of winds high in the atmosphere known as the jet stream.
One theory suggests that this is making heat domes more likely, although this is not clear cut.
2. More extreme rain
UK winters were 13% wetter, external in the decade from 2016 to 2025 than between 1961 and 1990, the Met Office says.
However, the large annual variation in rainfall makes it difficult to draw conclusions from a single decade, its scientists warn.
Globally, heavy rainfall events have become more frequent and intense over most land regions due to human activity, according to the UN's climate body, the IPCC, external.
For example, in October 2025, Hurricane Melissa became one of the strongest hurricanes to ever hit the Caribbean.
WWA researchers found that climate change increased extreme rainfall associated with the storm by 16%.
3. Longer droughts
Linking climate change with specific droughts can be difficult because there are lots of different factors that affect the availability of water.
Natural weather systems like El NiÃ±o can play a key role, as was the case with drought in southern Africa in early 2024.
But climate change is shifting global rainfall patterns. While some of the world is getting wetter, other parts are becoming drier, which can make them more prone to drought.
And heatwaves fuelled by climate change can worsen dry conditions when they do occur by increasing evaporation from the soil.
This makes the air above warm up more quickly, leading to more intense heat.
During periods of hot weather, increased demand for water, especially from farmers, puts even more stress on the water supply.
Climate-driven heatwaves worsened drought conditions throughout Europe this summer, according to the EU's Joint Research Centre, external.
Four of Europe's key rivers - the Loire, Po, Rhine and Danube - reached record low levels.
Drought was declared in all of Wales and two-thirds of England, with the highest category - "severe drought" - being used for the first time in parts of southern England.
Elsewhere, the WWA found that climate change intensified a severe drought in Jamaica and Puerto Rico from May 2026.
Global warming made extreme dry conditions 40% more likely, external in Jamaica and 30% more likely in Puerto Rico, the WWA said.
4. More fuel for wildfires
Fires happen naturally in many parts of the world.
It is difficult to know if climate change has caused or worsened a specific wildfire because other factors are also relevant, such as changes to the way land is used.
But climate change is making the weather conditions needed for wildfires to spread more likely, the IPCC says, external.
Extreme, long-lasting heat draws more moisture out of soils and vegetation.
These tinder-dry conditions provide fuel for fires, which can spread at incredible speeds, particularly if winds are strong.
In January 2026, fires in Chile and Argentina resulted in 55,000 evacuations. The area burned was around 36% larger due to climate change, according to a global report on wildfires, external.
More than 5,000 wildfires burned across Canada this summer, resulting in some of the worst air quality levels in the world being recorded in nearby cities.
Climate change made the conditions which enabled the fires to spread twice as likely, according to the WWA, external.
Many fires are started deliberately or accidentally by humans. But rising temperatures may also increase the likelihood of lightning in some forests, which can in turn trigger more fires.
The combined effects of shifting land use and climate change mean extreme wildfires are projected to become more frequent and intense globally, according to the UN Environment Programme (UNEP), external.
The number of the most extreme fires may rise by up to 50% by 2100, UNEP suggests.
2026 was the UK's second worst year for wildfires after 2022, according to provisional data, external from the housing department.
In Stourbridge, two fires destroyed 19 homes on the hottest day of the year.

Human activities are causing world temperatures to rise, posing serious threats to people and nature.
Things are likely to worsen in the coming decades, but scientists argue urgent action can still limit the worst effects of climate change.
What is climate change?
Climate change is the long-term shift in the Earth's average temperatures and weather conditions.
The world has been rapidly warming for around a century, causing weather patterns to change.
Since the 1980s, each decade has been warmer than the previous one, the Met Office says.
2024 was Earth's hottest year on record, with climate change mainly responsible for the high temperatures.
It was also the first calendar year to surpass 1.5C of warming compared to "pre-industrial" levels of the late 1800s, according to the Copernicus climate service, external.
Temperatures remained high in 2025, despite a slight cooling from a natural weather pattern called La NiÃ±a.
The opposite El NiÃ±o pattern, combined with climate change, makes it likely that 2026 will also rank among the hottest years ever recorded.
How are humans causing climate change?
The climate has changed naturally throughout the Earth's history.
But natural causes cannot explain the particularly rapid warming seen over the last century, according to the UN's climate body, the Intergovernmental Panel on Climate Change (IPCC).
This has been without doubt caused by human activities, especially the widespread use of fossil fuels - coal, oil and gas - in homes, factories and transport systems.
When fossil fuels burn, they release greenhouse gases - mostly carbon dioxide (CO2). This CO2 acts like a blanket, trapping extra energy in the atmosphere near the Earth's surface. This causes the planet to heat up.
Since the start of the Industrial Revolution - when humans began burning large amounts of fossil fuels - the level of CO2 in the atmosphere has risen by more than 50%.
The CO2 released from burning fossil fuels, external has a distinctive chemical fingerprint. This matches the type of CO2 increasingly found in the atmosphere.
What effects of climate change have already been seen?
Climate change has already had a huge effect, including:
- more frequent and intense extreme weather, such as heatwaves and heavy rainfall
- rapid melting of glaciers and ice sheets, contributing to sea-level rises
- the shrinking of Arctic sea-ice
- warmer oceans, which can fuel more intense storms and harm sea life
These changes are already having serious consequences for people and economies around the world.
Flash floods in Nepal killed more than 1,400 people in August 2026. Nepal's Finance Minister, Swarnim Wagle, said it could cost up to a tenth of the economy to rebuild.
Climate change increased the chances of the glacier collapse which triggered the flood, World Weather Attribution group scientists said.
Why does 1.5C matter and how will future climate change affect the world?
The more the world warms, the worse the impacts of climate change become.
Nearly 200 countries pledged to try to limit global warming to 1.5C above pre-industrial levels in the 2015 Paris agreement.
That target is generally understood to mean an average annual increase of 1.5C over 20 years rather than a one-off rise in a single year.
Long-term warming of 1.5C would bring serious consequences for many populations.
But an increase of 2C or more would bring even greater impacts, the IPCC says.
These include:
- more people exposed to extreme heat
- increased risks to food security in some regions due to more extreme weather
- greater chances of some climate-sensitive diseases spreading, such as dengue
- more species being threatened with extinction
The call to restrict temperature rise to 1.5C was partly designed to avoid crossing so-called "tipping points".
It is not clear exactly where they sit, but once these thresholds are passed, changes could accelerate and become irreversible.
These could include the collapse of the Greenland Ice Sheet, warm Atlantic Ocean currents or further loss of the Amazon rainforest.
About 3.3 to 3.6 billion people are highly vulnerable to climate change, the IPCC says.
People living in poorer countries are expected to suffer most as they have fewer resources to adapt.
This has led to questions about fairness, external, because these places have typically only been responsible for a small percentage of greenhouse gas emissions.
However, knock-on impacts could be felt over wide areas. For example, crop failures linked to extreme weather could raise food prices globally.
What are governments doing about climate change?
Reaching net zero CO2 emissions is essential to limit global warming, the IPCC says.
This means reducing emissions as much as possible and actively removing any remaining emissions from the atmosphere.
Most countries have, or are considering, net zero targets, external.
There has been encouraging progress in some areas, such as renewable energy and electric vehicles.
But humanity's CO2 emissions are still at record highs, causing long-term warming to reach 1.4C in 2025.
The latest UN Emissions Gap Report, external said the 1.5C limit was likely to be breached in the coming years.
A return to 1.5C by 2100 was possible, but it would require "urgent and stringent cuts to greenhouse emissions", the report added.
Otherwise, global warming could reach nearly 3C by the end of the century, the UN said.
World leaders meet every year to discuss their climate commitments.
In 2025, the COP30 climate conference ended without any new agreements on fossil fuels or deforestation in the final deal.
Countries had previously agreed on the need to "transition away from fossil fuels in energy systems" at the COP28 talks in 2023.
At COP29 in 2024, richer countries committed to giving developing nations at least $300bn (Â£223bn) a year by 2035 to help them tackle climate change. But this is far less than poorer countries say they need.

In Paris in 2015, almost 200 countries signed a landmark agreement designed to limit global warming to 1.5C and avoid its worst impacts.
But despite some progress in areas like renewable energy, the world has continued to warm at a rapid pace.
A recent UN report said the target was likely to be breached in the next few years and that "urgent and stringent" action would be needed to return the world to 1.5C.
What is the Paris climate agreement?
The Paris Agreement is at the heart of the international commitment to tackle rising global temperatures.
It came into force on 4 November 2016 and saw almost all the nations of the world agree to cut the greenhouse gas emissions which cause global warming.
However, the United States - the world's second biggest greenhouse gas emitter - withdrew from the deal in January 2026 under President Donald Trump.
The US also withdrew during Trump's first presidency, but it rejoined in 2021 under his successor President Joe Biden.
The only other UN member states outside the Paris agreement are Iran, Libya and Yemen.
What does the Paris Agreement say?
The Paris Agreement lists a series of commitments:
- to "pursue efforts" to limit global temperature rises to 1.5C, and to keep them "well below" 2.0C above those recorded in pre-industrial times, generally considered to mean the late 19th Century
- to achieve a balance - known as net zero - between the greenhouse gases that humans put into the atmosphere and the gases that they actively remove, in the second half of this century
- each country to set its own emission-reduction targets, reviewed every five years to raise ambitions
- richer countries to help poorer nations by providing funding, known as climate finance, to adapt to climate change and switch to renewable energy
The 1.5C target is generally accepted to refer to a 20-year average rather than a single year.
So, while 2024 was more than 1.5C warmer than pre-industrial times, it did not mean the Paris Agreement threshold has been breached
Why does keeping global warming to 1.5C matter?
Every 0.1C of warming brings with it greater risks for the planet, such as longer heatwaves, more intense storms and wildfires, according to climate scientists.
But a very large body of scientific evidence shows that warming of 2C or more would bring far greater impacts, on top of those felt at 1.5C, UN scientists say.
These include:
- more people being exposed to extreme heat
- higher sea levels as glaciers and ice sheets melt
- increased risks to food security in some regions due to more extreme weather
- greater chances of some climate-sensitive diseases spreading, such as dengue
- more species being threatened with extinction
- the loss of virtually all coral reefs
Some changes could become irreversible if so-called "tipping points" are crossed.
It is not clear exactly where these sit, but once these thresholds are passed, changes could accelerate and become irreversible.
These could include the collapse of the Greenland Ice Sheet, warm Atlantic Ocean currents or further loss of the Amazon rainforest.
What does The Paris Agreement promise for poorer countries?
The Paris deal restated a 2009 commitment that richer countries should provide $100bn (Â£73bn) annually by 2020 to help developing nations deal with the effects of climate change and build greener economies.
Although only $83.3bn was raised in 2020, data from the OECD, external shows the goal was reached in each of the three years after 2022.
Almost two-thirds of the money in recent years has gone towards efforts to limit global warming, while around a quarter has been used to help nations adapt to climate change.
In 2023, countries agreed for the first time that a fund should be established exclusively for loss and damage. This is money to help countries recover from the impacts of climate change.
Nepal became the first country approved to receive money from the fund after a flash flood in August 2026 killed more than 1,400 people.
At COP29 in 2024, richer nations committed to providing $300bn (Â£219bn) a year to developing nations by 2035. Developing countries - which had hoped for more - criticised the "paltry sum".
What has happened since the Paris Agreement?
World leaders meet every year to discuss their climate commitments at international summits known as COPs (Conference of the Parties).
All COPs since 2015 have tracked how countries are building on what they promised in Paris.
At COP28 in 2023, countries agreed for the first time to "contribute" to "transitioning away from fossil fuels", although they were not forced to take any specific action.
Countries also agreed to treble the global capacity of renewables - such as wind and solar - by 2030.
But the final deal at COP30 in 2025 failed to directly mention fossil fuels. Instead, the host of the conference, Brazil, published a voluntary roadmap for moving away from fossil fuels, which will be discussed at COP31.
That COP is taking place from 9 to 20 November 2026 in Antalya, Turkey and is co-hosted by Australia.
A "coalition of the willing" composed of 57 countries has also organised its own conferences separate from the COP process to discuss phasing out fossil fuels.
The first meeting was held in Santa Marta, Colombia in April 2026, and another conference is scheduled for July 2027 in Tuvalu.
Is the world on track to meet the 1.5C target?
The long-term 1.5C global warming target has not yet been breached.
But the latest UN Emissions Gap Report, external said the limit was likely to be exceeded in the next few years after "decades of insufficient climate action".
In the "lowest possible" scenario, warming would still reach 1.7 to 1.8C by the mid-century, the report said.
A return to 1.5C by 2100 is possible, but it will require "urgent and stringent cuts to greenhouse emissions", the UN added.
Specifically, emissions would need to be cut by 18% between 2025 and 2030.
