This article originally appeared in the Chicago Sun-Times. It has been republished with permission.
Joe Gamble knows what to expect when he arrives at work at the Bridgeport Art Center after days of heavy rain.
“There was raw sewage floating in the creek,” Gamble says after storms in early October. “The wind carried the smell for at least a block or two.”
The Bridgeport Art Center sits along the south branch of the Chicago River at a spot known as Bubbly Creek, a small body of water that marks the south fork of the river and divides Bridgeport and McKinley Park.
It’s a really disgusting spot after big storms.
Layers of feces, condoms, tampons and other items flushed down toilets float past and get stuck in the low-lying trees along the shoreline. There are so many condoms that they’ve picked up a nickname: “Chicago whitefish.”
More and more people have been drawn to the river in recent years for recreation, many of them taking to the water in canoes and kayaks.
Bubbly Creek appeals particularly to beginner rowers and paddlers because it’s calm and easy to navigate. After storms, though, it often stinks so badly that the smell clings to Gamble’s clothes even after he’s left the area.
“I am sometimes tolerant of smells,” says Gamble, who works at the Chicago Maritime Museum, “but it’s a different level.”
The culprit behind the stench? A sewage pumping station on Racine Avenue south of the Bridgeport Art Center building. The Racine Avenue pumping station has big pumps that help move sewer water—both wastewater and stormwater—to a treatment facility where it’s sanitized, then sent on to the Chicago Sanitary and Ship Canal, then the Des Plaines and Illinois rivers and ultimately to the Mississippi River down to the Gulf of Mexico.
But sometimes the Metropolitan Water Reclamation District of Greater Chicago, the government body that operates the station, says heavy rains mean it needs to dump untreated sewage directly into the river to prevent flooding of homes.
And it’s a lot of sewage. This year, the Racine station, which is nearly 90 years old, has dumped more than 10 billion gallons of sewage into the river. That’s more than it has since 2019. In Chicago, stormwater and wastewater go into one big sewer.
Like what happens at the Racine station on the South Side, the water reclamation district’s North Branch pumping station—at Lawrence Avenue and the river on the North Side, on the border of Albany Park and Lincoln Square—has spewed nearly 2 billion gallons of untreated sewage this year into the north branch of the Chicago River.
And all of this is happening despite the billions of dollars in taxpayer money that has been spent over 50 years on the Deep Tunnel project, the sprawling system of more than 100 miles of underground tunnels and massive reservoirs designed to capture floodwater in the Chicago area and help protect the river and Lake Michigan from pollution.
The Deep Tunnel is one of the many ways that government officials in Chicago and engineers have tried to adapt a big city that originally was built on a swamp and remains highly prone to flooding to its environment.
But climate change has complicated those efforts. It’s contributing to intensifying weather patterns that bring storms that drop rain faster and harder than ever before. That overwhelms our sewers, streets and homes.
These intense storms can bring us more than 8½ inches of rain in just 24 hours.
But Chicago’s sewer system, designed decades ago, can handle just 2 inches of rain before flooding is likely.
All of that sewage flowing into Bubbly Creek and the north branch of the river isn’t just gross. It also poses a health risk for people with weak immune systems because of the bacteria and other pathogens the water carries. The contaminated water also can wreak havoc with nature, wiping out fish populations for weeks. That’s bad for the larger ecosystem, something that environmental advocates and government officials have been working over the last three decades to restore.
Tara Hoffmann, executive director of Recovery on Water, a group that has a rowing team for breast cancer survivors, says she worries about keeping its members safe in the sometimes nasty water. Some of the women have compromised immune systems following their cancer treatment. And they are out on the water, rowing, much of the time during warm weather months.
Hoffmann recalls a particularly bad day on the creek in June, when the women were paddling through excrement.
“One of the first things you notice,” she says, “is fish up at the surface, gasping for air. They’re just desperate to breathe.”
A Threat to Wildlife
Both the Racine and North Branch pumping stations are owned by the water reclamation district. Since 2011, the independent government body that’s in charge of treating sewage and reducing flooding around Chicago has operated under a binding agreement with the U.S. Environmental Protection Agency over federal clean water violations related to the sewage.
District officials say the more intense storms we’re seeing mean that Chicago needs more flood prevention measures in addition to the Deep Tunnel, like creating green spaces and tapping other strategies in an effort to capture water before it reaches the sewers. The district has designed nearly 300 flood mitigation projects, many of them still in the planning stages.
Raw sewage is a clear threat to the river’s water quality, says Phil Nicodemus, who’s the research director for the organization Urban Rivers, which works to turn urban waterways in Chicago into wildlife sanctuaries.
“It dumps a bunch of nutrients into the water at the same time,” Nicodemus says of the sewage. “That causes a massive oxygen drop, which causes a huge die-off. If that happens enough times throughout the year, you might be talking about a whole summer without much oxygen at all. That creates an enormous problem for wildlife.”

In an interview with The Associated Press on Thursday, Schumer would not say if he would hold a Supreme Court vacancy open until after the next presidential election, as former Senate Republican Leader Mitch McConnell did in 2016. But he said that Democrats are "not going to allow any crappy nominees" to be confirmed to the Supreme Court — or to the lower courts or Trump's Cabinet, either. "The bottom line is we're not going to allow a right-winger on the court," Schumer said. Schumer's pledge came two days after Democrats won a decisive Senate majority in the midterm elections — a feat few predicted a year ago, when Schumer was facing intense criticism from progressives within his party and Senate Republicans were betting that a favorable map and backing from Trump would help them keep power. While there is still frustration with Schumer in some corners of the party, the New Yorker is expected to easily be reelected as leader by his caucus after leading them to wins in Republican-leaning states across the country. Democrats could have as many as 56 seats in the Senate if they win Mississippi and Alaska, which still have not been called — "a durable majority," Schumer predicts, that has been 20 years in the making as he has been directly or indirectly in charge of his party's Senate campaign operation. With so many seats, Schumer is betting that "it's not just a flip of the Senate once." And the party will have the power not only to reject any of Trump's nominees, forcing him to seek more moderate choices, but also to halt the Iran war and alter policies that they have been unable to counter in the minority. Navigating divided government, Schumer says focus will be on costs Schumer says the party's agenda will center around lowering prices, along with five issues that they have focused on in the minority — healthcare, housing, Trump's tariffs, childcare and lowering energy bills. He has said Democrats will try to ban federal elected officials from stock trades, and limit consumer costs from data center expansion. Democrats also want to investigate Immigration and Customs Enforcement raids across the country and scrutinize the Trump administration, which he says is the "most corrupted administration by far in American history." But Schumer would not get into specifics, or how he plans to get around Trump — who posted a picture of a red hat with the word "veto" in large letters on election night. Beyond Trump, Schumer will also have to navigate his own caucus, including progressives who have criticized him and incoming freshman who won red states and would not commit to supporting him for leader during their campaigns. And to pass any legislation, he will still have to win Republican support as well. He predicts that Republicans will suffer more losses "and keep following Trump over the cliff" if they don't work with Democrats in a bipartisan way. But that will not be easy. Schumer would not say if he would try and eliminate the filibuster, which he tried and failed to do when he was majority leader during President Joe Biden's term, to allow Democrats to pass legislation with a simple majority instead of 60 votes. "The focus has got to be on getting things done," he says. "That's all I am saying." Asked if he would support a third Trump impeachment after Trump was impeached and acquitted twice during his first term, Schumer responds that he would support an impeachment of Defense Secretary Pete Hegseth, an effort that House lawmakers have already launched. And Trump? "That's up to the House," Schumer said. Election wins two decades in the making Schumer first led his party's campaign arm in the 2006 cycle and has had a hand in every election since then, with mixed results. He attributes this year's wins to good candidates and a focus on local issues in Republican states — the effect of Trump's tariffs on farms in Iowa, where Democrat Josh Turek won, Trump's war with Canada in Maine, where Democrat Troy Jackson beat Republican Sen. Susan Collins, and data centers in Ohio, where former Sen. Sherrod Brown won after losing his seat two years ago to Republican Sen. Bernie Moreno. Still, the party's focus on lowering costs was "a message that resonated everywhere," he says. "That's a big difference than in the past." The Democrats who won were not all his recruits — in Michigan, Democrat Abdul El-Sayed represents the progressive wing of the party and beat Schumer's original choice for the seat, Haley Stevens, in the primary. But Schumer poured $67 million into that race to help El-Sayed and the two "talk regularly," he said. Schumer's future is unclear Even with his winning record this year, it is still unclear how long he will stay in power — and how long the party will support him as some call for a new generation of leadership. On his social media site, Trump praised Wiles and said she'd continue to work for his political organization. Wiles also released a social media statement Friday. "Serving President Trump in the White House has been the honor of a lifetime. I'm so proud to have been a part of what we've accomplished together from securing our border and cutting taxes to strengthening our economy and putting America First," Wiles said in a social media post shortly after Trump's announcement. She added that her commitment to "the President and the mission" will not change. Miller, long a key member of Trump's inner circle, is a key architect of the administration's hard-line immigration policies. President Donald Trump's hand reaches toward White House chief of staff Susie Wiles as they both attend a lunch with the Kennedy Center board members in the East Room of the White House in Washington, D.C., March 16, 2026. File photo by Jonathan Ernst/Reuters Wiles, the steely political operator and longtime adviser to Trump, was the first woman to ever serve in that post. The departure also came months after Wiles indicated she no longer showed evidence of breast cancer after she underwent months of treatment for the disease, a diagnosis she went public with in March 2026. Wiles is the longest-serving White House chief of staff for Trump, who cycled through four of them during his first four-year term. Miller is one of Trump's closest and longest-serving advisers, jumping on board during his longshot 2016 presidential campaign as a speechwriter. He currently serves as White House deputy chief of staff, and though he has a wide-ranging portfolio, Miller is most closely aligned with Trump's immigration policy and rhetoric on immigration. Cooper, Associated Press Share Copy URL https://www.pbs.org/newshour/politics/latino-voters-propel-democrats-to-big-wins-with-leftward-swing Email Facebook Twitter LinkedIn Pinterest Tumblr Share on Facebook Share on Twitter Latino voters propel Democrats to big wins with leftward swing Politics Nov 6, 2026 2:07 PM EST AN JUAN, Texas (AP) — Latino voters moved sharply to the left in the midterm elections, propelling Democrats to an improbable electoral sweep in Texas and in battleground House races from coast to coast. It's a remarkable pivot for a demographic that had shifted toward President Donald Trump just two years ago. "We showed our power and flexed our muscle during this election," said Democratic Rep. Gabe Vasquez, who won his battleground district in New Mexico by around 17 percentage points after winning by less than 1 percentage point in 2022. Democrats capitalized on voters' angst over rising prices and government corruption, riding a wave of frustration to retake control of the House and the Senate. Please check your inbox to confirm. Hispanics joined in that decisive repudiation of Trump and his Republican Party. In Texas, every county voted more Democratic than it did two years ago, when Trump beat Democratic Vice President Kamala Harris in the presidential race. But the more heavily Hispanic the county, generally the heavier the shift. "This is our lightning-in-the-bottle moment, that we were able to make such historic gains that we probably never conjured, especially here in Texas," said Johnny Garcia, a sheriff's deputy who won a newly created House district in the San Antonio area where Trump won by 10 percentage points in 2024. "The only way we did that is by going after the issues that were meaning the most to people." Republicans lost the gains Trump made with Hispanic voters in 2024 About one-third of Hispanic voters said they backed the Republican in their local U.S. House race, according to The AP Voter Poll, a survey of more than 100,000 midterm voters, while roughly 4 in 10 voted for Trump two years ago. The shift was especially pronounced in Texas, where voters flipped a Senate seat and the governor's office to Democrats along with every statewide office on the ballot. Roughly 7 in 10 Hispanic voters supported Democrat James Talarico in the U.S. Senate contest, while only about 3 in 10 voted for Republican Ken Paxton. The group was essentially split in the 2024 presidential election, according to AP VoteCast, an extensive survey of voters and nonvoters. Younger Hispanics' shift was even more pronounced, with swings of around 20 percentage points toward Talarico among Hispanic voters in Texas under 65 years old. Cindy Candia, a 56-year-old lifelong Democrat, was thrilled to see her party find success for the first time in her 20 years living in Texas. She was especially excited about the incoming governor, Gina Hinojosa, who grew up in the Rio Grande Valley, where Candia lives now. "She's a woman, she's Hispanic, she is from Brownsville, and I don't think anybody thought that Texas would vote for that, for that type of person," Candia said. Democrats won every House district that touches the U.S.-Mexico border — which includes seats in Texas, New Mexico, Arizona and California — for the first time since 2008. Even in the Senate race in Florida, where Republican Sen. Ashley Moody managed to narrowly win reelection, less than half of Hispanic voters supported Moody, while Trump definitively won this group two years earlier with 55% of Hispanics' support. In southwestern Kansas, three Hispanic-majority counties that voted overwhelmingly for Trump flipped to backing Adam Hamilton, who became the first Democrat in nearly a century to win a U.S. Senate contest in the state. Turnout also surged 27% over 2022 in the three counties, Finney, Ford and Seward. Fourteen Hispanic Democrats were newly elected on Tuesday, 10 of them in districts that are currently represented by Republicans or were redrawn to favor the GOP. The Congressional Hispanic Caucus will have more members than ever before, said Rep. Linda Sanchez of California, chair of the caucus' campaign arm, CHC BOLD PAC. Latino voters want someone who is "understanding of their issues" to represent them on Capitol Hill, said Leticia Gutierrez, a Democrat who won a Houston-area House district that Texas Republicans redrew in a failed attempt to pick up five more seats in the state. "I'm gonna carry all of those things with me to Washington to be able to have that lens," Gutierrez said. Manny Rutinel, a Democrat who defeated Republican Rep. Gabe Evans in Colorado, said voters responded to his life story, trusting that he understands their economic concerns after growing up in a family that sometimes struggled to make ends meet. "I think that they elected me because they know that for me it's deeply personal," Rutinel said. Democrats can't take Latino voters for granted In House districts where at least a quarter of the citizen voting-age population is Hispanic, the Democratic share in Tuesday's midterms averaged about 11 percentage points higher than Harris' 2024 performance. By contrast, other House districts saw a 7-percentage-point gain on average. In majority-Hispanic counties, Democratic Senate candidates exceeded their party's 2024 results by more than 15 percentage points. Latinos have been especially affected by Trump's immigration crackdown, which was a prominent issue alongside economic concerns in some of the most heavily Latino districts. d92dfc223175.text: By — Associated Press Associated Press Share Copy URL https://www.pbs.org/newshour/nation/3-charged-in-129-million-ai-scheme-targeting-thousands-of-companies Email Facebook Twitter LinkedIn Pinterest Tumblr Share on Facebook Share on Twitter 3 charged in $129 million AI scheme targeting thousands of companies Nation Nov 6, 2026 1:59 PM EST NEW YORK (AP) — Three people accused of using artificial intelligence to impersonate corporate executives and attorneys to steal about $129 million have been indicted on charges of wire fraud and aggravated identity theft, prosecutors said Thursday. Over more than a year and a half, Jacob Soall, 41, Sharon Hazan, 54, and Guy Sheetrit, 42, targeted thousands of companies across the world in their AI scheme, according to the indictment filed in a U.S. District Court in New York. Their victims included hospital systems in Missouri and California, a bank in Rhode Island, a financial technology company in the United Kingdom, a mutual fund company in Massachusetts and a pet food company in Florida, according to court documents. The defendants, from Spain, the UK, Israel and United Arab Emirates, were also charged with money laundering, according to the indictment. Lawyers for Soall and Sheetrit did not immediately respond to an email requesting comment. It was not clear whether Hazan had an attorney. The U.S. Attorney's Office for the Southern District of New York did not immediately respond to a voicemail left by The Associated Press. The three were arrested between June and September. In 2008, Hazan was convicted in a New York court of conspiracy to commit bank fraud, according to the U.S. Attorney's Office. The trio, who have nicknames that include "Rocky Balboa," "Superman Cash" and "Fat Boy," often targeted the companies' accounting departments. They would send an email purporting to be from the CEO and ask for help with a confidential financial transaction, according to court documents. They would also coordinate a phone or video call where the defendants used AI to mimic the voice and sometimes the image of the CEO, according to the indictment. The defendants would then tell them to contact an attorney at a major law firm, who the group was also ready to impersonate, according to court documents. Soall mainly impersonated attorneys from the UK and had a "handwritten script titled 'Lawyer Call' that he utilized to make himself seem like a real attorney when speaking with and defrauding victims," according to the U.S. attorney's office. The impersonated attorney would tell the employee to wire large payments to bank accounts across the world, according to court documents. The funds were then converted into cryptocurrency to try to conceal where they came from and then distributed to the trio and others involved, according to court documents. FBI Assistant Director in Charge James C. Barnacle, Jr. said the case shows how advanced technology can be used to commit large-scale fraud. "As criminals continue to weaponize emerging technologies, the FBI remains committed to rapidly adapting our capabilities to identify, investigate, and disrupt those who seek to harm New Yorkers and businesses operating in our communities," he said in a statement. If convicted, each of the charges have a maximum sentence of 20 years, except for aggravated identity theft, which is two years, according to the attorney's office. b0aeab50be6e.text: Calley Means , a former adviser to Health Secretary Robert F. Kennedy Jr. , said he resigned from the Trump administration over alleged internal corruption from a "concentrated group of people." Why it matters: Means left the Trump administration two weeks before the midterm elections that saw the GOP engulfed by a blue wave. He is one of the first former administration members to speak out about his time in the executive branch. What they're saying: "The simple reality in why I left is that there is a very concentrated group of people in the Trump administration that are antagonistic to what people voted for and are, frankly, — I think it's very clear — doing things for other reasons," Means said on Friday's episode of "The Joe Rogan Experience." "Particularly in many cases to enrich their families," he added. Editor's note: This is a breaking news story and will be updated with more information.

a13cd264a097.text: By — Ted Anthony, Associated Press Ted Anthony, Associated Press By — Jocelyn Noveck, Associated Press Jocelyn Noveck, Associated Press Share Copy URL https://www.pbs.org/newshour/arts/online-magazine-salon-announces-it-is-shutting-down Email Facebook Twitter LinkedIn Pinterest Tumblr Share on Facebook Share on Twitter Online magazine Salon announces it is shutting down Arts Nov 6, 2026 1:46 PM EST WASHINGTON (AP) — Salon, one of the early internet's most influential websites that featured sharp voices and political and cultural journalism with a liberal sensibility, announced Thursday it would shut down after 31 years of publication. "It has been an extraordinary privilege," the outlet said in a farewell note. The announcement, seen as a surprise, cited the fact that "the business realities of independent digital journalism have changed profoundly over the years." It did not immediately indicate what would become of its employees, though some reported they had lost their jobs. A spokesperson for the outlet said 19 full-time employees had been affected, as well as a handful of private contractors. "Over three decades, Salon has brought together politics, culture, criticism and ideas in a way that was distinctly our own," the unsigned farewell note said. "Our journalism examined power and politics, questioned assumptions, surfaced stories that deserved attention and made room for perspectives that were too often overlooked. Our writers and editors helped shape conversations about the forces changing our lives." It began shortly after the internet went big Salon began its life in the mid-1990s, barely three years after the internet itself went mainstream and a time when the "World Wide Web" was still written out in that fashion. It launched a decade before the newspaper and print magazine markets imploded — and a decade, too, before the rise of social media fragmented the journalism world. As its name suggested, Salon was initially styled as an online magazine and meeting place, a site where more provocative opinions and stories that might not be at home in daily newspapers or even then-dominant newsweeklies like Time or Newsweek could surface and generate discussion. It quickly became a place where writers wanted their work to appear. "The timing was right — readers were tired of bland, market-tested media products, and the internet allowed us to launch something original, something with a strong voice," founder David Talbot said on the outlet's five-year anniversary in 2000. It drew a cadre of high-profile writers and people who would become famous, including Jake Tapper and Glenn Greenwald. Two of its editors-in-chief, Talbot and Joan Walsh, went on to become prominent progressive political voices as well. As the internet grew, so did Salon's competition. Slate emerged the following year, and soon after, online magazines became the order of the day. Eventually, older print publications like The Atlantic began putting more content online and the marketplace of online ideas grew. Salon used Princess Diana's death in 1997 to go beyond its culture-and-criticism roots and wade into breaking-news coverage. Salon's archives will remain online for now Salon told The Associated Press that it had no immediate plans to take down its online archives, which include three decades of stories from across the world and across topics and genres. In its statement, Salon also made a point of thanking its readers. "You came to Salon for the journalism, the dialogue, the essays, the criticism, the unexpected discoveries and the sense that there was a place on the internet where ideas mattered," it said. "You read, shared, challenged, subscribed, wrote to us and kept coming back. Your engagement made Salon a publication and a community, and it gave our work meaning. We are so grateful for the time you spent with us." A free press is a cornerstone of a healthy democracy. Support trusted journalism and civil dialogue. 69d8b9db53bf.text: Democratic House members and members-elect are being bombarded with phone calls and emails urging them not to elect Minority Leader Hakeem Jeffries (D-N.Y.) as speaker, more than a dozen lawmakers and aides tell Axios. Why it matters: The calls point to a fundamental disconnect between House Democrats — most of whom are likely to vote for Jeffries — and at least a portion of their grassroots base. An incoming House Democrat told Axios they are "getting inundated" and have received "about 150" calls since the election urging them not to vote for Jeffries. A senior House Democrat said they received "over 500" calls in the last two days, telling Axios they also got asked about it in-person at a Chamber of Commerce meeting in their district. "I think our numbers are higher" than 500, said another House Democrat. "It's our No. 1 issue, and it's not close." State of play: Jeffries is in pole position to become speaker of the House after Democrats' landslide victory Tuesday, which is set to give them a massive majority of more than 250 seats. He has enjoyed the unanimous support of his caucus since becoming Democratic leader in 2022 and has never had a single House Democrat defect from him in a speaker vote. But the last speaker ballot was in January 2025, right before Democrats' grassroots base began railing against party leadership for what they perceived as insufficient resistance to the Trump administration. "Democrats in both chambers can't go back to business-as-usual politics. People want leadership that's ready to join the rest of us in this new era of politics," Ezra Levin, co-executive director of the progressive group Indivisible, said in a statement to Axios on Friday. A Democratic chief of staff who said their office got "about 300" calls told Axios: "Lots of people are saying make Jamie Raskin speaker." Raskin (D-Md.) has often been floated as a more progressive alternative to Jeffries, whose associations with pro-Israel groups and corporate PACs have long been a sore spot for the left. The top Democrat on the House Judiciary Committee, Raskin became a superstar among the party's grassroots after serving on the Jan. 6 committee. Raskin has expressed no interest in mounting a bid. A spokesperson for his office declined to comment. The intrigue: A third House Democrat, who said they've "gotten between 300-400" calls, told Axios that actor Mark Ruffalo's post on X calling for "a new speaker" has been driving much of the outreach. The post links to a Change.org petition that says Jeffries "is simply not the right choice." The petition had nearly 900,000 signatures as of Friday. The webpage includes a disclosure that the person who started the petition "receives compensation" as part of the " Change Ambassadors " program, which has raised eyebrows on Capitol Hill. Reality check: Jeffries remains the overwhelming favorite to become speaker, House Democrats say. Nobody has offered even a hint of a whisper that they would be willing to run against him. A fourth House Democrat, who said their office has gotten around 50 calls urging them not to vote for Jeffries, told Axios the odds of anyone else becoming speaker are "none." A fifth — a senior progressive who said they, too, have gotten a lot of calls — told Axios there is a "0.0%" chance of Jeffries not securing the gavel. Democrats' leadership elections are scheduled for Nov. 18-19, and a floor vote for speaker will occur when the new Congress convenes on Jan. 3. Between the lines: The volume of calls also varies, some members said, with progressives tending to receive more than moderates. "That's ridiculous. I haven't gotten one," Rep. Jim Himes (D-Conn.) told Axios, adding, "Jeffries absolutely will be speaker." Said Rep. Sam Liccardo (D-Calif.): "I'll be supporting Hakeem Jeffries, and anybody talking about a challenger is just selling tickets to a circus with no tent." Yes, but: Jeffries faces persistent skepticism and hesitance from incoming members — and not just from the progressive "Bloc." Axios interviewed nearly a half-dozen incoming House Democrats in deeply red seats Thursday who declined to state a firm position one way or another on voting for him. Don Leonard, an Ohio Democrat who won a seat President Trump carried by 10 percentage points, told a local outlet that he will be "shopping for a new leader" if Jeffries doesn't commit to changing his pro-Israel position. The bottom line: There was an expectation that the roughly dozen members of the "Bloc" would use a small majority to extract concessions from Jeffries. With a massive majority of dozens of seats, however, he has significantly more room to maneuver. His allies are confident they'll get enough Democrats to a "yes" to get him across the finish line — even if he doesn't get the unanimous vote he has enjoyed in the past.

2b041c43ffe3.text: By — Marc Levy, Associated Press Marc Levy, Associated Press Share Copy URL https://www.pbs.org/newshour/nation/opposition-to-ai-data-centers-in-the-midterms-foreshadows-tougher-regulations-ahead Email Facebook Twitter LinkedIn Pinterest Tumblr Share on Facebook Share on Twitter Opposition to AI data centers in the midterms foreshadows tougher regulations ahead Nation Nov 6, 2026 1:30 PM EST HARRISBURG, Pa. (AP) — After a campaign season filled with outrage against artificial intelligence data centers, the midterm elections ushered in a wave of Democrats pledging to clamp down on the energy-hungry behemoths. A tougher regulatory environment for AI giants and data center developers is expected to follow, even if President Donald Trump — perhaps the industry's biggest champion — stalls any federal crackdown. Data center regulation itself was not on most midterm ballots, and it wasn't among the top issues for most voters. But hard-line stances against the server warehouses were woven into the platforms of many candidates, including the Democrats who upended longtime Republican control of the governorships in Texas, Ohio, Georgia, Nevada and Iowa, many of which are data center hot spots. Skepticism of data centers, and their impact on electricity prices, often blended with the fight for affordability — a key campaign talking point for Democrats. In Texas, Clayton Tucker, the first Democrat elected state agriculture commissioner since 1986, said his pledge to fight data center development was critical to his victory. Everywhere he went, he said, ranchers worried that data centers posed an existential threat to their dwindling water supplies. "You know, there's an old saying around here that 'whiskey's for drinking and water's for fighting,'" Tucker told The Associated Press. "And that's exactly what happened." Data centers were a persistent bogeyman in attack ads According to data from AdImpact, campaigns large and small spent more than $380 million on television ads mentioning data centers. Democrats outspent Republicans on the topic by a more than 3-to-1 ratio. Sweeping wins by Democrats could have far-reaching implications for data centers. Besides taking control of Congress, Democrats flipped at least five governors' offices and took full control of state governments in five more states: Wisconsin, Minnesota, Pennsylvania, Nevada and Michigan. Data Center Watch, a project of AI security consultancy 10a Labs, said it tracked winning candidates for Congress and governorships and found the vast majority had expressed support for stronger regulation or even a moratorium. Among governors, 32 of the 34 victorious candidates in races where AP called a winner support stronger regulation or restrictions. Twelve of the 34 support bans or moratoriums, it said. During the campaign, Wisconsin Gov.-elect David Crowley, a Democrat, changed his position under pressure from his Republican opponent to take a harder line against data centers. Initially opposed to any moratorium, Crowley later said he supported one as well as abolishing the state's sales tax exemption for data center operators and developers. In an interview Thursday with AP, Crowley said he's having discussions now about what he'll propose once he takes office. In the mix are things like requiring developers to disclose more about their water and energy consumption, ensuring a community supports a project before it can go forward and insulating ratepayers and taxpayers from the energy costs of the projects, Crowley said. The industry sees a need to build trust AI giant OpenAI published a framework Thursday enumerating new commitments to the communities where it develops data centers. The company said it was asking federal, state and local policymakers to write "clear rules for how the industry builds." "Lawmakers should establish rules to advance responsible investment, protect residents, and ensure that the benefits of AI infrastructure are broadly shared," the post said. An industry association, the Data Center Coalition, echoed the sentiment that developers need to keep trying to build trust with public officials and communities. A coalition official, Dan Diorio, said the industry is aware many midterm winners have vowed to impose a moratorium. "We should expect them to want to deliver on those promises, but there are going to be real world consequences of that," Diorio said in an interview. Those consequences, Diorio said, could include host communities missing out on tax revenue or payments from tech companies. Data centers are also driving a broader economic expansion that encourages investment in domestic manufacturing, he said. Wall Street sees red lights ahead after the election The election of data center skeptics adds challenges to stock markets riding high on the AI boom. On Thursday, the Nasdaq, which is full of AI-related and other tech stocks, sank 11% below its all-time high amid worries that data center construction may slow because it's getting costlier to borrow money. AI data center construction is driving much of the U.S. economy's growth, and any slowdown could have a broader chilling effect. In an analyst report, Morgan Stanley said decisive results for Democrats carry "greater expectations for data center restrictions" that, under new state regulations, could "split the country into areas that are open to new data centers and those without." It singled out Texas' election of Democrat Gina Hinojosa for governor as the "most important election result" for data center development. Hinojosa has said she'd block a permit for a data center if it wasn't a good deal for Texans or residents hadn't gotten a say in the matter. She defeated Republican Gov. Greg Abbott, who had touted Texas as "the epicenter of AI development" before trying to clamp down on it late in the campaign. Morgan Stanley also said Ohio's election of Democrat Dr. Amy Acton as governor "creates significant risk of data center project delays in the state."

Meet Fu Shuang and Ping Ping: New giant pandas in Atlanta
Two 6-year-old pandas made their public debut at Zoo Atlanta in Georgia. Ping Ping and Fu Shuang arrived in late September but spent their first few weeks in quarantine adjusting to their new habitat. Zoo Atlanta is now one of three US zoos with giant pandas, alongside San Diego and the National Zoo in Washington DC. Giant pandas have been a symbol of US-China relations since Beijing gave a pair to the National Zoo in Washington DC in 1972.

0459a9efa976.text: By — Kelvin Chan, Associated Press Kelvin Chan, Associated Press Share Copy URL https://www.pbs.org/newshour/world/eu-accuses-tiktok-of-violating-its-digital-rules Email Facebook Twitter LinkedIn Pinterest Tumblr Share on Facebook Share on Twitter EU accuses TikTok of violating its digital rules World Nov 6, 2026 1:07 PM EST LONDON (AP) — The European Union accused TikTok of breaching the bloc's digital rules because its algorithm recommends a nonstop stream of personalized videos to users including those that it says could hurt mental health and body image. The short-video sharing platform must change the design of its "For You" feed so that users have more control over opting out of seeing certain content, the 27-nation bloc's executive arm said Friday. The platform failed to assess how its recommendation systems could lead people into "rabbit holes" that threaten their well-being, regulators said, by feeding them similar video clips based on what they've previously viewed or liked even if they are "triggering" such as clips about weight loss and mental health struggles. TikTok said the European Commission's findings are "fundamentally inaccurate and distort our platform's architecture and our commitment to user safety." "We have a strong record of protecting our community while giving users direct and intuitive control over their content experience," the company said in a statement. The company will have a chance to respond before the European Commission issues its final decision, which could include a fine of up to 6% of TikTok's total annual revenue. "Every time a user scrolls or likes a video on TikTok, the algorithm serves more of the same, leading users down rabbit holes they cannot easily escape from," European Commission Executive Vice-President Henna Virkkunen, who oversees tech sovereignty, said in a statement. "Today's preliminary findings show again that TikTok needs to step up its efforts to protect users' well-being, including those of minors." TikTok has added some measures, such as a "not interested" button to reduce the "rabbit hole effect," but the commission said they're ineffective in reducing how often harmful content is recommended. European regulators said they want TikTok to make changes to its "For You" feed, including giving more weight to 'explicit preferences' of people using the platform, stopping reliance on viewing time as a metric for recommending content, and making user controls more accessible. It's the latest in a series of enforcement actions targeting TikTok by EU regulators using the bloc's Digital Services Act, a wide-ranging rule book that requires tech companies to adhere to a framework under threat of hefty financial penalties. The commission opened its investigation into whether TikTok violated the DSA more than two years ago. This year, it has already issued two other sets of preliminary findings, accusing the platform of breaching the rules with " addictive design " features that lead to compulsive use by children and charging it with failing to adequately protect children's privacy rights. 'Permanent, serious' dialogue needed with China on AI: tech-focused lawmaker
“The Chinese Communist Party doesn’t want rogue AI agents hacking their systems and their water authorities any more than we do,” Rep. James Walkinshaw, D-Va., said Thursday.
Rep. James Walkinshaw’s vision for artificial intelligence regulation includes maintaining “permanent, serious” dialogue with China to mitigate the risk that powerful AI models pose.
That won’t be easy, but if the U.S. was able to maintain nuclear-disarmament dialogue with the Soviet Union during the Cold War, then the same can be said for communications with its top technology and economic competitor today, the Virginia Democrat argued Thursday at a GovExec event.
Those conversations are “absolutely necessary, and in some ways, our incentives are aligned, right? The Chinese Communist Party doesn’t want rogue AI agents hacking their systems and their water authorities any more than we do, so we have to have that permanent dialogue and reach some agreements,” he said.
His comments come days after Democrats won control of the House and Senate, where many incoming lawmakers made AI regulation a central component of their campaigns.
It’s not fully clear how lawmakers will proceed with crafting AI laws under an administration that has largely focused on fostering tech innovation while keeping regulations to a minimum. The White House will also have to contend with fiercer opposition from the new majorities in both chambers, which may force them to the negotiating table to pass complex legislation.
Walkinshaw is hardly the first member of Congress to advocate for U.S.-China AI dialogue, though his position gives the comments added weight. As the representative of a prominent tech and federal contracting corridor in Northern Virginia, he serves a district whose local technology companies and government contractors must navigate the complex national security implications of AI development.
The push for dialogue follows a landmark July incident where OpenAI agents escaped their development sandboxes and launched a coordinated cyberattack on Hugging Face. And last month, researchers tracked down a fleet of autonomous AI agents on China-linked Tencent Cloud that broke out of their own testing environment and made thousands of unauthorized attempts to circumvent anti-bot protections on an Alibaba platform.
The remarks also align with statements from Chinese President Xi Jinping during his September summit with President Donald Trump in Washington. Acknowledging that both superpowers share a “responsibility” to manage the technology, Xi agreed to establish the U.S.-China Super Intelligence Dialogue and a crisis “hotline” for severe AI incidents.
Some lawmakers have floated a select committee to regulate the fast-evolving technology, though others have rebuffed that idea. Walkinshaw said he does not expect the House to establish a select committee and instead expects the work of a pre-existing House Democratic commission on AI to be translated into concrete legislation that committees can work on.
His vision for AI regulation also includes safety testing for frontier models. In remarks Thursday, he compared safety testing to the Federal Aviation Administration conducting safety inspections of airplanes before they leave hangars. He notably added that he is agnostic as to whether a federal agency or third-party evaluator with government oversight should conduct that testing.

European Union prosecutors have begun investigating the possible misuse of EU funds meant for upgrading the Spanish railway line where a train crash killed 69 people last week.
Prosecutors backed by a special unit of Spain's Guardia Civil security force said they were conducting the inquiry at the offices of Adif rail infrastructure authority and rail safety agency AESF.
The 28 October accident on the Madrid-Seville high-speed line was one of the worst railway disasters in Europe this century.
It is the second EU fraud inquiry opened into Spain's railways this year, after 46 people were killed on the same line at Adamuz in January.
Last week, a train operated by state-owned operator Renfe ploughed into the back of a stationary train belonging to private Spanish company Iryo outside the village of Urda, around 130km (80 miles) south of Madrid.
The LZB communication system that monitors the position of trains had gone down, and the Renfe train had been given the all clear to start running at normal speed, even though the Iryo train ahead of it had been unable to restart.
The two accidents nine months apart on the same line have claimed 115 lives and dozens more injuries.
The European Public Prosecutor's Office (EPPO) said on Friday it had begun conducting investigative measures at Spain's rail authorities "after the opening of an investigation into possible fraud affecting EU funds, external allocated to the renovation and upgrading of safety, signalling and communications systems on the Madrid-Seville high-speed railway line".
The EPPO highlighted high public interest in the case, but said no further details would be made public.
As part of the process, a Spanish judge assigned to the case has to ensure the investigation complies with legal safeguards, including authorising any measures that might involve house searches or phone-tapping.
The Urda disaster has damaged the Socialist-led government of Prime Minister Pedro SÃ¡nchez ahead of a 29 November general election and the party is trailing the conservative People's Party (PP) in most opinion polls.
Close SÃ¡nchez ally Ãscar Puente resigned this week as transport minister, after seeing two deadly accidents on his watch this year.
The PP and far-right Vox say Puente's resignation is not enough and they have demanded that SÃ¡nchez resign too.
Many people in Spain have now become wary of taking the train, with reports of widespread cancellations and empty station platforms.
A funeral for the 69 victims at Urda will take place on Tuesday at Toledo cathedral, in the same province that the disaster happened.
Puente's successor, Carlos Cuerpo, has vowed to take all necessary measures to "restore the confidence of Spaniards in our high-speed rail".
Cuerpo met survivors of January's Adamuz disaster on Friday and they handed him a list of 11 demands for improving safety on Spain's railways.

The Leonid meteor shower is set to dazzle sky gazers across the UK throughout November.
The celestial spectacle takes place from now until 30 November with the peak taking place on the night of 17 November.
There could be the chance to spot up to 10-15 meteors per hour.
The shower is made up of dust particles from the Comet 55P/Tempel-Tuttle, which leaves a trail of debris as it follows its path around the Sun.
These particles enter the Earth's atmosphere at up to 44 miles (71km) per second - meaning these streaks of light are the fastest meteors in the sky.
How to spot the Leonids
Experts advise finding a safe, dark location away from sources of light pollution such as street lights.
The meteors will be visible with the naked eye, with no binoculars or telescope required.
However, giving your eyes some time to adapt to the dark - perhaps 20 or 30 minutes - will give you the best chance of spotting them.
A wide open space is the best place to be, giving a full view of the night sky.
Meteors could be visible anywhere but the Leonids' radiant - the point from which they seem to appear - will, as the name suggests, be around the head of the constellation Leo, meaning this is the best part of the sky to focus your gaze.
As with all celestial spectacles, clear skies will be a must.
What is the forecast on Saturday and Sunday evenings?
This weekend's forecast will not necessarily be great news for those hoping to catch the start of the shower.
While the weather will often be dry, large amounts of cloud are expected to fill the sky in many areas with the chance of a few spots of rain or drizzle.
At the moment the best opportunities for clear skies appear to be in southern and western areas of England and Wales on Friday and Saturday nights, with more cloud in northern England, Northern Ireland and Scotland.
By Sunday night it is likely that more parts of the UK will be clear.
However, fog could be an additional issue, forming in any areas where skies remain clear for any length of time, obscuring the view.
Overnight temperatures will drop into single figures with the chance of a touch of frost in a few locations so if you are looking at the night sky for any length of time you will want to wrap up warmly.
You can always check the hour-by-hour cloud, fog and temperature forecast for your area by checking BBC Weather online or the app.
And if you miss them this weekend then take heart that viewing conditions look particularly good around their peak in the middle of November. This is because the Moon will be below the horizon around midnight, meaning its reflected light will be less likely to spoil the view.

Alan Armstrong of Oklahoma entered the U.S. Senate to fill a vacancy in March with a clear priority: pass permitting reform that he argued was necessary based on his experience leading a major natural gas pipeline company.
Now, as he prepares to leave office, that goal is within reach—with big potential benefits for the company and him personally.
The bipartisan permitting bill slated for a vote next week would overhaul regulations for building all kinds of projects. But it also includes provisions Armstrong promoted that could push through a disputed pipeline that the Williams Companies, his former employer, has tried to build through New York for more than a decade.
When state regulators denied a water quality permit for the Constitution pipeline in 2016, it was a rare rebuke for an industry unaccustomed to having government officials block its projects. Provisions in the new bill would limit New York’s authority to deny it again.
Williams is now asking federal regulators to revive their approval of the pipeline from more than a decade ago.
Armstrong continued to hold at least tens of millions of dollars in Williams stock as of Oct. 22, according to his most recent financial disclosures. He also hired three former Williams colleagues to his staff, one of whom maintained his role as senior vice president and general counsel at the company while temporarily serving as Armstrong’s chief of staff in the Senate.
The Bipartisan American Affordability and Jobs Act would greatly restrict states’ and tribes’ ability to deny or place conditions on water quality certifications. The bill would also make other changes to accelerate approval of Constitution and other pipelines, including restricting judicial review and scaling back certain environmental reviews.
Environmental lawyers say changes to what’s known as a Section 401 certification of the federal Clean Water Act appear tailored to help a small number of gas pipeline projects. One of the companies that would benefit most is Williams, where Armstrong served as chief executive and chairman for 15 years until his appointment in March by Oklahoma’s governor to fill a vacated U.S. Senate seat.
Williams has already received extraordinary support from the Trump administration.
President Donald Trump claimed he made a deal with New York Gov. Kathy Hochul to get the Constitution pipeline built, which she denies. Environmental Protection Agency Administrator Lee Zeldin has pledged support for the pipeline, and his agency is finalizing a rule change that would restrict states’ and tribes’ ability to condition permits in order to safeguard water quality, similar to the permitting bill.
In October, the U.S. Department of Energy said it would devote up to $42 million under the Defense Production Act to pay permitting costs for the project.
Armstrong’s office did not respond to questions for this article, though he has frequently criticized what he calls a broken regulatory system that drives up costs.
“When every pipeline, transmission line, power plant and industrial project is treated as something to stop rather than something to build responsibly, the costs do not disappear,” Armstrong said in a Senate speech in July. “They accumulate slowly, until families are paying more, reliability is deteriorating, and investment is moving elsewhere.”
Williams spokesperson Blake Jackson said the company supports the permitting bill “and all its provisions to provide a tech-neutral and level-playing field for all energy infrastructure.”
Some residents of upstate New York see things differently.
A Threat to State Waters
Anne Marie Garti, a lawyer who owns a home near the Constitution pipeline route, fought the project the first time around. From the start, “there was a huge amount of opposition,” Garti said, “and skepticism.”
The Constitution project would run 125 miles from the Pennsylvania shale gas fields across upstate New York, eventually connecting to other interstate pipelines. The Federal Energy Regulatory Commission, also known as FERC, oversees interstate gas pipelines. But states retain authority under the Clean Water Act, which requires energy companies like Williams to apply for water quality certifications.
Garti called these permits the “weak link” in the regulatory process. Taking inspiration from an earlier permit denial in Connecticut, she and other residents focused their fight on the pipeline’s potential effects on 251 streams along its route. State regulators said 87 of those streams provided trout habitat.
Building the pipeline would require digging trenches across streams, diverting their flow and clearing trees and brush along their banks. The work would send sediment into clear waters, raise temperatures and temporarily damage habitat for trout and other species, according to the New York Department of Environmental Conservation’s 2016 denial.
State regulators rarely reject water quality permits, which are needed not only for pipelines but many federally regulated projects. In a recent survey of 24 states by the Association of Clean Water Administrators, no state reported a denial rate higher than 3.5 percent—most said they’d never denied a permit.
New York denied the certification for Constitution in 2016, saying the company had failed to address the project’s water quality impacts and had not provided sufficient proof that Williams would comply with state standards. The denial kicked off years of legal wrangling. In 2020, Williams said it would not pursue the pipeline and a federal appeals court ruling later vacated the federal permit.
Another permit denial followed in 2019 for a second Williams project: the Northeast Supply Enhancement (NESE) pipeline that would have run from New Jersey across the New York harbor. A few other pipeline proposals in the Northeast and mid-Atlantic faced similar fates, while in some cases regulators imposed conditions to protect waterways.

Immigration, once a political strength for Trump, became a liability after two years of mass detentions, deportations and armed agents in U.S. cities. Geoff Bennett: President Trump has replaced White House Chief of Staff Susie Wiles with Stephen Miller, the hard-line architect of his immigration agenda, following that crushing midterm defeat. Immigration, once a political strength for Mr. Trump, has become a liability after two years of mass detentions, deportations, and armed agents in American cities. Miller has called Democrats a -- quote -- "domestic extremist organization." Liz Landers reports on the appointment and the GOP's post-election reckoning. He gets it, very good politically, and he's a very good manager. He will do a great job, great manager. Liz Landers: The fallout from the midterm elections reaching his inner circle. She was the first woman to hold the role and was Trump's longest tenured chief of staff. Wiles will be replaced by Stephen Miller, the current deputy chief of staff. Miller is one of Washington's most polarizing power brokers. He's a chief architect of the administration's immigration crackdown, but his portfolio has expanded to include national security issues. Meanwhile, for Trump, a president who made loyalty to him a defining test of his party, criticism now comes from within it. Rep. Pete Hegseth, U.S. Defense Secretary: You see, they attack me, they attack us because we are effective. Liz Landers: The discontent isn't confined to Washington or even to Republicans. Arthur Young, Mississippi Voter: I just be believe people were just trying to send a message that we're tired. Liz Landers: For some voters like this one in Mississippi, the blue tsunami was a reflection of Americans' frustrations with a system they say stopped delivering for them. Arthur Young: We're tired of politicians enriching their pockets while everybody else is suffering. Liz Landers: But, in Mississippi, one of two Senate races, along with Alaska, that are still too close to call, the outcome remains uncertain. Scott Colom (D): We're going to follow the lawful process. Liz Landers: But back at the White House today, President Trump remains optimistic. Amna Nawaz: And Liz joins me now. So, Liz, let's start with the promotion of Stephen Miller to chief of staff. What is your reporting show the president is signaling with that move? Liz Landers: He's signaling that he's doubling down on this hard-line approach to immigration and that he is rewarding Stephen for his loyalty. I do think that's a big factor. The president alluded to that in the comments he made this afternoon. Stephen Miller is a fighter. He aggressively defends the president on television and behind the scenes, from what I have been told. And he is MAGA through and through. He believes in this agenda that the president is pushing. He is so pro-MAGA that he comes across as quite anti-Democrat. So he has made some of these recent TV appearances where he's called the Democrats the party of freaks, weirdos, losers, and crazies. So, even though President Trump claims that he is going to work with this Democratic majority that's incoming in January in Congress, we're already hearing from Democratic leaders like Hakeem Jeffries, who will likely be the speaker, calling Miller a reckless extremist today. The incoming chair of House Oversight, Robert Garcia, says that his committee plans to continue to investigate Miller. Amna Nawaz: And we know who Stephen Miller is now. But remind us how he got to this role. Who is he? Liz Landers: Miller is from Southern California. He has been politically active from a young age, really since he was in high school. When he went to Duke, he also kind of rose to national prominence at that time because he was doing television hits on national TV defending the lacrosse team against those false rape allegations at the time.
