The EU's former Brexit negotiator has warned that the UK cannot "cherry pick" which elements of the single market to which it subscribes, after Andy Burnham said he wanted to explore closer economic ties with Europe.
The prime minister has said rejoining the bloc's internal market was among options he could pursue as part of a reshaping of ties since the UK's exit from the EU nearly six years ago.
But Michel Barnier told the BBC's Sunday with Laura Kuenssberg that EU members would insist on the UK readopting certain conditions, such as the free movement of people, to gain access.
He said there was not a "single market Ã la carte" menu from which the UK could pick and choose what elements it wanted to adopt.
Barnier - who led the EU delegation during Brexit talks between 2016 and 2021, and had a three-month spell as French prime minister in 2024 - said the "door is open" within Europe to the UK rejoining as an EU member.
But he insisted that any move to rejoin the single market - which allows for goods to be freely traded without border controls - would require the UK to follow the same terms as other members.
He added that this included compliance with regulations designed to promote the circulation of goods, services, capital and people, referred to collectively within EU institutions as the "four freedoms".
"There will be no possibility to have one freedom and not the other. The four freedoms are clearly the four conditions to be inside a single market."
Since becoming prime minister in July, Burnham has suggested he could commit Labour to pursuing a much closer future relationship with Europe, including asking to rejoin the organisation as a full member, though he has ruled out major changes before the next election.
His predecessors have struck a series of deals with the EU on different aspects of how the UK and EU interact post-Brexit.
Both sides are hoping to use a meeting in Brussels in 10 days' time to unveil deals on food standards, youth visas and re-linking British industry to the EU's carbon trading regime.
Of the four freedoms, the free movement of people - which allows EU citizens to live and work elsewhere in the bloc without a visa - was a key issue during the 2016 Brexit referendum.
Burnham's immediate predecessor, Sir Keir Starmer, ruled out re-establishing it for the UK in Labour's 2024 election manifesto and any move to advocate it again would prove a key dividing line with the Conservatives and Reform UK at a future poll.
Burnham recently said in an interview that he would not re-establish free movement of people without a referendum, prompting Downing Street to clarify that he was not advocating its return at this point.
He has previously said he wanted to lay out "different options" for the relationship with Europe at the Brussels summit later this month, before trying to find a consensus with the British public on a new relationship.
Barnier also predicted that EU countries would reject reinstating the British financial rebate, first negotiated in 1985, that lowered UK contributions towards the EU's annual budget while it was a member.
The UK's decision to leave the bloc had created "a new situation", he said, meaning a new rebate would be "off the table".
'False promises and lies'
Barnier also compared Reform leader Nigel Farage to French politician Marine Le Pen. He said: "We have our own Farage. It is Mrs Le Pen. The same populism, the same lies, the same false promises."
Asked by Kuenssberg to clarify what he was referring to with his accusation of lies, Barnier said "for instance, when Mr Farage and Mr Johnson promised the UK people to get back [Â£350] million per week, it was not true, it was not possible. It was a lie".
The Vote Leave campaign, of which Boris Johnson became a key figure, has been criticised previously for the slogan on the side of their campaign bus that said Britain sent Â£350m a week to the EU, adding: "Let's fund our NHS instead".
Johnson said in 2017 that "once we have settled our accounts, we will take back control of roughly Â£350m per week. It would be a fine thing as many of us have pointed out if a lot of that money went on the NHS".
Critics have said that the Â£350m per week was an approximate sum which represents a "gross contribution" and did not take into account the UK's Â£75m-a-week rebate nor the EU's investments in the UK.
Johnson has since defended the claim, saying the Â£350m was based on the UK's gross contribution to the EU, and was in fact an underestimate as UK contributions were due to rise.
âIn his memoirs published in 2024, Johnson said EU money spent in the UK was not "democratically controlled by the British people", and "even if the net figure was only Â£175m, that was still a hell of a lot of money".
Farage, who led Leave UK and was not part of the Vote Leave campaign so not connected to the Â£350m claim, said: "It is the same old Barnier - arrogant, out of touch and a bully. He vindicates our decision to leave every time he opens his mouth."

94f4d6bdcc5c.text: By — Deepa Bharath, Associated Press Deepa Bharath, Associated Press Share Copy URL https://www.pbs.org/newshour/world/what-is-diwali-the-festival-of-lights-and-how-is-it-celebrated Email Facebook Twitter LinkedIn Pinterest Tumblr Share on Facebook Share on Twitter What is Diwali, the Festival of Lights, and how is it celebrated? World Nov 7, 2026 6:01 PM EST Diwali is the most important festival of the year in India, particularly for Hindus, and widely marked by prayers, family gatherings and the lighting of fireworks. More than one billion people across faiths celebrate it in the world's most populous nation and its diaspora. The name Diwali comes from "Deepavali," meaning "a row of lights." Celebrants place rows of traditional clay oil lamps outside their homes to symbolize the victory of light over darkness and knowledge over ignorance. The festival follows the Hindu lunar calendar, typically falling in late October or early November. This year, Diwali falls on Nov. 8. The victory of light over darkness While Diwali is a major religious festival for Hindus, it is also observed by Sikhs, Jains and Buddhists. Its origin stories vary by region but share a theme: the victory of good over evil. In southern India, Diwali celebrates Lord Krishna's victory over the demon Naraka, who is said to have imprisoned women and tormented his subjects. In northern India, it honors the triumphant return of Lord Rama, his wife, Sita, and his brother, Lakshmana, after 14 years of exile in the forest. Lights, fireworks and feasting A worker makes firecrackers at a factory ahead of Diwali, the Hindu festival of lights, on the outskirts of Ahmedabad, India, on Oct. 29, 2026. Photo by Amit Dave/Reuters Traditions vary by region but commonly include lights, fireworks, feasting, new clothes and prayers. In southern India, many people take an early morning bath with warm oil to symbolize bathing in the holy River Ganges for physical and spiritual purification. In the north, worship centers on the goddess Lakshmi, who symbolizes wealth and prosperity. Gambling is a popular tradition, reflecting a belief that those who gamble on Diwali night will prosper throughout the year. Many people buy gold on Dhanteras, the first day of the festival, believing it will bring good luck. Other traditions include setting off firecrackers and exchanging sweets and gifts with friends and family. Celebrations also feature rangoli — geometric and floral patterns drawn on the floor with colorful powders. Other faiths' traditions Jains observe Diwali as the day Lord Mahavira, the last of their great teachers, attained nirvana, or liberation from the cycle of birth, death and rebirth. Sikhs celebrate Bandi Chhor Divas, which overlaps with Diwali, to commemorate the release of Guru Hargobind from imprisonment under the Mughal emperor Jahangir. Some Buddhists mark the day as the anniversary of Emperor Ashoka's conversion to Buddhism in the third century B.C. Celebrations across North America in 2026 Disney World in Florida held several days of Diwali festivities ahead of the holiday, featuring more than 500 dancers. Diwali at Times Square marked its 11th year in New York City with international performers, cultural bazaars and a lighting countdown at the Ball Drop Tower. Other community events across North America include Diwali Eve on the Waterfront in Jersey City, Diwali Family Cruise Lights on the Hudson in New York, Diwali on the Bay in San Francisco and a Diwali Fusion Bollywood Boat Party in Vancouver, British Columbia. Last year, California became the third U.S. state to make Diwali an official state holiday. Israel's president says he will task opposition leader Gadi Eisenkot with forming a new coalition government.
Isaac Herzog has been holding talks with political parties after neither Eisenkot's bloc nor that of Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu secured a majority in Israel's parliament, known as the Knesset, following last week's election.
Eisenkot will now have 28 days to try to form a new administration, with a potential 14-day extension.
"Now is the time to form a national emergency government. I will do everything to ensure we are worthy," the former military chief wrote on X.
No political party in Israel has ever won an outright majority, meaning all governments have been coalitions.
Netanyahu's right-wing Likud party and its far-right and ultra-Orthodox Jewish allies won 53 seats in the 120-seat Knesset, while Eisenkot's centrist Yashar party and three other Jewish opposition parties in his bloc won 48.
Two Arab-led alliances, the United Arab List and the Joint List, together won an unprecedented 19 seats following a surge in turnout among Arab voters.
That positions them as potential kingmakers. However, all but one of the Jewish parties pledged before the polls not to work with them to form a government.
Herzog said that, after consulting all parties during the week, he would give Eisenkot the first chance to form a government.
A statement from the president's office said he had informed both Eisenkot and Netanyahu of the decision.
Following consultations with delegations from the incoming Knesset members, Eisenkot received 67 recommendations for the premiership and Netanyahu 46, the statement said.
The president has broad discretion to pick someone they believe has the best chance of building a coalition and does not have to choose the leader of the party with the most seats.
The election results had implied three possible options for the formation of a government: a national unity administration involving both Netanyahu and Eisenkot, a right-wing coalition involving Netanyahu and defectors from Eisenkot's bloc, or an Eisenkot-led government supported by the Arab parties.
Eisenkot and every member of his bloc bar one has previously refused to enter government with Arab parties, but there has been speculation that an agreement could be reached.
He could also attempt to reach a deal with ultra-Orthodox parties, but that too would be difficult.
There is precedent for a unity government. In 2020, following three deadlocked elections, Netanyahu and his centrist rival Benny Gantz agreed a power-sharing deal in which the leadership rotated between the two.
During his consultations with the parties, Herzog had said that to prevent another round of elections and to build a stable government, he expected "factions and their representatives to understand that, in the current reality, not every commitment and promise can be fulfilled".
In the period 2019 to 2022, one of the most politically fractured in Israeli politics, there were five separate elections as Netanyahu and his rivals struggled time and again to co-operate.

61b0cc7c10fa.text: By — Grace Abels, PolitiFact Grace Abels, PolitiFact By — Madison Czopek, PolitiFact Madison Czopek, PolitiFact Share Copy URL https://www.pbs.org/newshour/health/sen-chris-murphys-stroke-at-53-highlights-a-trend-strokes-among-younger-adults-have-risen Email Facebook Twitter LinkedIn Pinterest Tumblr Share on Facebook Share on Twitter Sen. Chris Murphy's stroke at 53 highlights a trend: Strokes among younger adults have risen Health Nov 7, 2026 4:14 PM EST This article originally appeared on PolitiFact. After U.S. Sen. Chris Murphy, a 53-year-old Democrat representing Connecticut, was hospitalized Oct. 31 following a stroke, his chief of staff said she was "optimistic" he will make a full recovery. Stroke rates are higher overall among older adults, so a stroke at his age may sound surprising — but it's become more common. WATCH: Sen. Chris Murphy discharged from hospital after stroke Stroke rates among adults ages 20 to 54 years old have risen in the last 30 years. Researchers found that the stroke incidence rate among adults from 1993-94 nearly doubled in 2020, jumping from 33.90 cases per 100,000 people to 62.18 cases. Stroke rates remain much higher overall among older adults, but the rate for older people declined during the same period. When Centers for Disease Control and Prevention researchers compared stroke incidence data from 2011-13 with 2020-22, they found that stroke prevalence increased 14.6% among people 18 to 44 and 15.7% among people 45 to 64. There isn't one single explanation for the rise, but risk factors for stroke such as high blood pressure and obesity are up among young people, too. A study in Florida found that from 2014 to 2022, young patients (18 to 55 years old) who experienced the most common form of stroke increasingly had existing vascular risk factors such as hypertension, coronary artery disease, diabetes or sleep apnea. READ MORE: Connecticut Sen. Chris Murphy is in the hospital after having a stroke, his office says To decrease stroke risk, health professionals advise people to quit smoking and using drugs recreationally and to eat a balanced diet that incorporates many colorful fruits and vegetables. It's important to maintain an active lifestyle and manage conditions such as high blood pressure, diabetes and cholesterol. High blood pressure significantly increases a person's stroke risk, and some people can feel completely healthy even if they have hypertension, Dr. Elizabeth Rosen, neurologist at Tufts Medical Center, told Prevention. Regularly seeing a health care provider can help people identify stroke risk factors early, Dr. Aaron Shoskes, a University of Utah neurologist, said in April. A visit with a primary care doctor can reveal information about a person's weight, family history of stroke and other health conditions. "Once those numbers are known, the next step is working with a clinician to manage them," Shoskes told the university. "Early intervention makes a big difference." 3db08aefcfb9.text: Nvidia CEO Jensen Huang is facing increasing congressional scrutiny after multiple reports Friday night suggested he had a romantic relationship with a purported Chinese spy. Why it matters: Huang is arguably the world's most powerful CEO, the man who runs one of the world's largest companies and whose products are central to the world's most important technology. The mere suggestion that he was in some way compromised by a Chinese intelligence agent could quickly become a major, bipartisan focus of the incoming Congress. What they're saying : Sen. Chris Coons (D-Del.) promised a probe of the latest Times report and Huang's relationships. "The more I learn about the insane relationship between the Trump Administration, Chinese spies, and AI billionaires, the more I'm convinced there is nothing this administration does that isn't corrupt. Congress will investigate and get answers," Coons posted to X, linking in another post to the Times' story. Catch up quick: A series of reports over the last 10 days has raised concerns about an allegedly illicit relationship with an undercurrent of espionage. Oct. 29 : The New York Times reported that Jensen Huang and a tech executive named Alice Huang had a "close relationship," that U.S. authorities had concerns about her intelligence connections with China, and that President Trump had been briefed on the situation. Oct. 31 : The Wall Street Journal reported that intelligence authorities in the U.S., Singapore and Taiwan all had reason to believe that Alice Huang might be a Chinese spy. Nov. 5: A group of House Republican committee chairs asked Jensen Huang to give them a briefing on his relationship with Alice Huang and Nvidia's controls over sensitive information, saying they need to determine "the extent to which U.S. national security has been placed at risk." Nov. 6: Both the New York Times and Financial Times reported that Alice Huang was in fact a Chinese spy, recruited by top intelligence officials specifically to spy on Jensen Huang. Her purported goal: to convince him to lobby U.S. officials to allow chip exports to China. The FT also reported that Jensen Huang and Alice Huang had a romantic relationship. For the record: Nvidia has repeatedly and firmly denied that Jensen Huang's relationship with Alice Huang was anything but a typical business contact, and insisted that no sensitive information would have been shared with her or anyone else. The company did not respond to Axios's request for comment on Saturday. The Chinese government has also publicly denied engaging with Alice Huang to spy on Jensen Huang. The big picture: President Trump and his administration have staked the country's future on beating China in the race to develop and control advanced AI. Nvidia's chips are central to that vision, and Jensen Huang has been close to Trump throughout this term. There've been back-and-forth fights over whether Nvidia's chips can be sold to China or not, but also extensive reporting that those chips are making their way to Chinese companies regardless. What's next: The Republican chairmen who requested a briefing from Jensen Huang gave him a Nov. 11 deadline to set a date for their meeting.

Trump, while he was at his golf club in Florida, posted on social media that he made the offer to "the Great Dana White, a violent Fighter and Warrior" to become the Republican president's chief spokesperson. 563c91d03004.text: Single-holder executive offices only; excludes courts, commissions and federal offices. Data: Associated Press; Axios analysis; Chart: Andrew Pantazi/Axios Democrats' midterm gains extended deep into the machinery of state government: They swept every statewide executive office on the ballot in Texas, Georgia, Nevada, Wisconsin and Arizona. Why it matters: These low-profile victories will shape what millions of Americans pay for electricity, what their kids read in class and which party runs the 2028 presidential election in key states. The big picture: Democrats captured five Republican governorships, in Texas, Georgia, Ohio, Iowa and Nevada. But the scale of their gains becomes clearer farther down the ballot. Georgia: Democrats wrested all eight statewide executive offices on the ballot, including governor, attorney general, secretary of state and school superintendent. Texas: They flipped all six posts, defeating Gov. Greg Abbott and Lt. Gov. Dan Patrick in a state that hadn't elected a Democrat to statewide office in 32 years. Nevada: Democrats won all six executive offices, flipping governor, lieutenant governor and controller. Wisconsin: Democrats completed their Badger State domination, picking up the office of treasurer, the sole statewide office still held by a Republican. Arizona: Democrats held governor, attorney general and secretary of state. They lead in the three other executive races: treasurer, school superintendent and mine inspector. Data: Associated Press; Axios analysis Between the lines: The Democratic gains reach offices that decide which policies advance, which don't and which get challenged in court. Attorneys general: Nathan Johnson in Texas and Tanya Miller in Georgia will decide when their states sue the Trump administration and what corporations they investigate. Secretaries of state: Democrats flipped these offices in Georgia, Ohio and Indiana, putting new officials in charge of running the 2028 presidential election there. Texas' lieutenant governor: Vikki Goodwin will preside over the Senate, where the lieutenant governor picks committee chairs and decides which bills get a hearing. The intrigue: Some offices are hyper-specific and rarely command national attention, but they have a big influence on the issues Democrats championed this election. Utility bills: Shelia Edwards' victory and Peter Hubbard's reelection give Democrats a 3–2 majority on Georgia's Public Service Commission, which sets utility rates and approves long-term electricity plans, putting Democrats in charge of decisions that affect the climate and affordability. Oil and gas: Jon Rosenthal's victory breaks Republicans' monopoly on Texas' three-member Railroad Commission, which, despite its name, regulates oil and gas production and pipeline safety . Classrooms: Democrats won three Republican-held Texas State Board of Education seats and lead in a fourth that would change the majority. Publishers have historically tailored the nation's textbooks to the Texas board's conservative curriculum standards. It recently adopted social studies changes that Muslim advocacy groups criticized as discriminatory. The courts: Democrats won all four Texas Supreme Court seats on the ballot, cutting an all-Republican court to a 5-4 GOP majority. They also swept Texas' 15th Court of Appeals, which hears appeals involving state government . Data: Axios research; Chart: Andrew Pantazi/Axios Case in point: Democrats flipped New Hampshire's Executive Council, giving them veto power over Republican Gov. Kelly Ayotte's nominees and major state contracts. Republican councillors repeatedly rejected family-planning contracts with Planned Parenthood . A Democratic majority could force compromises. The bottom line: Many voters couldn't name the officials they just put in charge of their power bills, textbooks and ballots. But they'll soon feel their decisions.

Climate change readiness and helping people access the countryside are among priorities in a five-year plan for a national landscape.
The North Pennines National Landscape Management Plan 2026-31 has been adopted by the Cumberland, Westmorland and Furness, County Durham and Northumberland councils.
Work to ensure the North Pennines was "as prepared as possible for future climate challenges" included restoring peatland to help reduce flooding and equipping farmers with wildfire fighting equipment such as drones.
Chris Woodley-Stewart, director of the North Pennines National Landscape (NPNL), said: "In many ways, its the most ambitious plan that we've ever had, but also the most realistic."
National landscapes were formerly known as areas of outstanding natural beauty, and the North Pennines features heather moors, dales, woods and one of England's highest waterfalls High Force.
NPNL is mainly funded by the government and other charitable organisations.
One of the priorities in its management plan announced last month was adapting to "warmer, wetter winters and hotter, drier summers".
NPNL said uplands were "especially vulnerable to the effects of climate change" through rising temperatures, altered rainfall patterns, and increased frequency of extreme weather events.
Mitigation work like protecting existing woodlands and restoring carbon-rich peat soils would help safeguard upland ecosystems but also support downstream communities by "improving water quality and reducing flooding", it said.
One of the area's largest land managers, Raby Estates, said it worked with NPNL on wildfire prevention measures including managing its farmers' fuel loads and providing firefighting equipment.
Duncan Peake, chief executive at Raby Estates, said drone equipment to help spot fires was a "really significant, additional tool in our wildfire control kit".
As part of the management plan, NPNL said it was would also work with farmers who wanted to get the skills and equipment for farm visits.
Peake said farmers on their estate were already taking groups of mostly young people "who wouldn't normally have an opportunity to come to the countryside" to help them understand how farming works.
Woodley-Stewart said: "You can't make people come to the countryside and invest in the local economy, but you can help to create circumstances in which they feel this landscape is for everybody."
He said the five-year plan would guide the policy of the local authorities but would not be compulsory.
"There's no stick here, it's all carrot," Woodley-Stewart said, adding: "Everyone has a role to play in its implementation."

More than 430 seagrass shoots have been discovered in the Fowey Estuary, giving conservationists hope that one of the UK's most important marine habitats can be brought back to Cornwall's waters.
The new growth was recorded across 50 patches of seabed during summer surveys carried out by Cornwall Wildlife Trust.
The findings come despite fears the restoration trial might not succeed when only six seedlings had emerged by the end of April.
Chloe James, of Cornwall Wildlife Trust, said the shoots were "hugely encouraging" after an "uncertain start to the spring".
Volunteers collected seagrass seeds from a donor meadow in Torpoint in autumn 2025 before planting them in the estuary. The seeds remained buried through the winter before beginning to grow in spring.
"The new growth is a powerful reminder of why restoration work takes time, persistence and a willingness to keep learning," said James.
Earlier work involved some of the trust's first attempts to restore seagrass meadows in Cornwall's estuaries, with volunteers collecting and planting thousands of seeds while researchers tested different restoration methods.
Seagrass, which may not look remarkable, is often described as the sea's equivalent of a woodland, said the trust.
It provides shelter and nursery grounds for fish and other marine life, helps improve water quality, locks away carbon and reduces coastal erosion.
The trust said mainland Britain had lost up to 92% of its seagrass meadows over the last century. Previous research highlighted by the project found seagrass could capture carbon up to 35 times faster than tropical rainforests.
The restoration effort has not been without setbacks. In the Helford Estuary, algal growth appeared to wipe out planted seedlings at one site, although three plants were later found to have survived and had started spreading.
More seeds are due to be planted in the Fowey Estuary and Helford Estuary, with further monitoring planned for spring 2027.

Republicans are in soul-searching mode after the coalition that powered Donald Trump to three straight presidential nominations imploded in spectacular fashion in the 2026 midterms.
The stunning election defeat immediately raised questions about the party's future post-Trump.
But there are no easy answers as Republicans face the choice of doubling down on Trumpism or trying to chart a new path forward in his final years in office.
The depth of the problem was captured by outgoing Florida Governor Ron DeSantis, who called the midterms "close to an extinction-level event for Republicans".
Others struck a more optimistic tone. Vice-President JD Vance, who blamed the midterm results on public anger over the war with Iran, argued the party could turn things around. Nevertheless Vance acknowledged the fallout will be messy.
"There will be a lot of infighting and arguing over what happened and why," Vance said.
The wide range of reactions on the right highlights deep fault lines in the party that formed around Trump's improbable rise to the presidency in 2016 and never really went away.
It's too early to tell which faction will win out. But while Republicans are still licking their wounds, the intraparty battle Vance predicted is already under way.
The party must decide whether it will be "centred on one figure, one guy, or on a wider set of ideas like conservatism that can win outside the deepest red places," Rina Shah, a Republican strategist, told the BBC.
Critics on the right - the "Never Trumpers" who opposed his first White House campaign - are pushing for a return to the Republican Party's pre-Trump roots, citing the historic losses around the country on election night.
But simply turning back the clock on Trump will be extremely difficult if not impossible to do.
The party has been wholly transformed during Trump's decade-long reign. Most Republicans have shifted to the right on domestic issues like immigration, and rejected the interventionist foreign policy of the George W Bush era that led to the wars in Iraq and Afghanistan.
In Congress, the more moderate establishment wing of the party that disliked Trump from the start has almost entirely disappeared, replaced by conservative Trump backers who echo his nativism and populist rhetoric.
That trend continued this year, as old-guard Republicans like John Cornyn in Texas and Maine's Susan Collins, both of whom clashed with Trump over the years, were voted out of office.
Three days after the election Trump appointed Stephen Miller as his new White House chief of staff, replacing Susie Wiles.
The move signalled Trump has no plans to moderate his policies or message in his remaining years in office. Miller, who had been serving as the president's chief domestic policy adviser, is a longtime Trump aide known for his hardline immigration policies.
One of the architects of the Make America Great Again (Maga) movement, Steve Bannon, predicted a "civil war" in the party after the midterms.
Afterwards, he blamed the Republicans' defeat on the economy and "foreign wars". "I don't think we implemented the Maga programme," he said, calling on Trump to double down on mass deportations.
But other Republican strategists said the midterms were a wake up call for Make America Great Again (Maga) loyalists who want Trump's political movement to outlast his presidency.
"There's still plenty of Maga voters out there who have supported Donald Trump through thick and thin," said Whit Ayres, a Republican strategist.
"But there is also a significant portion of the Republican Party that's non-Maga, and that's a majority now."
Should Republican hopefuls distance themselves from Trump?
The party lost control of the House and Senate, as well as governorships and state legislatures in red states like Texas and Kansas where Democrats had been shut out of power for decades - and where Trump won by double digits when he was on the ballot.
The stunning upsets underscored the fickle nature of political coalitions.
Trump expanded the Republican base in 2024, increasing support with Latinos and younger voters among other key groups. Republicans hailed the gains as a sign of future strength for the party.
Just two years later, the party lost ground with nearly every critical voting bloc. According to a New York Times analysis of voter data, Latino support for Democratic candidates increased by 29 percentage points from 2024-26. Support from young voters 18-29 years old increased by 33 points.
The swings reflected polling ahead of the midterms that found widespread disapproval with Trump's handling of the economy, immigration and the war with Iran.
Democrats also capitalised on a public perception that the Trump family and administration is rife with self-dealing and corruption. The president's focus on the White House ballroom and other Washington construction projects also contributed to a sense among voters that he was more focused on his legacy than addressing affordability issues.
It's a sentiment shared by Benjamin Shrader, the leader of the Young Republicans in Austin, who was still shell-shocked when he spoke to the BBC in Texas the morning after his party was almost wiped out in the state by a Democratic "blue tsunami".
Shrader said Trump was still a "force of nature" when asked to reflect on how the president had used his first public appearance after the results to show off the White House ballroom project.
He hesitated before adding: "I would focus on issues that are not ballrooms, that are not renaming things. I would focus on what matters."
The evidence in the immediate aftermath of the midterms suggests that Republicans could benefit by distancing themselves from Trump ahead of 2028.

New Zealand voted in a new government as fog choked the capital, Wellington, on Saturday - and the mood was as palpable as the grey weather.
"It's pretty flat," 21-year-old Imogen Vlutger says. "There's this kind of apathy and a bit of dread."
"Tired. I think we're all tired," Symone, 28, admits.
"I didn't even vote," one man in his 40s sheepishly confesses. He couldn't bring himself to tick any of the boxes, he explains, declining to chat further.
"Wellington's a bit of a bubble," another voter says, expressing a caveat I heard often, before describing feeling disillusioned.
But polling shows this is a pervasive sentiment across the country: the national mood is low and faith in politics is even lower.
More than half the country no longer sees it as a land of opportunity, a recent study found, while a similar portion fears that the future looks even worse.
Many Kiwis feel the economy is in ruins, there are no jobs, the cost of living has become sky high, the sense of community that used to be a source of national pride is breaking down and there's no sense of genuine progress on policy solutions.
A record number of them are abandoning ship in search of brighter futures elsewhere.
Saturday's election also saw a record number of voters desert the two major parties, giving neither a clear mandate.
But it brought new highs for parties across the spectrum: the left-leaning Greens, the right-wing libertarian Act Party and the centrist Opportunity Party â the latter of which had never won a seat in parliament before but could now hold the balance of power with seven.
"You have voted to change New Zealand politics for good," the party's ecstatic leader Quilae Wong told Kiwis on election night. "I personally came into this because I was frustrated at the slow pace of change."
It will likely be weeks before we know exactly who will make up the governing coalition and what deals have been made to form it.
But this is only the first of many challenges facing whoever is the next prime minister of a country at a crossroads.
A perfect storm
New Zealand hasn't always felt like this.
For a long time, the country was viewed as a land of milk and honey â literally â for those who worked hard, with its people ranking amongst the most positive in the world.
A satisfying career, access to quality healthcare, and a close network of family and friends â which research suggests are the three most important building blocks of a happy life â were all there for the taking, University of Auckland Prof Robert MacCulloch says.
"The lifestyle was good," the world-leader in the study of happiness economics tells the BBC. "You weren't the highest paid, but you could get by nicely."
Not anymore.
Many who spoke to the BBC said the country's decline accelerated into a dive during the Covid pandemic.
Unemployment is now at an 11-year high and rising. For Kiwis aged under 24, things haven't been this bad in three decades: jobs are so scarce that one in three either cannot get enough work or have none at all.
Michael Dawson says he did everything he thought he was supposed to: finished school, studied a trade and obtained a qualification, and has applied for dozens of jobs.
But it's been a year now and the job market is so dire he hasn't had a single interview.
"It has sucked. A lot... I'm somewhat cynical with the way I think [about the future] now," the 20-year-old says.
Zainab Ali, chief executive of support service Youth Inspire, has never seen demand so high, with waitlists for its employment aid workshops stretching into the hundreds.
The young people who do make it through their doors on the outskirts of Wellington are disheartened.
"The things we used to hear from everyone's grumpy uncle around the Christmas table sometimes, our young people are now starting to give us that same feedback: like, 'What's the point?'"
Meanwhile, household electricity bills have jumped drastically, partly driven by global supply shocks. New Zealand remains one of the least affordable places on Earth to rent or buy a home. High inflation means every dollar is having to stretch further.
The island nation produces enough food to feed its population eight times over, but about a quarter of adults are skipping meals because the price of groceries â set by a supermarket duopoly â is among the highest in the developed world.
And the headlines are full of healthcare crises: long waiting lists, chronic understaffing, crumbling health infrastructure and climbing costs for patients. Few stories have captured the state of the system like the death of a man who collapsed in an emergency department toilet after a nine-hour wait in July.
"There's a segment of the population that are facing real material hardship... and then there's another segment of New Zealanders that are quite anxious that they could be next," political scientist Luke Oldfield, from Victoria University of Wellington, says.
Increasingly polarised public debate â around topics like MÄori rights and the Treaty of Waitangi, healthcare for LGBT+ people and immigration â have added to the mental load for many in those communities.
"There's been a few groups feeling like they're being used as a political football," Dr Lara Greaves, who studies Indigenous politics, says.
This perfect storm is driving about 180 people to leave the country every day â a record-breaking exodus that is dividing families, shrinking communities and draining talent pools.
Siblings Sam and Emily tell the BBC that they love New Zealand but find it hard to keep finding reasons to stay. Their friends are leaving en masse and even their parents have considered moving to Australia.
"It's not just that you're being rewarded for going to Australia, it's that you're kind of actively being punished for staying here," Sam says.
There are still large parts of the country that feel differently, though.

055b243a044b.text: No state looms larger, more dominant or more instructive about the future of American politics, governance and AI than Texas . Why it matters: Texas is suddenly — and unexpectedly — the American story. It's the battleground and proving ground for immigration policy, AI, data center growth, Hispanic voting patterns, and the direction of the Democratic Party. Put simply, it seems nearly impossible for Republicans to retain the presidency in 2028 without the Lone Star State. And it seems nearly impossible for AI to keep growing so fast if Texas rejects or dramatically slows it. Texas is so populous, so wealthy, so Hispanic, so energy-rich — and now so top-to-bottom blue — that both parties see it as a de facto nation-state capable of reordering ... everything. "Texas is everything," Steve Bannon, one of the top voices of MAGA, told us. Bannon has been so Texas-obsessed all year that he took his influential podcast, " War Room, " on the road to the " forward lines " of Texas for months at a time. Bannon said Texas needs to be an early focus for Stephen Miller, the new White House chief of staff. Houston Mayor John Whitmire on Friday directed police to limit cooperation with ICE, saying : "Elections matter." Bannon said he expects many more such actions, with Texas becoming a sanctuary state "quickly unless dramatic action is taken." "Trump is going to be forced to federalize the border," Bannon said, either with National Guard troops or federal law-enforcement agents. The big picture: Texas was red as blood on Nov. 2, the day before midterms. Now it'll have a Democratic governor ... lieutenant governor ... attorney general ... comptroller ... land commissioner ... agriculture commissioner ... Texas House ... and U.S. senator, 37-year-old James Talarico. Talarico won by double digits over state Attorney General Ken Paxton, and Gina Hinojosa — who'll be Texas' first Latina governor — upset three-term Gov. Greg Abbott. Democrats won all four state Supreme Court seats on the ballot and are set to flip Texas' Board of Education. The new Texas House speaker is likely to be an 87-year-old Black woman, Senfronia Thompson , a Houston Democrat first elected during the Watergate era. Everything's bigger in Texas , especially in politics going forward: 1. South Texas' border counties broke the GOP's thesis. Republicans built their Texas future on South Texas Hispanics, based on President Trump's performance there in 2024. Talarico won Hidalgo by 46 points, Cameron by 38 and Webb by 47. Trump had narrowly carried all three! The lesson: The Valley didn't realign. It swung — or came home to Democrats, as many South Texans would say. 2. Immigration came home, too . Republicans' border-security argument was undermined as President Trump's ICE, cheered on by Abbott, hit South Texas' rural counties and then moved hard-line enforcement into cities across the state. Hidalgo voters were driven by a sluggish economy and the historic immigration crackdown. In Harris County (Houston), voters cited immigration, corruption and GOP leaders' policies as motivating their votes — and 72% of voters in Hispanic precincts in Harris County backed Hinojosa. The takeaway: Voters wanted a secure border and undocumented criminals removed. They didn't sign up for enforcement in their own neighborhoods. 3. Texas is now ground zero for the AI wars. Elon Musk, the world's richest person , moved to business-friendly Texas from California along with other tech elites , and brought along Tesla's headquarters . Musk posted a reminder Saturday to incoming leaders: "SpaceX and Tesla have prospered in Texas, because we were not constantly operating under an oppressive and extractive state government. ... As California became increasingly difficult, due to extreme taxes and overregulation, we moved our major domestic expansions and HQ to Texas." Musk made himself a midterm issue , spending $225 million on races in Texas — about half of his national total . Talarico ran straight at him : "This Senate seat doesn't belong to Elon Musk." After the rout, Musk said on X that data centers in space were looking "pretty appealing." Texas was on track to become home to one of the world's largest concentrations of data centers, but that buildout is now at risk . In August, 57% of Texan registered voters in a University of Texas/Texas Politics Project poll opposed a data center in their own community, including 43% of Republicans, 60% of suburbanites and 60% of rural voters. Gov. Greg Abbott (R) tried to pivot from his bullishness on data centers but still lost reelection . On Aug. 3, he paused new data center grid connections. Hinojosa called data centers a physical manifestation of a governor doing the bidding of monied interests. Sid Miller, the Republican ag commissioner, said he didn't vote for Abbott and blamed him for not listening to Texans on data centers: "He needs to go." 4. All-of-the-above energy now has a Democratic landlord. Texas pumps the oil, drills the gas, harnesses the wind, runs its own grid — and powers the AI boom. Hinojosa pledged a moratorium on new data center approvals until the Legislature passes protections in 2027. One energy lawyer called it "a brand-new day in Texas" for policy once considered settled. The challenge: Wage war on oil and gas, and Texas snaps back red. Govern like Texans have through much of the state's history, and Democrats could get a lease measured in decades. 5. The Hispanic vote is America's biggest swing bloc . Texas had a record-setting surge in Latino turnout, and Talarico won 68% of them . Two years ago, that same bloc gave Trump the Valley. This time, the more heavily Hispanic the county, the heavier the leftward shift . 6. Republicans suddenly have a 2028 math problem. Texas has the second-most electoral votes, after California. Tough choices, uncertainty, and scrutiny may lay ahead for defense contractors
With a new Congress in 2027, companies could see more anti-corruption probes.
New and existing defense programs may face funding delays or challenges, and companies could see a flurry of Congressional anti-corruption inquiries when the new Democrat-majority Congress takes office next year, experts say. Until then, industry can expect a push for funding by the current majority.
“There'll be a lot of pressure on the Republicans to get something passed during the lame duck [session] because they know how hard it will be after that. And defense hawks will be pushing very hard,” said Mark Cancian, a government budget expert and senior adviser with the Center for Strategic and International Studies.
While Republicans being able to amass enough support to pass $350 billion in reconciliation funding for defense “looks iffy,” he said, passing the base budget of around $1.1 trillion is “quite doable.”
But that reduced funding ceiling—along with the possibility of another continuing resolution—means the Pentagon will need to choose what gets funded.
“At $1.5 trillion, [the Pentagon] could do everything. In other words, they could fund a lot of legacy systems, but also fund a lot of new systems. And a $1.1 trillion dollar budget will require them to make some trade-offs—which [ones] get protected will be an important question,” Cancian said.
Defense spending, overall, typically garners bipartisan support. But this year, the U.S.-Israel war on Iran has been a source of political contention—from the Trump administration starting it without Congressional approval to the downstream economic effects.
Also, the administration has, again, tethered funding for several prominent national security programs to a supplemental funding bill instead of the regular defense budget. Those programs include the White House’s massive missile defense effort dubbed Golden Dome, some shipbuilding, and munitions production.
A failure to secure that extra funding could constrain some of the Pentagon’s modernization programs, said Shaun McDougall, lead defense analyst for Forecast International, a sister brand of Defense One.
If Congress passes a long-term continuing resolution instead of a new budget for 2027, the Army would not be able to start building its MV-75 program, to replace the UH-60 Black Hawk, or its Bradley replacement, XM-30.
“They're wanting to start production on those using FY27 funds,” McDougall said.
Navy shipbuilding programs that would take a hit include “new submarine tenders [and] work on the new frigate,” while the “Air Force has several missile programs, and…the collaborative combat aircraft.”
And, when that potential stopgap funding expires, it may be replaced by another continuing resolution—or result in a government shutdown.
“You have the possibility of a government shutdown if there's disagreements over using the Iran War as a bargaining chip or something like that. So there's a lot of potential for budget disruptions, and that's been one of the big struggles for the Pentagon in general,” McDougall said.
However, Democrats could opt to pass the more-than-trillion-dollar defense budget to cover big expenses like munitions.
And in that case, “the war funding is essentially covered” if the base budget includes “a little flexibility to move money around,” CSIS’s Cancian said. “The biggest piece is munitions,” though it likely would also include other operational costs of the Iran war.
Plus, even as polarizing as the Iran war is, stockpiles of the exquisite munitions that were used must be replenished.
“Democrats obviously aren't happy with the war and how it's going, but replacing all those munitions, it has to be done, whether you support how those munitions were used up in the first place,” McDougall said.
Under the microscope
A Democrat-led Congress will likely focus on anti-corruption, with probes into companies that have close ties to the White House and broader Trump administration, said Kristina Moore, a partner with Womble Bond Dickinson law firm in Washington, D.C.
The “first wave of investigations” would likely explore “where there is evidence that a family member close to the president or the administration had an unfair advantage, or somehow benefited directly financially because of a transaction—an acquisition, a merger, a government loan or a contract,” Moore said. “Was a contribution made, say to the White House ballroom, and—close in time—a policy outcome or a contracting decision, right?”
Then, Congressional oversight and defense committees may examine individual policies for potential wrongdoing.
Venezuela, Iran, drones, AI use: “What is that oversight angle there? Was there a no-bid contract awarded in one of those scenarios? What influenced the administration's policy? Who benefited from a change in the administration policy? And then there's just simply who holds information,” which could be interesting to investigators, said Moore, who was previously a Congressional investigator and has advised clients undergoing such probes.
“You kind of get there either because you were involved in a transaction that looks suspicious, or you were involved in a policy area that is of interest and under scrutiny.”
That means companies must know how to navigate public opinion, and the risks that arise because Congress is investigating.
“They operate in the court of public opinion. Who are those third parties that might be amplifying this? What is that specific risk that exists because Congress cares about us? And what's our fact pattern…our narrative?” she said. “Is there any alignment between what the Congress is looking for in our actions or activities?” and is there “internal awareness of what people were saying to the administration?”

b2c29abf32ef.text: House Republican leaders are bracing for enough GOP defections to impeach Defense Secretary Pete Hegseth when the measure comes to a vote this week. Why it matters : Republicans who were defeated in Tuesday's election-night bloodbath have little left to lose and could be more willing to back impeaching Hegseth, whose overall support has eroded since the start of the Iran war. Hegseth doesn't have "a lot of love" on Capitol Hill, retiring Rep. Don Bacon (R-Neb.) told Fox News. Bacon told Axios he's undecided on this week's vote. Driving the news: Rep. Thomas Massie (R-Ky.) is planning to force a vote on his resolution to impeach Hegseth for allegedly defying Congress and illegally continuing the U.S. war in Iran. Republican leaders avoided the measure before Election Day after Speaker Mike Johnson (R-La.) canceled votes and sent lawmakers home early. Johnson has denied his decision to send members home was related to the impeachment vote, but it would have been a politically difficult vote for Republicans just weeks before the midterms. The political calculus has now shifted dramatically since Tuesday, with the GOP's crushing defeat fueling anger within the conference and increasing the number of Republicans willing to back impeachment. The big picture: The blame game is already in full swing among House Republicans, with the Iran war emerging as a top target of their ire. "Iran, Iran, Iran ... We should have never done the war before the midterms," a GOP lawmaker told Axios. Hegseth is the face of the war for many on Capitol Hill, putting him in the crosshairs of frustrated Republicans. Another GOP lawmaker told Axios that Hegseth's tone and rhetoric have been "very damaging to our ability to get the facts out to the American people on why the strikes targeting Iran's nuclear facilities, and the additional military actions, were necessary." Zoom in: Hegseth is also on "thin ice" with the Trump administration, with some officials pushing for his ouster, Axios' Marc Caputo and Alex Isenstadt reported . Trump defended Hegseth on Wednesday, telling reporters he has every intention to "keep him" in his post. If Hegseth is still around come January, the new Democratic majority will have the power to pursue investigations and impeachment proceedings. The other side: Hegseth is fighting back, calling the impeachment effort a "sham" led by a "disgruntled, defeated congressman" in a video posted on X Thursday. Massie, who lost his primary to a Trump-backed opponent, fired back, urging Trump to replace Hegseth while Republicans still control the Senate. "There is one contingency in which I won't reintroduce the articles of impeachment: Hegseth resigns," Massie wrote . Chief Pentagon spokesman Sean Parnell said in a statement to Axios: "Secretary Hegseth will not back down or be deterred by politicians seeking to score partisan points or launch phony investigations where no wrongdoing exists. The Department of War has followed the law, and our Secretary will continue to stand and fight every single day to support and defend the Constitution, lead our troops, and protect America." "We will continue to drive President Trump's agenda at the Department of War — despite threats of sham witch hunts from Democrats — and Secretary Hegseth is 100% committed to leading the Department until the end of President Trump's term in office." Reality check: Even if the House impeaches Hegseth, removing him from office would require a two-thirds vote in the Senate, a threshold that would be difficult to achieve, even when Democrats take control of the chamber in January.

Habitat work and a monitoring scheme have helped hazel dormice thrive at a National Trust site, despite declines elsewhere, experts have said.
Killerton National Trust has 100 nest boxes across its estate in Devon. Rangers weigh and record details of each mouse between April and October.
The trust said the animals "continue to thrive" in the area - a sign it was "doing something right" by creating a "healthy, diverse and well-connected habitat for wildlife".
The People's Trust for Endangered Species said populations had declined by over two thirds in the UK since 2000. Experts said the decline was largely down to "habitat fragmentation".
The trust hopes the mammals, which typically weigh between 20g and 40g, will have gained enough weight to begin hibernating in the coming weeks and survive the winter ahead.
Fi Hailstone, senior ranger for the National Trust at the Killerton estate, said: "When we have warmer weather, it wakes them up and when we have wet springs, that affects their ability to forage when they do wake up.
"So having a resilient ecosystem with lots of shelter for them, lots of scrub, lots of things for them to eat [is important]."
"They love bramble, and I know that bramble has a bit of a bad reputation with a lot of gardeners," Hailstone said.
"But bramble is the life source, really. It has flowers in the spring, it has berries on it. â©It's also protective in terms of cover from other predators, so it's a really great place for them to nest."
When they are not hibernating, they are shy and nocturnal.
Hailstone said Devon was "a bit of a stronghold for dormice" because "there is such a strong hedge network".
"We've been monitoring our dormouse population at Killerton since 2018, and during that time, we've noticed that they are fairly stable, which does buck national trends."
Hailstone said: "We are finding them in new areas which indicates them spreading across the estate.
"We think this is because we're planting a lot more hedges, a lot more trees."
"We might be planting lots of woodland now, which is great, but we won't see the effects of that for dormice for another 100 or so years," Hailstone added.
"It's really important to manage the woodlands that we already have in a positive way."
Anyone who finds a dormouse in the winter is urged not to pick it up but to alert the RSPCA or local animal shelter.

LAHAINA, Hawaiʻi—As Mikey Burke walked into her acupuncture appointment on a Wednesday morning in May, she felt the energy shift, just as she always does.
Noelani Ahia, 51, an acupuncturist and Hawaiian healer, greeted Burke, 42, with a smile and a hug, and led her away from the sunlit, open-air courtyard of the Lahaina Comprehensive Health Center and into a dark room, walled in with dividers and empty except for a single bed, a chair and a few small tables. As they settled in, they spoke about Lahaina.
Burke, a mother of four, has been going to the local health center since her home burned down three years ago in the deadliest U.S. wildfires in more than a century. Sometimes, it feels like these appointments are the only time she can truly breathe.
“I don’t think people realize how hard a time people are still having,” said Ahia, who directs Maui Medic Healers Hui, a community organization that operates out of the state-run center. “Pretty much no one is fine.”
“And we’re almost worse off now than we were right after the fires,” Burke replied.
“Can you say a little bit more about that,” Ahia asked, softly.
Burke’s appointment was one day before a construction crew would pour the cement foundation of her family’s future home, and the same week that the Maui Wildfire Exposure Study might be shutting down for good.
As she started to speak, Burke fought back tears.
“The fire was a point in time,” she began, her voice breaking as she laid out a chronology that disaster survivors know all too well.
In the immediate aftermath, the first, most acute trauma was that everything was gone, she explained. But now there’s a slower, unrelenting ordeal of all that has fallen apart since.
It’s not just about the destruction of her family’s house, which she’d fought for years to find and secure. It’s her family’s mental health, the loss of friends and neighbors who were priced out and moved away, the fights to address water access, regain local control of land rights, advocate for her children’s Hawaiian immersion school and protect her people’s ability to be Hawaiian in this place that has been taken over by colonizers and corporate interests again and again. She and her neighbors have to be strong for every battle. Everything feels too important; nothing can fall through the cracks.
It was in this building that Burke found out about the Maui Wildfire Exposure Study, a University of Hawai‘i research project both quantifying the health impacts of the wildfires and helping survivors navigate them. Burke participated in MauiWES with her husband and four boys, and it was through the study that she learned that her twins, then just 10, were showing signs of post-traumatic stress disorder. It was also how she’d enrolled them in therapy.
But keeping the study funded had been an ongoing struggle, and a few days before Burke’s acupuncture appointment, organizers held a weekend-long event to collect survivors’ health information for what they feared could be the last time.
It made Burke angry. She’d seen what the study had done for her boys. She felt how deeply her community was still struggling. If no one tracked her community’s health, then how would they know, years from now, how the fires changed them? How would they know how to heal?
“There’s always something that we have to fight,” she continued, her tears now falling fast. “We can’t even just be in our own grief.”
The Maui wildfires on Aug. 8, 2023, destroyed more than 2,200 buildings and killed more than 100 people. The Burkes were among the nearly 13,000 displaced.
For months after the fires, Mikey, her husband, Rob, their four sons and four dogs were shuttled between family and friends’ homes, hotel rooms and finally to the two-bedroom, one-bathroom rental where they’re now living, another waystation in the long wait for a new home.
Three years out, she was still meeting people who hadn’t heard about the Lahaina Comprehensive Health Center or MauiWES, who had been so swept up in surviving, day-to-day, they hadn’t had time to seek support. It was clear to her there was a pressing need for these health resources.
In the dimly lit room at the health center, the magnitude of it all rose and took over. She fell into Ahia’s arms, shaking, and the older woman stroked her back with strong, fluid movements.
“I’ve got you,” Ahia said. “You’re carrying so much.”
Burke took a deep breath through her tears.
“Just for today, just for this little bit of time, we’re gonna set it down,” Ahia continued, her voice low and calm. “We’re going to take the pōhaku out, even though the pōhaku is your kuleana.”
Her worldly responsibilities, her kuleana, are like pōhaku, stones, weighing her down every day, Ahia explained. But for now, she could set them aside.
Burke’s shoulders softened, the tension of the morning dissipating.
This is a central part of Ahia’s work. Her clients come in with a lifetime of wounds, small and large, their nervous systems shot by unending, compounding traumas. She refers to it as colonial inflammation, how years of layered injustices pile on and manifest in a physiological response to stress. A Native Hawaiian diaspora kid who grew up on the continent and returned to Hawai‘i as a young adult, Ahia blends teachings from Hawaiian healing and traditional Chinese medicine into her practice.
She co-founded what grew into Maui Medic Healers Hui in 2019 to care for protesters opposing an observatory on Mauna Kea, a volcano on Hawai‘i island considered sacred by many Native Hawaiians. After the 2023 fires, the organization mobilized to support survivors. Now, many of Ahia’s patients are still feeling the disaster’s aftershocks.

LAHAINA, Hawaiʻi—Early on a Saturday morning in May, Ruben Juarez took the 45-minute flight from Oʻahu to Maui, just like he’d done dozens of times over the past three years.
This one felt different.
Juarez landed in Kahului Airport with his partner, Alika Maunakea, and drove on a long winding highway beside the piercing blue ocean until they reached the Lahaina Comprehensive Health Center.
A cool breeze wafted in from the Pacific less than half a mile below as they set up stations for blood collection, lung function tests and mental health check-ins, directing a team of Ph.D. students and local healthcare providers. Then they waited for the fire survivors to arrive.
On Aug. 8, 2023, Maui was hit with the deadliest wildfires the U.S. has seen in over a century. They killed at least 102 people, displaced nearly 13,000 residents and destroyed more than 2,200 buildings. Three years later, just 15 percent have been rebuilt.
Juarez, an economist, and Maunakea, a biomedical scientist, never expected to focus on disaster recovery. But after the fires, they were thrust into the space by the overwhelming scale of need. The two University of Hawaiʻi professors dreamed up the Maui Wildfire Exposure Study, or MauiWES, as a form of rapid response: an effort to track the impacts of the fires on survivors’ health.
Three years and 2,500 participants later, the study has blossomed into a combination of research and intervention, a web of community organizations working together to give participants not just free testing but also therapy, food assistance, cash support and help connecting with doctors and insurance. Some even say the study saved their lives.
The researchers hope MauiWES could become a national blueprint for public health response after disasters. Experts across the country are paying attention. One longtime disaster researcher, David Eisenman at the University of California, Los Angeles, said the study’s holistic approach is “singular.”
But critical federal support to keep the effort going for at least a decade was running out, and its renewal was uncertain—grant applications had been met with silence for months. And just two weeks before Juarez and Maunakea landed on Maui, state funding they were counting on fell through.
Now, here they were at what might be their last big event to understand how survivors were doing and what help they needed.
Juarez was distraught: It felt like the end. But Maunakea, usually the pessimist of the pair, refused to believe it. He felt the study had to continue. The need was too great. They would find a way.
At the health center that Saturday morning, Maunakea greeted Lisa and Nilsson Panis, a pair of siblings born and raised in Lahaina. As he checked them into the study, he explained what they’d do that day. Urine samples to track environmental exposures. Saliva collection for biomarkers of stress and aging. Blood tests for metabolic function. Two assessments of lung health. Recordings of blood pressure, height and weight. A mental health screener.
At the end of it all, they’d meet with a volunteer physician who would help them understand their test results, and they’d each walk away with $100, compensation for their time.
“We’re trying to do this every year,” Maunakea told the Panises.
He was determined to make that happen.
A Different Kind of Research Study
The lobby of the health center had a dark stain on its ceiling where water had leaked in just a month before.
The building—run by the state’s Department of Health and loaned to MauiWES for the weekend—sits near the base of the sprawling West Maui mountains. That weekend, the foothills above the center were covered in dry, yellowing grass that was nonetheless much greener than usual, courtesy of recent Kona low storms.
The storms swept water damage into construction sites and homes that had just been rebuilt. They busted up highways and caused torrential flooding, triggering millions of dollars in damage across the county. They also kicked off an unusually verdant spring, with flowers blooming on the trees outside the center and along the highway below. Wetness that early can heighten the fire risk later in the year, fueling grass and brush growth that dries out and becomes plentiful tinder, susceptible to heat and strong winds.
Lisa Panis had an appointment with MauiWES that day, but she was hoping they’d have room for her older brother, too. In a fluorescently lit room just beside the center’s main lobby, she introduced Nilsson to Maunakea and explained that he had been a first responder after the wildfires, cleaning up debris in the burn zone. Maunakea immediately instructed the Ph.D. students working the check-in desk to sign him up, along with Nilsson’s girlfriend, another survivor.
MauiWES had limited resources, especially with funding so up in the air. But on an island already suffering from a severe healthcare provider shortage, Maunakea and Juarez didn’t like turning anyone away.
Maunakea listened to Nilsson explain what his life looked like in the months after the fires: 12-hour days, seven days a week, clearing the burn zone for a construction company. He wore full-body gear to keep as much of the dust out as possible, but he still ended each day coated in grime. Though he’d never been tested, Nilsson felt confident the constant inhalation of ash and the debris that covered his body as he worked had impacted his health.

“Are you still doing that, or pau?” Maunakea asked.
“Pau,” Nilsson replied. Finished. Now he was working as a mason, bringing his sister on whenever he could. It wasn’t steady. He hoped jobs would pick up in the summer.

How the deadly shooting in Krakow unfolded
Six people were killed and several others injured when a gunman opened fire in central Krakow, Poland's second largest city, on Saturday.
Footage authenticated by BBC Verify shows about a dozen people running inside two buildings before a black car with its front window open passes, followed by a police car.
Another video shows the moment that gunshots were heard in the city's main market square.
Poland's interior minister described the suspect - a 25-year-old Polish citizen - as being inspired by "far-right ideologies"; police said he used "military weapons" in the attack.
Hours after the attack, Polish PM Donald Tusk said three other bodies were found at the suspect's home, which is still being searched.

Perched on a ridge high up in the spectacular scenery of the German Alps lie the burned-out ruins of a mountain house called The Eagle's Nest, which is now at the heart of an intense debate about Germany's Nazi past.
Known in German as Kehlsteinhaus, the retreat was built by the Nazis in 1938, and frequented by Adolf Hitler and other high-ranking Nazis and their guests. After World War Two it was classified as a historical monument recalling the Nazi era.
Last month it was gutted by fire in a suspected arson attack, and some believe it should be completely destroyed, the site returned to nature and all memory of its Nazi past forgotten.
But others want it either partially or completely rebuilt, wary of the risk of turning it into a site for Neo-Nazi pilgrimage at a time when Germany is witnessing the resurgence of the far-right.
Germany has an "everlasting responsibility to communicate, to deal with our Nazi past", said Isabel Heinemann, professor of contemporary history at Munich's Ludwig-Maximilians-UniversitÃ¤t (LMU).
But rebuilding the site completely, she warned, would mean putting "highly ideologised or highly ideological architecture" back in place.
Before it was burned down during the evening of 23 October, the Eagle's Nest had been a popular tourist attraction, owned by the state of Bavaria and operating for many years as a restaurant.
Visitors would take a bus and then ride the original brass and mirror-panelled lift through the mountain to the Kehlsteinhaus to savour the magnificent views above the town of Berchtesgaden.
Once there, they could eat sausages in the beer garden on the Obersalzberg at 1,834m (6,017ft) above sea level, overlooking the Alps.
Unlike Hitler's nearby summer residence, the Berghof, which was bombed in World War Two and demolished in 1952, the Eagle's Nest survived the war.
Tens of thousands of tourists visited each season, providing an important source of income to the region.
In the 1990s, amid concerns that the site did not do enough to confront the crimes of the Nazi past, a museum, the Obersalzberg Documentation Centre, was opened close by.
Around 15 years ago, a photo exhibit was opened in the Kehlsteinhaus about its history.
Although the Eagle's Nest itself was "largely destroyed" by the fire, according to police, the documentation centre survived unscathed.
The authorities have not commented on a possible motive, but a 33-year-old man with a history of mental illness has been detained in a secure psychiatric hospital on suspicion of arson.
Some feel this is the moment to allow the site to fade into history.
"It's been torched now. It's been destroyed. I think they should just clear away the rubble and leave the mountain as it should be in its natural state," said Prof Sir Richard J. Evans, a specialist in Nazi Germany at the University of Cambridge.
That has happened with "quite a few other Nazi sites", he argued, including the bunker in Berlin where Hitler killed himself: "The bunker was filled in with concrete and a children's playground put on the top of it on the ground."
The Kehlsteinhaus was just "a Nazi vanity project" since romanticised by the name Eagle's Nest, he said.
But Bavaria's authorities take a different view about the site's future.
Both the state's interior minister, Joachim Herrmann, and its minister for the arts, Markus Blume, have spoken out in favour of rebuilding the Kehlsteinhaus.
"We can hardly leave a ruin standing there," Herrmann said.
Sven Keller, head of the Obersalzberg Documentation Centre, believes it is important not to leave the site in ruins, as that could encourage Neo-Nazi pilgrims, who would be able to hike up there completely undisturbed.
"We have quite some experience at Obersalzberg with what happens if we clear those sites. Hitler's Berghof was demolished in the 1950s, and in our experience, this does not remove such sites from the mental maps of people," he told the BBC's Today programme.
Nor does he believe "a one-on-one reconstruction" of the site is possible, and Blume has made clear on Bavarian radio that "it should not and must not cost the taxpayer anything".
Herrmann said they would look for a sensible solution in consultation with historians, given the historically complex circumstances surrounding the building.
Heinemann, who also heads the Leibniz Institute for Contemporary History, believes full-scale reconstruction should be "out of the question".
"I rather think we can document the state left by the fire and also document the historical remains of the Kehlsteinhaus, and then reconstruct parts in a modern design, to make clear the different layers of time that can be seen in this building," she told the BBC.
Germany and Austria have long struggled to deal with the fraught legacy of buildings and sites connected to the Nazi era.
With the recent rise of the far-right AfD and the Austrian Freedom Party, the debate over Erinnerungskultur (Culture of Remembrance) has taken on a new urgency.
A row broke out recently in Germany when AfD and conservative CDU councillors in a town in Saxony decided to ban "stumbling stones" memorials - embedded small brass plaques in the streets - to victims of the Nazis.
In Austria over the summer, a police station was opened in the house where Hitler was born in Braunau am Inn. It followed years of controversy about how the house should be used.
The Austrian government said the police presence would help prevent neo-Nazi pilgrims.
But others had wanted the house to become a centre of responsibility, actively confronting the Nazi past.
As one resident of Braunau am Inn told me, it was a delicate balance between how much to remember and how much to forget.
